# 9. Maroubra Central


# 9.1. Locality statement

The Maroubra Central Local Character Area (LCA) is located at the geographical core of the Randwick LGA and covers the inland part of the Maroubra suburb (west of Malabar Rd and north of Beauchamp Rd) to the LGA boundary at Bunnerong Road. It includes the regional sport and recreational facility of Heffron Park and Maroubra Junction town centre at the intersection of Anzac Parade and Maroubra Road.


# 9.2. Locality map

![page 30 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


*Figure 7: The Maroubra Central Local Character Area*

![page 30 img 2 (593x808)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0030-e89132e7f1b1.png)


<!-- SRC: b1-local-character-areas.pdf | PAGE: 31 -->


# 9.3. Desired future character

Maroubra Central LCA will provide a range of housing styles and densities that responds to its diverse community and demographics.

New development will capitalise on the flat terrain to improve walking and cycling infrastructure for enhanced connectivity between the LCA and Kingsford Light Rail Station.

In other areas to the east where the terrain is more undulating, development will complement the

topography rather than amend existing ground levels through excessive cut and fill. Development in these areas will be carefully articulated in terms of bulk and scale to ensure consistency with adjoining development and streetscape, as well as retention of views from public and private land. View corridors east across to Maroubra Beach and west across the LCA, as well as internal vistas provided by the street pattern is maintained.

Maroubra Junction town centre will be the primary commercial centre and support increased opportunities for housing as part of new mixed-use developments. New development within the centre will support economic vibrancy along with streetscape and public domain improvements. Active street frontages will ensure the centre functions as a key economic hub of the LCA and provide for enhanced safety and experience for visitors both during the day and night.

Smaller commercial centres along Maroubra Road, Anzac Parade and Bunnerong Road will continue to provide retail and hospitality services at a smaller, intimate village scale. Each commercial centre will retain 2 storey street wall heights to provide pedestrian scale and retain existing built form.

The establishment of green grid connections enriches the open space network across the LCA, promoting ecological sustainability and a sense of natural continuity. Rear yards of residential lots, as well as public parks will provide opportunities for planting of canopy trees. Street planting will further provide opportunities for increased canopy trees and green links, noting significant mature planting and ecological communities along Anzac Parade. Improved access to Heffron Park will ensure both residents and visitors can enjoy the recreational amenities it offers.

The LCA will retain its balanced lot size and frontage character. The distinct built form character of The Coral Sea Estate and surrounding social housing area will be preserved in terms of its subdivision layout following a radial pattern around the park, connected by ring roads.

Building heights and forms are carefully considered to complement the surrounding built form integrated by the roof pitch and contextually fitting the predominate architectural style. Construction materials are selected to complement and appreciate the predominant construction style and materials of the street and local area. The use of masonry facades, terracotta tiles and sandstone within fencing and landscaping elements will ensure new development translates with the historic development pattern of the area. Low or permeable front fences provide views of building facades and front gardens.

New developments incorporate consistent front setbacks to reinforce the building edge along the streets ensuring a cohesive streetscape that contributes to the overall aesthetics and walkability of the area. The use of natural building materials, such as sandstone, are incorporated into sites where they interface with the public domain. Basement car parking should be non-discernible from the street and not result in building heights and building façade presentations incongruous to the predominant character of the area. Car parking structures and driveways within the front setback are to be minimised to ensure streetscapes characterised by building facades, front fencing, gardens and street tree planting is reinforced.

The environment will be aesthetically pleasing and welcoming for both visitors and residents, achieved through streetscape enhancements that form an integral part of Council's broader strategy for open space and tree planting. Pedestrian and cycling safety along Anzac Parade and its surroundings are prioritised which is essential to create a liveable and accessible community. Larger lots will provide opportunities for planting of large canopy trees within front and rear setbacks. Smaller lots will provide front gardens that are enhanced by low and permeable fencing to provide connections with the street and adjoining public domain.

![page 31 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 31 img 2 (405x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0031-ba4489de861e.png)


<!-- SRC: b1-local-character-areas.pdf | PAGE: 32 -->


# 9.4. Key characteristics

- Continuous tree canopy along typically generous street verges, with footpaths adjacent to property
- Front gardens in setbacks are visually and spatially connected to each other, and connected to the street, only separated by low brick walls
- Local topographical changes, between properties and streets, is managed with low sandstone retaining walls
- Verandas, balconies and sheltered outdoor spaces address front gardens and streets, at both ground floor and upper levels
- A constantly changing skyline of variegated roofscapes defines the streetscapes, generally at 2-3 storeys
- Car parking entries, driveways and carport structures integrated into built form and landscape spaces.

# 9.5. Development guidelines

Development must comply with Section B1.3 General Development Guidelines. In addition, development must satisfy the following:


## a) Locality

- Establish clear visual and physical connections to formal and informal open spaces, including Snape Park, Nagle Park, Latham Park, Heffron Park, Coral Sea Park and the Anzac Parade corridor, through building siting, orientation, landscaping and pedestrian access. Development must respond to local topography and reinforce the established streetscape pattern and architectural character of the locality
- Preserve and enhance key views from and across the public domain, including district and street view corridors, such as views east to Maroubra Beach and west across the LCA and beyond.

## b) Landscaping

- Retaining walls and landscaping structures visible to the public domain is required to be constructed of sandstone, and a style that is complementary to both the dwelling style and era, as well as the predominant streetscape
- Retain and enhance natural landscape features including sloping topography, sandstone or bedrock walls.

## c) Car parking and movement

- Ensure development facilitates and improves pedestrian and cycle connectivity between key open spaces areas throughout the Local Character Area, including Snape Park, Latham Park, Nagle Park, Heffron Park and Coral Sea Park
- Utilise streets as key movement corridors to support increased pedestrian and cycle permeability, particularly along higher order and commercial streets, including Anzac Parade, Maroubra Road and Fitzgerald Avenue. Development must contribute to safe,
![page 32 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: b1-local-character-areas.pdf | PAGE: 33 -->

legible and continuous pedestrian and cycle connections between centres, open spaces and surrounding neighbourhoods.


## d) Land use and subdivision

- Retain the existing and historical pattern of retail and commercial uses
- Residential and ancillary development must contribute to the enhancement of rear laneways by promoting pedestrian movement, active frontages, and high-quality residential amenity
- Development adjacent laneways must incorporate design measures that support laneway activation, landscaping, passive surveillance, and pedestrian amenity
- Development is to maintain the diversity of demographics in the area
- Maintain and support a diverse mix of land uses. Development must respond to the established land use pattern and reinforce the presence of residential, commercial, community, and recreational uses that reflect the neighbourhood's diverse residential demographics, social, cultural, and economic identity.

## e) Mixed-use and non-residential development

- Retain the existing pattern of retail and small scale commercial uses fronting Maroubra Road, Moverley Road, Avoca Street and Bunnerong Road
- Ground floor retail and small scale commercial uses are to reinforce the established fine grain lot pattern resulting in narrow shop frontages with awnings
- Retail and small scale commercial uses will meet local convenience demands for retail, food and beverage services.

# 10. Bunnerong Creek


# 10.1. Locality statement

Bunnerong Creek Local Character Area (LCA) is located in the south east of the LGA and includes the northern part of Matraville, Chifley and the western part of Little Bay. It is characterised by low density residential housing stock and large areas of open space.


# 10.2. Locality map

Figure 8: Bunnerong Creek Local Character Area

![page 34 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)

![page 34 img 2 (642x878)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0034-1a240e7eb185.png)


<!-- SRC: b1-local-character-areas.pdf | PAGE: 35 -->


# 10.3. Desired future character

The LCA ' s unique landscapes and open space are preserved further. New developments acknowledge and respect the cultural significance of Indigenous landscapes and sites as an integral part of the development, fostering a harmonious coexistence between development and heritage.

Building on the existing green grid and biodiversity connections within the LCA will further reinforce the commitment to environmental sustainability and ecological balance. The Bunnerong Creek Area from Barwon Park in the north to Woomera Reserve in the south, including the La Perouse Pony Club and Chifley Sports Reserve, will be protected to maintain the unique remnant coastal creek character of the area. Opportunities for bushland regeneration and improved biodiversity will include:

- Further extension of native vegetation, replacing weeds throughout Bunnerong Road bushland, Wassell Street, Anzac Parade and Woomera Reserve
- Improvement in the ecological condition of creek and riparian zone on the Crown Land between Franklin Street and Bunnerong Road
- Connecting areas of high biodiversity at Kamay Botany Bay National Park (La Perouse), Malabar Headland National Park and Botany Wetlands through strategic habitat reconstruction along the Bunnerong Road and Franklin Street corridors
- Continued mitigation of threats affecting habitat loss and reduced biodiversity.
The environment will be aesthetically pleasing and welcoming, achieved through streetscape enhancements that form an integral part of Council ' s broader strategy for open space and environmental restoration. Improvements to the active transport network will make movement across and within the LCA by bicycle more appealing to a wider demographic. Improved accessibility around the coastal area with improved signage and wayfinding will benefit tourists and visitors to the area. Improved pedestrian and bicycle paths along Anzac Parade will provide direct north south connectivity along the edge of the LCA. East west paths that connect into the Anzac Parade route will ensure accessibility around the LCA is strengthened, including connections to Matraville Centre and Botany Bay. Improved signage and wayfinding will benefit both residents and tourist visitors in the area.

The maintenance of the predominantly 1-2 storey detached brick bungalow residential character will ensure that new developments seamlessly integrate with the established architectural identity, preserving the community's unique suburban charm reflected in the strong grid subdivision pattern and prevalent lot sizes. Basement car parking should be non-discernible from the street and not result in building heights and building façade presentations incongruous to the predominant character of the area. Car parking and car parking structures are set behind building lines to ensure setback lines of dwellings within the streetscapes are not disrupted and front gardens and landscaping is the predominant feature within the streetscape.

Simultaneously, Matraville town centre as the LCAs main commercial centre will evolve into a vibrant community-focused local village that is compact and pedestrian friendly, with plenty of choice in housing styles and affordability, great speciality shopping, and enjoyable walks to parks, sporting and outdoor play areas. New mixed-use development within the centre will seek to improve the economic vibrancy and enhance the public domain with active ground floor day and night uses sustaining a revitalised centre, supported by high quality architecture and high amenity buildings.

The LCA's unique industrial functionality will be preserved. Designated industrial lands which are crucial for supporting the employment of the local population and the establishment of local industry and business are retained. The precinct will maintain a range of small and medium size lots (including strata buildings) to continue to cater for smaller industrial operations. Managing the residential interface is also important to protect residential amenity.

![page 35 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 35 img 2 (47x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0035-e45dae205f00.png)
![page 35 img 3 (47x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0035-a0461c04d38f.png)
![page 35 img 4 (3830x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0035-89d4ecf8d9b4.png)


<!-- SRC: b1-local-character-areas.pdf | PAGE: 36 -->

Access and connectivity of industrial lands to the wider LCA and Randwick City will be improved with pedestrian and cycle connections.


# 10.4. Key characteristics

- Low walled front gardens visually and spatially connected to each other and the street, with large canopy trees within the gardens
- Generous spacing between adjacent buildings allow spatial and visual connections to densely planted back gardens and local and regional topography and the ocean
- Parking entries, driveways and carports beside buildings, and set either behind buildings or well back from the street
- Building entries are distinct from driveways, identifiable within the front gardens and directly address the street
- The space of the wide streets and generous verges are punctuated by individual high canopy trees, and singular building elements, typically 2 storeys high
- Verandas, balconies and sheltered outdoor spaces address front gardens and streets, at both ground floor and upper levels.

# 10.5. Development guidelines

Development must comply with Section B1.3 General Development Guidelines. In addition, development must satisfy the following:


## a) Locality

- Ensure view corridors within the Local Character Area and to the coast are maintained from public spaces.

## b) Built form elements

- Development must avoid large, continuous building forms and achieve a fine grain built form that reflects the established subdivision pattern of the Local Character Area. This is to be achieved through:
- articulation of façades, including recesses and projections
- modulation of building width and depth
- variation in roof forms and materials
- clear expression of individual building components
- designing development on consolidated lots to read as multiple smaller built forms
- Upper level built form must minimise visual bulk and reinforce the predominant lowscale streetscape character, including through appropriate setbacks from street frontages and site boundaries
- Development must provide a graduated transition in scale, bulk and intensity at interfaces with open space, ecological corridors, low density residential areas and industrial land
- At interfaces with ecological corridors, public reserves and open space:
- buildings must be set back to accommodate deep soil planting and canopy trees that extend the landscape character of adjoining land
- built form must minimise visual and physical impacts on the ecological setting
- At residential - industrial interfaces:
- development must incorporate setbacks, landscape buffers and building orientation to minimise impacts from noise, light spill and activity
- building design must incorporate appropriate acoustic mitigation measures, including orientation of habitable rooms, building materials or use of nonhabitable spaces as buffers.
![page 36 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 36 img 2 (86x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0036-d7aeab707ec4.png)


<!-- SRC: b1-local-character-areas.pdf | PAGE: 37 -->


## c) Landscaping

- Landscaping is to work in conjunction with built form to provide ecological buffers, visual screening and transition between development and sensitive landscapes, including Bunnerong Creek and associated corridors
- Retain and enhance natural landscape features including sloping topography, sandstone or bedrock walls
- Development must strengthen connections to adjoining open space and ecological corridors, including the Bunnerong Creek corridor, through building siting, orientation and landscaping that reinforces the subdivision pattern, landscape character and ecological function of the locality
- Development must retain and strengthen ecological corridors between identified open space areas through the provision of continuous native planting, with particular emphasis on sites adjoining public open space, drainage corridors and road verges forming part of the Bunnerong Creek landscape system
- Sites adjoining identified ecological corridors, including the Bunnerong Creek area, Barwon Park, Woomera Reserve and Wassell Street Reserve, must provide deep soil zones that align with adjoining public land and neighbouring properties to facilitate continuous planting and habitat connectivity across boundaries
- Where fencing is provided within or adjacent to ecological corridors, it must be designed to be permeable to fauna movement, including through open fencing types, gaps at ground level, or similar design measures
- Development adjacent to open space and ecological corridors must minimise hard boundaries and incorporate landscaping that visually and ecologically integrates private land with the adjoining public domain
- Landscaping across Local Character Area must prioritise locally endemic species to support biodiversity, habitat creation and ecological resilience
- Development adjacent to identified ecological corridor streets (Anzac Parade, Bunnerong Road, Wassell Street) must contribute to continuous canopy planting and landscaping that reinforces the ecological and visual connection of the corridor.

## d) Car parking and movement

- Utilise streets as thoroughfares for increased pedestrian and cycle permeability, such as Anzac Parade, Little Bay Road, Franklin Street, Daunt Avenue and Pozieres Avenue.

## e) Land use and subdivision

- Development is to maintain the existing diversity of population demographics in the Local Character Area through retention of existing land uses
- Maintain and support a diverse mix of land uses. Development must respond to the established land use pattern and reinforce the presence of residential, commercial, industrial, community, and recreational uses that reflect the neighbourhood's social, cultural, and economic identity.

## f) Mixed-use and non-residential development

- Retain the existing and historical pattern of retail and commercial uses within the Local Character Area, including those along Anzac Parade and Bunnerong Road
- Development must demonstrate alignment between built form and the public domain, ensuring access, sustainability and residential amenity improvements are achieved.

![page 37 img 2 (2937x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0037-b45369aa8cec.png)

# 11. The Port


# 11.1. Locality statement

The Port Local Character Area (LCA) encompasses the port and industrial land of Randwick City aligning with boundaries established under State Environmental Planning Policy (Transport and Infrastructure) 2021 (Transport and Infrastructure SEPP) for land nominated as Port Botany. The LCA includes the southern section of Brotherson Dock and the Bulk Liquids Berth area and supporting industrial lands. At its southernmost point is Molineux Point which contains a lookout and green space.

This DCP Part does not apply to land within the Port LCA that is governed by the Transport and Infrastructure SEPP.


# 11.2. Locality map

Figure 9: The Port Local Character Area

![page 38 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)

![page 38 img 2 (656x825)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0038-a46e5915afea.png)


<!-- SRC: b1-local-character-areas.pdf | PAGE: 39 -->


# 11.3. Desired future character

The LCA's unique industrial functionality will be preserved. Designated industrial lands which are crucial for supporting the efficient operation of the port will be maintained. The precinct will retain large lots and avoid strata and small lot subdivision to cater for large and port related industries.

New developments will be of a bulk and scale that is compatible with adjoining residential areas and public open space, incorporating generous setbacks and landscaping, including layered planting and canopy trees, to provide a visual buffer between industrial, residential, private and public recreation zones.

Landscaping will play a key role in mitigating the visual scale of large industrial buildings and protecting the amenity of adjoining areas.

Development must have regard to and not compromise the heritage qualities associated with adjacent heritage conservation areas.

New developments preserve the picturesque views extending to Molineaux Point and Botany Bay, protecting the natural beauty of the waterfront. Molineaux Point lookout will be transferred into a significant environmental and scenic site to enhance public spaces while preserving the ecological integrity of the area. Increased tree canopy will promote the greenery and biodiversity of the area.

Environmental qualities and marine ecosystems of adjacent Yarra and Frenchmans Bays will not be compromised by new developments. The remnants of a row of Canary Island Palms along McCauley Street are preserved, as are the group of Norfolk Island Palms on the corner of Beauchamp and Botany Roads and Port Jackson Figs on Botany Road. Similarly, remnant Eastern Suburbs Banksia Scrub (ESBS) found around, and mature landscape elements associated with the former Bunnerong Electricity Substation should be preserved.

The LCA will achieve a greater accessibility through increasing transportation options, incorporating public transport, walking, and cycling routes to seamlessly connect the community to this waterfront locality.

Trucks are the main mode employed to move and deliver products, materials and equipment around the industrial area. The larger sites on Military, Botany and Beauchamp Roads are serviced by large and b-double vehicles, while the smaller operations around Raymond Avenue and Perry Street are serviced by smaller light weight trucks/ vans, and some larger vehicles.


# 11.4. Key characteristics

- Expansive views to landscape and water between large-scale buildings and at ends of streets
- Setbacks from street propagate major landscape offerings, with low-level planting, mature canopy trees and water management within the landscape
- Transparent fences to properties connect internal landscapes to street planting, and mediate scale of development
- Setbacks between sites manage level changes between sites with heavily planted landscapes, retaining walls and water management
- Heroic scale of industrial buildings and infrastructure mediated by large openings between them, and equally generous landscapes, including high-level tree canopies
- Segregated carriageway, cycleway and pedestrian routes, and distinct access points into sites and buildings.
![page 39 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 39 img 2 (3830x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0035-89d4ecf8d9b4.png)

# 11.5. Development guidelines

Development within the LCA will largely be guided by the State Environmental Planning Policy (Transport and Infrastructure) 2021.

Development must comply with Section B1.3 General Development Guidelines. In addition, development must satisfy the following:


## a) Locality

- Preserve and enhance street views corridors from the public domain, particularly views to Botany Bay
- Ensure that new development does not negatively impact the public domain, public amenity and the enjoyment of public spaces through excessive overshadowing, inappropriate driveway location, vehicle and pedestrian conflict, reduced casual surveillance, and reduced impacts on walkability and opportunities for active transport
- Sightlines and connections beyond the site boundaries are important considerations for building placement, orientation, paths of movement and framed views.

## b) Built form elements

- Setbacks shall enable substantial landscaping and planting of canopy trees
- Ensure setbacks are consistent with the predominant setting in the street
- Building massing and scale must be comparable to surrounding development
- Massing of new development is to be setback from boundaries to ensure appropriate and sympathetic alignment with adjoining sensitive land uses
- Taller building elements must be centred within sites away from site boundaries.

## c) Landscaping

- Retain established trees within the public and private realms and include perimeter planting to increase shade and amenity, provide green links and visual buffers to adjacent sensitive land uses
- Retain and extend street tree plantings on all streets to enhance the streetscape character, provide green links and improve pedestrian amenity. Notably along Beauchamp and Botany Roads, and McCauley Street
- Fencing shall be transparent to maintain visual connection between the site and the street
- Landscaping is to be used with fencing to provide obstruction of views where required for security and/or amenity
- Establish a connection to adjoining open space, the waterfront and Botany Bay through landscaping and built form, drawing on the area's topography and coastal setting to reinforce visual relationships and provide a transition between industrial development and surrounding land uses
- At interfaces with residential areas and public open space, development must provide setbacks that accommodate deep soil planting and substantial landscaping, including canopy and layered planting, to form an effective visual and environmental buffer and reduce the visual scale and bulk of large buildings.

## d) Materiality

- Ensure materials, finishes and architectural detailing contribute to a sustainable and contemporary built form that responds to the coastal character of the locality
- Fences must be of a paling or cyclone style and dark in colour.
![page 40 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 40 img 2 (3344x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0040-6faa5abf60d6.png)


<!-- SRC: b1-local-character-areas.pdf | PAGE: 41 -->


## e) Car parking and movement

- Facilitate and improve pedestrian and cycle movement throughout the precinct, particularly along Botany Road, Military Drive and Prince of Wales Drive
- Ensure car parking is provided on-site and vehicular entry/exit locations clearly visible
- Pedestrian movement to and from sites must be clear and legible from the street and separate from vehicular entries.

## f) Land use and subdivision

- Retain the existing and historical pattern of industrial development associated with the functions of Port Botany.

## g) Mixed-use and non-residential development

- Ensure ancillary retail and commercial uses are at ground level, clearly visible and are safely accessible from the street by pedestrians
- Development, including building layout, scale, and setbacks, must demonstrate responsiveness to adjacent development patterns, including building typologies, street layouts, and open space networks
- Designs must support permeability and open spaces
- Development must demonstrate adaptability to evolving land uses and contribute positively to the public realm, ensuring long-term integration with surrounding uses.

# 12. Northern Coast


# 12.1. Locality statement

The Northern Coast Local Character Area (LCA) is situated on the northern coastal side of the Randwick LGA and incorporates the ocean bays of Clovelly, Gordons, Coogee and Lurline. It includes many significant and iconic open spaces and coastal vistas, the vibrant Coogee town centre and the urbanised coastal areas of Clovelly, Coogee, the east side of South Coogee and a northern section of Maroubra situated around Lurline Bay with their mix of heritage and contemporary built forms. It also includes Wedding Cake Island, a focal viewpoint offshore. The area has an extremely high natural value, landscape relevance and significant vistas.


# 12.2. Locality map

![page 42 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


*Figure 10: Northern Coast Local Character Area*

![page 42 img 2 (585x809)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0042-98581248fd92.png)

# 12.3. Desired future character

The Northern Coast LCA comprises buildings that contribute to coastal character and its landscape setting. New buildings or additions offer innovative and contemporary design responses while complementing the existing building form and scale of the area to ensure new development sits comfortably within streetscapes, noting the undulating terrain and prevalence of Federation, Pre-War, Inter-War, Art Deco and mid-century architectural designs. Development will conform to existing landforms rather than amending ground levels through excessive cut and fill. Development will be carefully articulated in terms of bulk and scale to ensure consistency with adjoining development and streetscape, as well as retention of views to the coast and across the LCA from public and private land. Consistent front setbacks reinforce the building edge along the streets. Building heights and forms complement rather than dominate the rhythm of development, including roof pitch and massing at ground and upper levels when viewed from the public realm to contextually fit with the predominate architectural style.

Materials complement and give appreciation to the predominate construction style and material of the area. The use of masonry facades, slate and terracotta tiles, as well as sandstone will ensure new development translates with the historic development pattern of the area.

Buildings must demonstrate high-quality architectural design that is responsive to the coastal setting, incorporating materials, colours, and forms that reflect and complement the natural landforms, vegetation, and visual qualities of the foreshore landscape. Development should minimise visual intrusion, maintain low-scale built form where appropriate, and integrate sensitively with the topography to preserve the scenic and ecological values of the area.

Private gardens will compliment dwellings and respond to lot sizes, with larger lots providing opportunities for substantial planting. Low or permeable front fences provide views of building facades and front gardens. Use of sandstone in landscaping, including fencing and retaining walls, will complement its use amongst dwellings and where visible within the public domain.

Where present, car parking structures are located at the rear of buildings with access from rear lanes to provide continuous, uninterrupted footpaths for pedestrian friendly streets. Basement car parking should be non-discernible from the street and not result in the presentation of a 3storey building where the predominant character of the area is 2-storeys. Where car parking occurs in the front setback, hardstand and ancillary structures are recessive to the dwelling and landscape.

The commercial centre of Coogee will be the primary commercial centre within the Northern Coast Local Character Area, supporting mixed-use development, retail, tourism and improved public domain outcomes, while maintaining a strong sense of place and human scale informed by its coastal setting. New development will contribute to day and night-time economic vibrancy and active street frontages, supported by streetscape and public domain improvements. These active street frontages will reinforce the centre 's role and function as the primary commercial and mixed - use activity centre within the Northern Coast LCA, supporting economic vibrancy, improved safety, and enhanced visitor experiences during both day and night.

Smaller commercial centres, including those on Clovelly Road, will continue to provide retail, business, and hospitality services that support the local community. Development within all commercial centres will retain predominant building street wall heights to provide pedestrian scale and retain existing built form where historical architecture, including building awnings, roof form and façade detailing contribute to the streetscape.

Public open space along the coastline will be prioritised to provide opportunities for planting, recreation and pedestrian movement. Development adjacent areas of public open space will not compromise the enjoyment and amenity received by users, as well as opportunities for the rehabilitation of native fauna and flora.

![page 43 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 43 img 2 (270x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0043-b32a41096984.png)


<!-- SRC: b1-local-character-areas.pdf | PAGE: 44 -->

Improved active transport opportunities, particularly facilitating easy access to the nearby Randwick Health and Education Precinct will improve the connectivity and encourage sustainable and healthy lifestyles.


# 12.4. Key characteristics

- Front gardens in setbacks provide privacy to residences, but are also visually and spatially connected to the street, only separated by low brick walls
- Continuous tree canopy along typically generous street verges, with footpaths adjacent to property
- Built form responds to dramatic changes in site topography, with stepped buildings, multilevel terraces and retaining walls
- Changes in site and precinct topography, between sites, and between properties and streets, are mediated in the landscape with low sandstone walls
- Rear lanes are extensively used, for parking and service access, cycling and informal play
- The interior of aggregated street blocks create a mass shared landscape, providing amenity to all houses in the block, and creating significant habitat pockets
- Building entries are distinct from driveways, identifiable within the front gardens and directly address the street.

# 12.5. Development guidelines

Development must comply with Section B1.3 General Development Guidelines. In addition, development must satisfy the following:


## a) Locality

- Development must respond to adjoining open spaces and the coastline through siting, orientation, landscaping and built form, drawing on the area's distinctive topography to reinforce coastal views and the coastal streetscape character
- Preserve and enhance key views from and across the public domain, including district and street view corridors, such as views towards and along the coast, public open spaces and prominent landmarks, including Coogee Beach, Goldstein Reserve and St Brigid's Parish Church .

## b) Built form elements

- Development must minimise building bulk and visual prominence when viewed from the coastline, public reserves, and key public vantage points, including streets that provide views to the coast
- Development must not obstruct or visually interrupt identified public view corridors to the coastline, beaches and prominent landmarks, and must be designed to maintain and frame views from streets and public open space
- Development must be designed to respond to the natural landform, including stepping built form with the slope of the site, minimising excavation and avoiding large-scale cut and fill that alters the visual expression of the terrain.

## c) Landscaping

- Retaining walls and landscaping structures visible to the public domain is required to be constructed of materials and a style that is complementary to the coastal setting and responsive of natural materials endemic to the area
![page 44 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 44 img 2 (3461x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0044-5353aade3949.png)
![page 44 img 3 (918x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0044-4f6c96f21d78.png)


<!-- SRC: b1-local-character-areas.pdf | PAGE: 45 -->

- Retain and enhance natural landscape features including sloping topography, sandstone or bedrock walls
- Establish a connection through landscaping , drawing on the area's distinctive topography and connection to the coastal landscape
- Maintain and enhance formal planting, including avenue planting along Arden Street and around Coogee Beach
- Retain and enhance areas of open space, their accessibility, amenity and ability to support recreational, habitat and biodiversity outcomes
- Plant species must be capable of withstanding exposed and windy coastal environments. Where possible, compliment coastal heathland character.

## d) Materiality

i. Exterior colour schemes must compliment natural elements in coastal areas.


## e) Car parking and movement

- Utilise streets as thoroughfares for increased pedestrian and cycle permeability, particularly along streets that support commercial and retail premises, provide access to the nearby Education and Health Specialised Centre, as well as coastal open spaces, including Coogee and Clovelly Beaches.

## f) Land use and subdivision

- Where lot subdivision or consolidation occurs, the design of buildings must include modulation to a similar dimension and scale created by the historical subdivision pattern
- Retain the existing and historical patterns of retail and commercial uses within the Local Character Area, particularly those along and around Coogee Bay Road and Clovelly Road
- Secondary dwellings and ancillary development enhance rear laneways and maintain a high standard of residential amenity
- New development must maintain and support a diverse mix of land uses
- New development must respond to the established land use pattern and reinforce the presence of residential, commercial, community, and recreational uses that reflect the neighbourhood's social, cultural, and economic identity.

## g) Mixed-use and non-residential development

- Retain the existing pattern of retail and small scale commercial uses fronting Clovelly Road, Carrington Road, Coogee Bay Road, Dolphin Street, Dudley Street, Havelock Avenue and Malabar Road
- Ground floor retail and small scale commercial uses are to reinforce the established fine grain lot pattern resulting in narrow shopfront articulation
- Awnings must be provided to street frontages of commercial premises along Clovelly Road, Carrington Road, Coogee Bay Road, Dolphin Street, Arden Street, Dudley Street, Havelock Avenue and Malabar Road to support pedestrian amenity and streetscape continuity. Where this is not feasible due to existing built form, heritage constraints or architectural design, alternative design responses must achieve a consistent and coherent street frontage
- Provide active ground floor uses along primary street frontages within local centres, including retail, food and drink premises, and other uses that support the day-to-day needs of residents and visitors.

# 13. Southern Coast


# 13.1. Locality statement

The Southern Coast Local Character Area (LCA) stretches from Mistral Point at Maroubra Bay to Congwong Bay. The area is known for its high natural value, landscape relevance, and significant vistas. Key features include Aboriginal cultural places, archaeological sites, landscape heritage, large open spaces, national parklands, dramatic rocky coastlines, bays and beaches. The Local Character Area includes a number of small commercial centres that serve areas of urban development located along the coast.


# 13.2. Locality map

![page 46 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


*Figure 11: Southern Coast Local Character Area*

![page 46 img 2 (621x818)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0046-33b5025b26a5.png)


<!-- SRC: b1-local-character-areas.pdf | PAGE: 47 -->


# 13.3. Desired future character

Development which occurs in the Southern Coast Local Character Area (LCA) must be consistent with or seek to achieve the desired future character of the area.

The LCA will retain and enhance its large expanses of open space and national parklands, securing these areas as invaluable resources for future. Increased opportunities for bushland and biodiversity are appropriately resources and expanded through:

- restoration efforts at Council managed sites
- mitigating threats to remnant bushland and prioritising restoration and protection work around areas of high biodiversity value
- increase buffer plantings to protect remnant bushland in the Anzac Parade median, Arthur Byrne Reserve, Pioneers Park, Cromwell Park and the Little Bay fauna corridor
- Continue to link patches of remnant bushland through appropriate indigenous plantings and create effective fauna corridors along Anzac Parade road easement.
New developments ensure that public views of the ocean remain unobstructed, preserving the distinctive coastal scenery and environment of the LCA. These developments are designed to blend seamlessly with the coastal landscape, enhancing rather than diminishing its natural beauty.

Buildings must demonstrate high-quality architectural design that is responsive to the coastal setting, incorporating materials, colours, and forms that reflect and complement the natural landforms, vegetation, and visual qualities of the foreshore landscape. Development should minimise visual intrusion, maintain low-scale built form where appropriate, and integrate sensitively with the topography to preserve the scenic and ecological values of the area.

Urban areas are well connected with the coastline through increased green street links focusing on native trees to seamlessly merge coastal and urban environments. Urban areas will maintain a low density, 1 and 2 storey, residential character supported by active transport connections, including cycle paths and links to the coastal walk.

The environment will be aesthetically pleasing and welcoming for both visitors and residents, achieved through streetscape enhancements that form an integral part of Council ' s broader strategy for open space and environmental restoration. Improvements to the active transport network will make moving across and within the LCA by bicycle more appealing to a wider demographic. Improved pedestrian and bicycle paths along Anzac Parade will provide direct north south connectivity along the edge of the LCA. East west paths that connect into the Anzac Parade route will ensure accessibility around the coastal area is strengthened, along with improved signage and wayfinding to benefit tourists and visitors in the area.

New developments respect the cultural sensitivity and significance of Indigenous landscapes and sites, fostering a harmonious coexistence.

Public domain upgrades at commercial centres will be more inviting, contributing to a vibrant community atmosphere, notably at Maroubra Beach.

Large-scale redevelopments are approached with a keen understanding of the coastal character, as well as key infrastructure considerations such as public transport access to and within the LCA.

# 13.4. Key characteristics

- Front gardens are spatial buffers from the wide streets, visually and spatially connected to the street through the use of low masonry walls
- Front garden planting concentrated to street edge and building edge, leaving large areas of usable space
- Generous spacing between adjacent buildings allows expansive views to regional landscapes and the ocean
- Due to the separations noted above, individual buildings act as distinct points in variegated streetscape, differing formally, but all within a consistent height datum
- Building entries are distinct from driveways, identifiable within the front gardens and directly address the street
- Coastal landscapes are predominant, in both private and public domain: rolling, undulating topography, and low, dense endemic plants, sparsely punctuated by low-lying trees
- Verandas, balconies and sheltered outdoor spaces address front gardens and streets, at both ground floor and upper levels.

# 13.5. Development guidelines

Development must comply with Section B1.3 General Development Guidelines. In addition, development must satisfy the following:


## a) Locality

- Establish a connection to formal and informal open spaces and the coastline through landscaping and built form, drawing on the area's distinctive topography to reinforce the open landscape character and visual connection to surrounding coastal environments
- Ensure view corridors within the Local Character Area and to the coast are maintained from public spaces
Preserve and enhance key views from and across the public domain, including district and street view corridors, such as views towards and along the coast, public open spaces and prominent landmarks.


## b) Built form elements

- Development must minimise building bulk and visual intrusion when viewed from the coastline, public open space and surrounding landscapes, ensuring built form remains subservient to the dominant coastal setting
- Development must not obstruct or diminish public views to and along the coastline, including views from open space, coastal pathways and streets, and must maintain the openness of the coastal landscape
- Development must be sited and designed to follow the natural landform, with building elements stepping with the terrain and avoiding extensive cut and fill that would disrupt natural ground levels and coastal landforms.

## c) Landscaping

- Retaining walls and landscaping structures visible to the public domain is required to be constructed of materials and a style that is complementary to the coastal setting and responsive of natural materials endemic to the area
- Retain existing landform, natural ground levels and rock formations
![page 48 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 48 img 2 (3366x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0048-06c910ec9419.png)


<!-- SRC: b1-local-character-areas.pdf | PAGE: 49 -->

- Establish a connection through landscaping to formal and informal open spaces, drawing on the area's distinctive topography, coastal landscape, abundance of open space and the presence of national parklands
- Development must incorporate canopy trees within front and rear setbacks
- Plant species must be capable of withstanding exposed and windy coastal environments. Where possible, compliment coastal heathland character.

## d) Materiality

- Exterior colour schemes must compliment natural elements in coastal areas.

## e) Car parking and movement

- Utilise streets as thoroughfares for increased pedestrian and cycle permeability, particularly along streets that support commercial and retail premises, and access between Maroubra Beach and Coogee Beach to the north
- Maintain and enhance pedestrian movement along the coast ensuring access to Maroubra and Malabar Beaches, and Little Bay, as well as connections to Coogee to the north.

## f) Land use and subdivision

- Where lot consolidation or subdivision occurs, the design of new dwellings must be built to a similar dimension and scale that reflects the predominant detached dwelling character
- Retain the existing and historical pattern of retail and commercial uses within commercial centres
- Maintain and support a diverse mix of land uses
- Development must respond to the established land use pattern and reinforce the presence of residential, community, government and recreational uses that reflect the neighbourhood's social, cultural, historic and environmental identity.

## g) Mixed-use and non-residential development

- Retain the existing pattern of retail and small scale commercial uses fronting Anzac Parade, Prince Edward Street and Bay Parade
- Ground floor retail and small scale commercial uses are to reinforce the established fine grain lot pattern resulting in narrow shopfront articulation
- Awnings must be provided to street frontages of commercial premises along Anzac Parade and Prince Edward Street to support pedestrian amenity and streetscape continuity. Where this is not feasible due to existing built form, heritage constraints or architectural design, alternative design responses must achieve a consistent and coherent street frontage
- Provide active ground floor uses along primary street frontages within local centres, including retail, food and drink premises, and other uses that support the day-to-day needs of residents and visitors.

# 14. The Bays


# 14.1. Locality statement

The Bays Local Character Area (LCA) consists of the coastal zone from Bare Island to Bumborah Point including the coastal environments of Botany Bay, including Yarra Bay, Frenchman's Bay and Bare Island. Its eastern boundary follows Anzac Parade and Bunnerong Road and it is bordered by the industrial area of Port Botany to the north and west. It includes the La Perouse neighbourhood centre, Chinese Market Gardens, Yarra Bay Bicentennial Park, Eastern Suburbs Memorial Park and a pocket of residential zoned land east of Bunnerong Road. Key features of The Bays LCA include the Aboriginal Community's unbroken connection to the land, that can be traced to 7,500 years, the rich variety of marine and estuarine habitats , being First Nation's Gamay Sea Country, and the heritage significance as a first contact area.

# 14.3. Desired future character

The character of The Bays LCA will be established by the protection of its natural landscapes, indigenous storytelling and connection to country, views across the LCA and along the coast, as well as historical built form and landscapes. It will celebrate its relaxed coastal charm and develop an authentic brand which strengthens its coastal and indigenous identity.

Preservation of the area ' s unique biodiversity and continued protection and rehabilitation of its landscapes and ecosystems will ensure the conservation of local flora and fauna, including:

- improvements to the existing green grid and biodiversity corridors
- extension of native vegetation throughout the Yarra Bay Bicentennial Park
- connecting dune vegetation between Bumborah Point and western edge of Yarra Beach
- mitigating threats affecting remnant bushland
The establishment of green grid connections will enrich the open space network across the LCA, promoting ecological sustainability and a sense of natural continuity. Rear yards of residential lots, as well as public parks will provide opportunities for planting of tree species endemic to the area. Street planting will further provide opportunities for increased canopy trees and green links, noting significant mature planting and ecological communities along coastal zones. Improved access to La Perouse Park will ensure both residents and visitors can enjoy the recreational amenities it offers.

Aboriginal heritage and culture and significant sites will be respected in new developments adhering the cultural richness of the area and the local indigenous population ' s connection to country.

The existing character of La Perouse will be enhanced by maintaining the low-density detached dwelling scale at 1 to 2 storey building heights. New dual occupancy and semi-detached infill development will present as a single dwelling to the street to ensure this characteristic is achieved. Built form will seamlessly integrate with the coastal character, ensuring that developments coexist with, and enhance the natural beauty of the surroundings. Development will complement the topography rather than amend existing ground levels through excessive cut and fill. Development in will be carefully articulated in terms of bulk and scale to ensure consistency with adjoining development and streetscape, as well as retention of views from public and private land. View corridors to Botany Bay and across the LCA are maintained. Front fences are discouraged to promote the coastal landscape setting. In the absence of fences, front boundaries will be delineated with landscaping. Where front fences are proposed, they will be low, permeable, and integrated with vegetation endemic to the area to ensure structures at the interface with the street are non-discernible.

La Perouse neighbourhood centre (generally bounded by Anzac parade, Endeavour Avenue and Goorawahl Avenue) is the primary commercial centre and will support increased opportunities for greater economic vibrancy as a result of transport access to the area and tourism opportunities, capitalising on the Kurnell to La Perouse ferry service. The neighbourhood centre will be characterised by its nil street setbacks and 2-3 storey elevation along Anzac Parade and Endeavour Avenue. It will promote pedestrian activity and street activation, with a focus on retail and hospitality services at ground level to connect with the boatshed café, located between Anzac Parade and the waterfront, to create an intimate coastal village scale.

New development will maintain and enhance the landscape quality of streetscapes, particular for streets that provide a visual connection to the coastline and Botany Bay. New developments incorporate consistent front setbacks to reinforce the building edge along streets, ensuring a cohesive streetscape that contributes to the overall aesthetics and walkability of the area. The use of natural building materials, such as sandstone, are incorporated into sites where they interface with the public domain. Basement car parking should be non-discernible from the street and not result in the presentation of a 3-storey building heights. Car parking and car parking structures are set behind building lines to ensure setback lines of dwellings within the streetscapes are not disrupted and front gardens and landscaping is the predominant feature within the streetscape.

![page 51 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 51 img 2 (47x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0035-a0461c04d38f.png)


<!-- SRC: b1-local-character-areas.pdf | PAGE: 52 -->

The environment will be aesthetically pleasing and welcoming for both visitors and residents, achieved through streetscape enhancements that form an integral part of Council's broader strategy for open space and environmental restoration. Improvements to the active transport network will make visiting La Perouse by bicycle more appealing to a wider demographic. Improved accessibility around the coastal area with improved signage and wayfinding will benefit tourists and visitors to the area.


# 14.4. Key characteristics

- The rolling coastal landscape is the main spatial experience, low-lying hills and valleys undulating towards the coastal cliffs, with views of the ocean omnipresent
- Built form is a predominant cottage typology, consisting of single-story, flat roof, built form, set well back from wide streets
- Generous and continuous spatial curtilage around the houses and between houses and the street, typically without walls or fences between properties and between properties and the street
- There are very few hardscape parking areas or parking structures; and fewer in front of the predominant building alignment
- The above open spatiality allows for intermittent street parking, in dedicated, brick-paved parallel parking bays along the street
- The widely separated buildings allow for continuous spatial connection and views across the rolling local landscape, and to the ocean
- Changes in the gentle rolling topography are expressed across the precinct in natural rock outcroppings and shelves, instead of built-up masonry walls.

# 14.5. Development guidelines

Development must comply with Section B1.3 General Development Guidelines. In addition, development must satisfy the following:


## a) Locality

- Protect views to Botany Bay, Heritage Items and HCAs from the public domain, including but not limited to Goorawahl Avenue, Anzac Parade, Adina Avenue, Adina Way, Murrong Place, Goonda Avenue, Elaroo Avenue, Tasman Street, Oorana Avenue and Canara Avenue
- Development in the La Perouse local centre is to support local convenience retail for residents and also attract visitors by providing recreational retail, food and beverage services that respond to the area's coastal location and character.

## b) Built form elements

- Development must minimise building bulk and visual presence within the landscape, ensuring built form does not dominate the open coastal setting when viewed from public spaces along coastal edges and public reserves
- Development must not obstruct or fragment expansive public views across the coastal landscape and towards Botany Bay, and must maintain the visual continuity of the open and connected landscape setting both along the coast and to inland open space areas, including Chinese market gardens, Eastern Suburbs Memorial Park, and beyond

- Development must be designed to respond to the natural topography, stepping with the landform and avoiding built-up platforms, retaining walls or cut and fill that disrupt the natural expression of the rolling coastal terrain
- Maintain nil setbacks and 3 storey scaled shop-top housing for development within La Perouse neighbourhood centre, bounded by Anzac Parade, Endeavour Avenue and Goorawahl Avenue.

## c) Landscaping

- Retaining walls and landscaping structures visible to the public domain is required to be constructed of materials and a style that is complementary to the coastal setting and responsive of natural materials endemic to the area
- Establish a connection through landscaping to formal and informal open spaces, drawing on the area's distinctive topography, connection to Botany Bay and national parklands and the broader coastal cultural landscape
- Development must incorporate canopy trees within rear setbacks
- Front boundary treatments must prioritise landscaping and low planting of locally appropriate species to maintain the open coastal landscape character of the streetscape, respond to natural site topography and support visual and ecological continuity. Solid front fencing is discouraged. Where fencing is provided, it must be visually permeable and designed to allow for fauna movement, including through open fencing types, gaps at ground level or similar measures
- Development must maintain visual openness and continuity of the coastal landscape across sites, streets and adjoining open space areas.
- Landscaping must prioritise locally endemic species and be designed to support ecological connectivity, habitat creation and links between coastal and inland environments
- Development adjacent to open space, coastal edges and ecological corridors must minimise hard boundaries and incorporate landscaping that visually and ecologically integrates private land with the public domain.

## d) Materiality

- Ensure external materials and finishes respond to the natural surrounding environment through the use of lightweight construction, recycled materials, sandstone, timber and natural textures
- Exterior colour schemes must compliment natural elements in coastal areas.

## e) Land use and subdivision

- Maintain and support a diverse mix of land uses
- Development must respond to the established land use pattern and reinforce the presence of residential, community, and recreational uses that reflect the neighbourhood's social, cultural, historic and environmental identity.

## f) Mixed-use and non-residential development

- Ensure ground floor retail and commercial uses reinforce the small-scale village character of La Perouse. Retail and commercial uses will support both residents and those visiting the area and be complimented with awnings to protect and promote outdoor dining and pedestrian movement

## g) Aboriginal cultural landscape

- Site planning and landscaping must respond to and reflect the cultural landscape, including through retention of natural landforms, use of locally appropriate plant species, and integration with the open coastal and ecological setting
- Major development must incorporate meaningful design responses that recognise and communicate the Aboriginal cultural significance of the locality, including through public art, landscape design, materials or built form elements integrated into the development and public domain
- Development must be sited and designed to avoid or minimise impacts on Aboriginal cultural heritage and culturally sensitive areas, and where in proximity, demonstrate a design response that respects and responds to their cultural significance.

# 1. Introduction

Randwick City's heritage is rich and diverse and includes buildings, structures, Aboriginal and archaeological sites, parks and reserves. They are valued because they are associated with significant phases of history, or with important people and events in Randwick's development and cultural heritage. Collectively, this heritage contributes to the community's cultural life, sense of place, and shared identity, fostering pride and continuity across generations.

It is important to recognise that the legal owners of a state or local heritage-listed property are not merely owners, but custodians entrusted with the care of a significant cultural asset. While they have a legal responsibility, they also have a unique opportunity to help preserve and celebrate the significance and character of these places for future generations. By maintaining and respecting heritage features, owners contribute to a shared sense of identity and help keep the stories of our community alive.

Heritage is a living part of our environment, and its preservation is a collaborative effort that benefits everyone.

This section of the DCP applies to heritage listed items and heritage conservation areas (HCAs) identified under Schedule 5 of the Randwick Local Environmental Plan 2012 (RLEP) and should be read in conjunction with other sections of the DCP for specific development types, locations or sites, if relevant to the application.

Where there are inconsistencies between this section and any other DCP sections, this section will prevail.


## General objectives

The general objectives of this section of the DCP are to:

- Retain and conserve Randwick's rich and diverse environmental heritage .
- Provide detailed guidelines to manage change to the environmental heritage of Randwick as defined and identified in RLEP
- Ensure development proposals consider the impacts to the cultural significance of heritage items, HCAs, archaeological sites, and places of Aboriginal cultural significance.

# 1.1. Burra Charter

The Australia ICOMOS Charter for the Conservation of Places of Cultural Significance (the Burra Charter) is widely adopted as the standard guidelines for heritage conservation in Australia and sets out a standard of practice for those who provide advice, make decisions about or undertaking works to places of cultural significance, including owners, managers and custodians.

Development affecting a heritage item or property within an HCA is assessed having regard to the principles and practices contained in the Burra Charter .

F or the purposes of this DCP, 'Cultural Significance' (significance), 'Fabric' , 'maintenance', 'preservation', 'restoration', 'reconstruction', 'adaptation', 'use', 'compatible' and 'setting' definitions are based on the Australia ICOMOS Charter for the Conservation of Places of Cultural Significance 2013 (Burra Charter).

![page 5 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 5 img 2 (3722x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-638502fa4ec5.png)
![page 5 img 3 (3720x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-86fb628b9c1c.png)
![page 5 img 4 (3598x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-e8fdd78ffbd9.png)
![page 5 img 5 (2056x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-df0544f4aaa3.png)
![page 5 img 6 (2051x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-7562ee55a98e.png)
![page 5 img 7 (330x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-bcbad94b06ce.png)
![page 5 img 8 (686x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-5c6cb0c7a1bd.png)
![page 5 img 9 (2287x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-c9b50038aba6.png)
![page 5 img 10 (1292x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-04588a70747b.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 6 -->

Cultural significance means aesthetic, historic, scientific, social or spiritual value for past, present or future generations. Cultural significance is embodied in the place itself, its fabric, setting, use, associations, meanings, records, related places and related objects. Places may have a range of values for different individuals or groups.

Fabric means all the physical material of the place including elements, fixtures, contents and objects. Fabric includes building interiors and sub-surface remains, as well as excavated material. Natural elements i.e. bed rocks of a place may also constitute fabric. Fabric may define spaces and views, and these may be part of the significance of the place.

Maintenance means the continuous protective care of a place, and its setting. Maintenance is to be distinguished from repair which involves restoration or reconstruction.

Preservation means maintaining a place in its existing state and retarding deterioration.

Restoration means returning a place to a known earlier state by removing accretions or by reassembling existing elements without the introduction of new material.

Reconstruction means returning a place to a known earlier state and is distinguished from restoration by the introduction of new material. New material may include recycled material salvaged from other places. This should not be to the detriment of any place of cultural significance.

Adaptation means changing a place to suit the existing use or a proposed use.

Use means the functions of a place, including the activities and traditional and customary practices that may occur at the place or are dependent on the place.

Compatible Use means a use which respects the cultural significance of a place. Such a use involves no, or minimal, impact on cultural significance.

Setting means the immediate and extended environment of a place that is part of or contributes to its cultural significance and distinctive character. Setting may include structures, spaces, land, water, and sky; the visual setting including views to and from the place, and along a cultural route; and other sensory aspects of the setting such as smells and sounds. Setting may also include historical and contemporary relationships, such as use and activities, social and spiritual practices, and relationships with other places, both tangible and intangible.


# 1.2. Heritage places in Randwick City

This DCP section applies to the environmental heritage within Randwick City as identified in the RLEP:

- Heritage items (local, state, and national)

## Heritage conservation areas

- Archaeological sites
- Aboriginal heritage (places and objects)
The requirements, objectives and controls in this section apply in addition to the heritage conservation requirements, principles and practices contained in the Burra Charter, RLEP Clause 5.10 , policy guidelines contained in the Heritage Inventory Assessment Report (State Heritage Inventory Report available online at the Department of Environment's heritage website), development requirements of other relevant parts of this DCP, and relevant conservation management plans.

![page 6 img 2 (3825x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0006-b73e19198d4b.png)
