Heritage items, HCAs some archaeological sites and Aboriginal places and significant landscape elements and geological sites are listed in Schedule 5 of the RLEP.


# 1.3. Heritage advice

Prior to lodging a Development Application (DA) or undertaking maintenance works to a heritage item or a property located within an HCA, or if works are likely to affect an Aboriginal object, Aboriginal place of cultural significance or historical archaeological site, applicants are advised to discuss their proposal with Council's specialist Heritage Officer.

Where major work is proposed, applicants are strongly advised to obtain professional assistance from a recognised expert in heritage conservation.


## 1.4. Consent requirements


## 1.4.1. Development not requiring consent

Heritage Exemption Certificate for maintenance and repair works to Local items listed under the Randwick Local Environmental Plan

Maintenance and repair works are encouraged for heritage items and properties in HCAs and may not require development consent from Council if they are of a minor nature and would not adversely affect the significance of the item or HCA.

Applicants must consult with Council prior to undertaking any maintenance or repair works to confirm whether development consent (i.e. a Development Application) is required. A written advice must be obtained from Council prior to the commencement of any works.

Where it is determined that the proposed works do not require development consent, and relate to a heritage item or property within a Heritage Conservation Area, the applicant must obtain a Heritage Exemption Certificate (HEC) from Council prior to commencing works.

A Heritage Exemption Certificate application form can be found on Council's website or HERITAGE-MINOR-WORKS-WITHOUT-CONSENT.pdf.

Maintenance and repairs can include non-structural external works such as:

- Essential maintenance and reinstatement of original heritage features
- Replacing broken windows frames, panes and fly screens
- Minor repairs to roofing, brickwork, timberwork, metal work, fencing and tessellated tiles
- Repainting surfaces which are already painted, including timberwork and metalwork
- Repointing brickwork and masonry
Maintenance and repairs can also include non-structural internal works such as:

- Patching, painting and decoration to the interior of the building
- Installation of joinery
- Repairing timber floors
- Plumbing and gas fitting work
- Electrical work and communications cabling
- Installation of insulation
Additionally, the installation of solar panels and associated equipment within a HCA may be considered under a HEC, if they provided the works do not involve:

- Solar panels positioned on the primary roofs or verandahs facing/visible from the main street
- Heritage items that form part of a continuous group or row of properties
![page 7 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 7 img 2 (2656x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0007-7edfeefa914d.png)
![page 7 img 3 (733x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0007-b679cae45c3b.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 8 -->

- Slate or timber shingle roofs
- Complex primary street facing roofs
- Very small primary street facing roofs (smaller than 4m)
- Any works that require structural modifications to support the solar panels
- Any works that involving removal of roof elements, such as chimneys, capping, parapet walls.
Further, the installation of surveillance systems and devices on heritage items and within HCAs may be considered where they:

- are not visible from the public domain
- do not involve alteration, damage or the removal of significant fabric.
Any new penetrations must be limited in number and made through non-significant fabric or mortar joints only.


### Exempt development

Under the State Environmental Planning Policy Exempt and Complying Development Codes 2008 (The Codes SEPP) some categories of minor internal works are permitted as Exempt Development for buildings within HCAs, but not for heritage items. The classification of Exempt Development refers to works that have minimal environmental impact and therefore does not require Council's consent. The Codes SEPP does not permit external building alterations to heritage items or properties located within HCAs.


### Standard exemption for State Heritage Register items

Certain activities and work are exempt from approval under the Heritage Act 1977 for items listed on the State Heritage Register or subject to an interim heritage order. Standard exemptions include maintenance works where t hese have little to no impact on the item's heritage significance and support its ongoing management.

These standard exemptions are made under the Heritage Act 1977 and published in the NSW Government Gazette - https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/topics/heritage/apply-for-heritageapprovals-and-permits/state-heritage-register-items/standard-exemptions

Before any activity or work takes place, follow these steps to:

- understand what 'significant fabric' is
- determine if your proposed activity or work can be carried out under a standard exemption and therefore you do not need to lodge an application for approval
- understand how to comply with standard exemption requirements.

### Note

To determine if a property is heritage listed, search the State Heritage Inventory online database using the Heritage NSW website, or check Schedule 5 of RLEP and Heritage Map. You can also search the Australian Heritage Database for National listings and inquire with Council or Heritage NSW for the most accurate information.


## 1.4.2. Development requiring consent

A DA is required for the carrying out of development which relates to a heritage item, development in an HCA, Aboriginal place or archaeological site. RLEP Clause 5.10 (2) identifies those instances where development consent is required.

![page 8 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 8 img 2 (3630x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0008-fbeea19926c9.png)
![page 8 img 3 (1692x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0008-8c666a92425c.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 9 -->

Additionally, it is important to carefully consider the following guidelines for DAs impacting Aboriginal objects and places of cultural significance, historical archaeological sites, and state listed heritage items.


### Aboriginal objects and places of cultural heritage

Aboriginal objects and places provide evidence relating to Aboriginal habitation of an area and are of cultural significance to Aboriginal people because of their spiritual, ceremonial, historic, social or educational values. Aboriginal objects and places are protected under the NSW National Parks and Wildlife Act 1974.

Part 4 of Schedule 5 under the RLEP identifies the former Prince Henry Hospital site as an area containing Aboriginal cultural heritage. Other Aboriginal objects and places in Randwick City are not listed in the RLEP due to the sensitive nature of these sites. This is common practice for protecting Aboriginal cultural heritage in NSW.

Development consent is required to disturb or excavate land containing Aboriginal objects or an Aboriginal place. It is an offence to harm or desecrate an Aboriginal object or place. If Aboriginal objects are present or likely to be present and an activity will harm those objects, an Aboriginal Heritage Impact Permit (AHIP) will be required.

Clause 5.10(8) -Aboriginal Places of Heritage Significance - , Council may require a Statement of Heritage Impact to assist in its consideration of the effect of the proposed development on the cultural significance of the Aboriginal object or place, or to identify the potential for the discovery of Aboriginal cultural heritage on a particular site. As part of the heritage impact assessment, consultation with local Aboriginal groups must be undertaken and the outcomes of such consultation provided to Council with a development application.


### Historical Archaeological sites

Archaeological sites provide physical evidence of the past and can include objects and artefacts from the lives of previous generations, such as tools and household items, as well as remains of early buildings and structures.

A number of archaeological sites are listed in Schedule 5 of the RLEP. Archaeological sites or relics that have local or state significance are protected under the NSW Heritage Act 1977.

Development consent is required for disturbing or excavating an archaeological site while knowing or suspecting that the work may result in a relic being discovered, exposed, moved, damaged or destroyed. Council may request an archaeological assessment to confirm the likelihood and potential significance of relics on the site and recommend appropriate action in the context of the proposed development.

When intending to disturb or excavate land where such archaeological relics have been identified or are considered likely to occur, it is the responsibility of the property owner to seek relevant approvals, including an excavation permit or an exception under Section 139 and Section 140 of the Heritage Act 1977.

RLEP Clause 5.10(7) Archaeological Sites outlines consultation requirements with respect to carrying out development on an archaeological site.


### State Heritage Register items

Heritage items of State significance are listed on the NSW State Heritage Register (SHR) and should be identified under Schedule 5 of the RLEP. The NSW Heritage Council is the consent authority for any development proposal affecting SHR Items under the NSW Heritage Act 1977.

Consent from the NSW Heritage Council requires either the submission of an Integrated DA, or a prior Section 60 application under the NSW Heritage Act 1977. Applicants are advised to consult with either Council or the Heritage NSW, in relation to works affecting SHR Items.

![page 9 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 10 -->


### Note

To view the Codes SEPP, refer to www.legislation.nsw.gov.au Further information on permits relating to Aboriginal objects and places of significance, obtaining approvals relating to archaeological sites, and NSW Heritage Register is available from the NSW Department of Environment and Heritage: www.environment.nsw.gov.au


## 1.4.3. Development in the vicinity of heritage items and heritage conservation areas

All development adjacent to or in the vicinity of a heritage item or HCA must carefully consider its potential impact on cultural significance, fabric, and setting of the item and/or HCA. Applicants should address any potential impacts of the development on a heritage item or HCA and measures to mitigate this impact in their Statement of Environmental Effects and/or Statement of Heritage Impact (SOHI).

The proposal must also consider how development may impact on heritage items and HCAs in neighbouring's LGAs (i.e. Daceyville in Bayside LGA).


## 1.4.4. Infill buildings

A new building within a heritage conservation area, referred to as an infill building, must be designed to respect and be sensitive to its heritage context. It should be sympathetic to neighbouring buildings in terms of established setbacks, scale, form and materials.

New development must reflect the established site coverage pattern and urban grain of the original subdivision and development of the suburb. In accordance with the Burra Charter principles, infill buildings should be clearly identifiable as contemporary additions and must not attempt to replicate historic buildings or mimic traditional detailing.


### Note

For further guidance refer to 'Design in Context: Guidelines for Infill Development in the Historic Environment' jointly produced by the Heritage Council of NSW and the Royal Australian Institute of Architects (NSW Chapter).


## 1.4.5. Adaptive reuse

Council supports the continuation of the original use of a heritage building as it helps retain the original floorplan, decorative features and enhances cultural significance. However, where continuation is not feasible due to changes in technology and market/social trends, adaptive reuse of a heritage item may be considered acceptable on heritage grounds.

Development must comply with the Burra Charter definition and guideline for 'compatible use':

Compatible use respects the cultural significance of the place and involves no or minimal impact on cultural significance.

Where the original use of a place is of cultural significance it should be retained wherever possible (e.g. Post Office, Bank, Religious, Educational, Library, etc.).


### Note

Refer to 'New Uses for Heritage Places: Guidelines for the Adaptation of Historic Buildings and Sites' prepared by the Heritage Branch, Office of Heritage and Environment, for further guidance on the adaptation of heritage buildings.

# 1.5. Heritage management documents


## Heritage conservation management plans

A Conservation Management Plan/Schedule (CMP/S) and/or a Heritage Asset Action Plan (HAAP) may be required where Council considers that the significance of a heritage item or a contributory item and the extent of proposed changes warrant a more detailed and rigorous assessment.

A CMP/S or HAAP identify conservation polices and management mechanisms to ensure the cultural significance of a place is retained. They are particularly useful where building fabric has deteriorated, and to facilitate master planning of larger sites and long-term asset management is needed. A CMP/S or HAAP must be prepared by a specialist heritage consultant. RLEP Clause 5.10(6) of the Randwick LEP outlines HCMP/S or HAAP considerations relevant to the CMP/S and HAAP preparation.


## Statement of Heritage Impact

A Statement of Heritage Impact (SOHI) - also referred to as a heritage impact assessment - evaluates the extent to which a proposal may affect the significance of a heritage item or HCA. A SOHI must establish the cultural significance of a place, assess the impact of the proposed development on that significance, and propose design and planning measures to mitigate adverse impacts.

A SOHI is generally required for development effecting heritage significance of a heritage item or a HCA, archaeological sites, and Aboriginal places and objects. A SOHI may also be required for development adjacent to or in the vicinity of a heritage item or HCA, where there is potential for indirect heritage impact.

For major changes or alterations, the required SOHI must be prepared by a specialist heritage consultant who can advise on alternative design solutions to reduce heritage impacts.


## Note

For more guidance, refer to 'Assessing Heritage Significance' and 'Statements of Heritage Impact' (2023) prepared by the then Department of Planning and Environment (DPE). Council's Heritage Planner can also clarify whether a DA requires the submission of a Heritage Impact Statement, Heritage Conservation Management Plan, and Heritage Asset Action Plan. Additional resources on preparing a Heritage Conservation Management Plan and Heritage Asset Action Plan are available at Heritage NSW

# 2. Development controls


# 2.1. Heritage items and Heritage Conservation Areas


## Explanation

This section contains objectives and controls to protect and enhance Randwick City's heritage items and HCAs. It aims to ensure that development affecting heritage items or properties within HCAs or within the vicinity of an item or a HCA is sympathetic to the heritage values by achieving a balanced approach between contemporary design expectations, environmental sustainability, embodied energy, character, and protecting cultural significance.

Buildings and sites within HCAs are identified on the DCP map as being contributory, neutral, or detracting to the character and significance of the HCA.

Contributory buildings provide good evidence of the main development period(s) and make a positive contribution to the character and/or heritage significance of HCAs. They have a collective significance, and their retention is essential if the character of the area is to be maintained.

Non-contributory (neutral and detracting) buildings may have limited historic values but nonetheless respects the surrounding context or display qualities which do not add to the character of the heritage conservation area. They are not to be considered as a precedent for new work when assessing the merit of an application. Non-contributory buildings may be demolished and replaced by new development sympathetic to the character of the heritage conservation area.


## Objectives

- P rotect and enhance Randwick City's heritage items and HCAs
- Ensure development and alterations and additions to heritage items and/or within an HCA respects and does not distort, obscure or detract from the cultural significance of the place or its interpretation and appreciation
- Ensure the adaptive reuse of heritage items enhances its historic and cultural significance and does not result the unnecessary removal of significant fabric.

## Controls


## All development

- All new development in an HCA or in the vicinity of a HCA or a heritage item must respect the design, scale and character of neighbouring buildings and the key heritage values of the item and the area
- All development proposals within, adjacent to, or in the vicinity of a heritage item or HCA must demonstrate that they have considered the likely impact on cultural significance and fabric of the item and/or HCA
- Proposals to alter or add to a heritage item or a building in an HCA must consider assessment of the significance of individual building elements, the broader area, and the relationship to neighbouring properties and the streetscape
- Alterations and additions to heritage items and contributory buildings must be designed and sited to retain contributory features of the building and maintain the streetscape character of the HCA
![page 12 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 12 img 2 (3845x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0012-5124e8409a02.png)
![page 12 img 3 (2458x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0012-ebb16857ec90.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 13 -->

- A new building, or additions visible from the street or an HCA, must respect and respond to the HCA and streetscape character. A detailed streetscape analysis must be included in the site analysis submitted with any DA
- When proposing adaptive reuse of a heritage item, the proposal must ensure that the significance and original fabric of the heritage item is not adversely affected by the change of use
- Alterations and additions to group items must consider the impacts on the entire group, in particular the existing pattern of rear additions and location of alterations.

## Neutral buildings

- Alterations and additions to a neutral building must:
- remove unsympathetic alterations and additions, including inappropriate building elements
- ii) respect the original building 's bulk, form, scale and height
- iii) minimise removal of heritage fabric and building elements
- iv) use appropriate and sympathetic materials, finishes and colours that complement the HCA and do not diminish its significance.
- Demolition of neutral buildings will only be considered where it can be demonstrated:
- restoration of the building is not reasonable
- ii) the replacement building will enhance and not compromise the significance of the HCA.
- Where demolition of a neutral building is approved, Council may require a photographic archival record of the building to be submitted to Council as a condition of consent.

## Detracting buildings

- Development on sites containing detracting buildings must aim to improve the contribution of the site to the character of the HCA
- Alterations and additions to, or redevelopment of, detracting buildings must:
- remove inappropriate and unsympathetic additions and modifications that are intrusive to the significance of the HCA
- ii) respect the prevailing bulk, form, scale and height of the surrounding streetscape.
- Contemporary design is acceptable where it is sympathetic to the character of the HCA and/or nearby heritage items.

# 2.2. Demolition and excavation

Demolition of a heritage item or contributory building in a heritage conservation area is generally not supported, unless there are overriding reasons such as structural damage. The demolition of a non-contributory building and replacement by an appropriately designed infill building can be supported where carefully demonstrated (refer to section 2.1 above).

In assessing a DA for the demolition of a heritage item or a contributory building, Council will consider:

- The heritage significance of the item or building
- The structural condition
- Comparative analysis of all options; and
- The contribution the item or building makes to the streetscape.
![page 13 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 13 img 2 (102x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0013-2610dfdc49fa.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 14 -->

Council may require the submission of a report by a structural engineer with heritage experience to determine whether the building is, or is not, structurally capable of reasonable and economic use.

Where demolition of a heritage item or a contributory building within a heritage conservation area is approved it will generally be conditional upon the submission of a photographic archival recording using either film or digital capture to provide a stable and long-term record. A photographic plan sheet of the building should be used to show the location and direction of all photographs and the sequence in which they were taken. The Heritage Branch guidelines include requirements for cameras, film and digital image storage. Applications for demolition of a heritage item or buildings in a heritage conservation area are required to provide details on the replacement development.

Excavation beneath, adjacent to, or in front of early buildings has the potential to compromise their structural integrity is generally not supported. To assess the impact of excavation applicants must provide detailed information on:

- The nature and method of construction
- The structural condition of all buildings on the site
- The potential impacts on neighbouring heritage-listed buildings and HCA properties
- The ground conditions of the site and adjoining properties

## General controls

- Demolition of heritage items and contributory buildings is not permitted
- Excavation will not be permitted where:
- o it occurs under a heritage item or common walls and footings, freestanding boundary walls, or under any other part of a heritage item
- o it occurs beneath or forward of the front façade of a heritage item
- Where excavation is proposed beneath and/or within 1.5m of a heritage item, adjacent heritage items or buildings within an HCA, a Geotechnical Report and Structural Report must be prepared by a professional with heritage experience to demonstrate that the works will not have any adverse effect on the structural integrity of those items.

# 2.3. Design and character


## Explanation

The design of new development should achieve a sympathetic blend of old and new, maintaining the heritage character of the area while allowing for contemporary expression. This can be achieved by respecting the established scale, form, siting, setbacks, materials and finishes of the streetscape without being overly imitative. Careful attention must be paid to adjacent development within the vicinity of heritage items and the character of HCA.


## Objectives

- Promote high quality design that complements and enhances the streetscape character and significance of the heritage item or HCA
- Ensure new development does not adversely impact on the setting, streetscape character or views associated with any heritage item or HCA
- Ensure additions or changes to the external appearance of heritage items and contributory buildings within HCAs respect the original, built form, architectural style and character
![page 14 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 15 -->


## Controls


## All development

- Development must demonstrate how it respects or responds to the heritage values of the heritage item or the HCA (including within the statements of significance of the item or the HCA and its key characteristics outlined in Section 4 of this DCP)
- A streetscape analysis must be prepared to demonstrate how the development has identified, incorporated, and enhanced the contributory character elements and features of the streetscape such as view corridors, built form, scale, setbacks, fencing styles, extent of soft landscaping, significant trees/landscape elements and garages and driveway locations. A streetscape analysis must be prepared and submitted to Council for review at DA stage
- New development should be consistent with important horizontal elements of buildings in the streetscape, in particular ground floor levels and eaves lines, where appropriate
- Large blank areas of brick or rendered walls should be avoided. Where this is not possible, contrasting building materials and treatments must be used to break up the visual mass
- Alterations, extensions, or additions to the building, and its grounds, that are considered visually or architecturally incompatible with the original character of the site must be removed. Unsympathetic elements should be replaced with new works that are designed to be in harmony with the original building style, scale, materials, and detailing. Original features should be reinstated using materials, construction techniques, and forms that closely match or replicate the original design, ensuring the heritage significance and visual integrity of the property are preserved or enhanced.

## Heritage items and contributory buildings

- Street-facing elevations and visible side elevations must not be significantly altered. Additions must be located to the rear or side of the building to minimise visual impact on the streetscape
- Additions or alterations must complement the existing building in scale, form and detailing while remaining visibly distinguishable from the original fabric on close inspection. New and old design are not to be confused, or the boundaries/junctions blurred.
- New work must respect and retain the significant heritage fabric, including internal and external features and proportions, chimneys, fireplaces, doors, windows, openings, balconies, and verandas.

# 2.4. Scale and form


## Explanation

Bulk and scale refer to the height and size of a building, while form and massing relate to the arrangement of its component parts. In heritage contexts, these elements must be carefully managed to ensure new development does not dominate or detract from existing heritage significance.


## Objectives

- Ensure that alterations and additions to heritage items and contributory buildings and other development, including buildings, structures, and works within and in the vicinity of HCAs are consistent with the scale and form of these items or contributory buildings, and do not dominate or compete with the heritage significance, including fabric, design, form, scale, character, and setting
![page 15 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 16 -->

- Ensure that scale and form of new development is consistent with the heritage significance and character of the HCA, and adjacent heritage items and/or contributory buildings

## Controls


## All development

- In streetscapes characterised by consistent single storey development, upper-floor additions are only appropriate if not readily visible from the street/public domain. Ground floor rear additions are the preferred form of development
- Attic style additions may be permissible, where they are sympathetic to the original roof form and not visible from the street/public domain especially for previously unaltered buildings or semi-detached pairs
- Front dormer windows are discouraged on heritage and contributory items and on relatively unaltered semi-detached pair or terrace rows as they detract from the integrity of the original roof forms and consistency of the streetscape
- Dormer windows and skylights must not be located on street elevations or where they would be visually prominent from a public domain or detract from the original roof form. Dormer windows must be sympathetic in scale and form, proportion, and detailing to the architectural style of the building.

## Heritage items and contributory buildings

- Additions to existing buildings, and other development on the same site, must be subordinate to the original building, and must not visually dominate, compete with, or obscure its form and massing, including significant roof forms
- Additions to heritage items, and other associated development, must not introduce prominent design elements that compete with or detract from the architectural features, materials, or detailing of the existing building
- Single storey rear additions to dwelling houses must be designed so as not to compromise the form and integrity of the main roof, and must be lower in scale and visually subordinate to it
- Development proposal to the main roof of single storey dwelling houses may be acceptable where they are wholly contained within the existing roof space and do not alter the roof form, pitch, or eaves height
- Additions to single storey dwelling houses, particularly two storey additions, should adopt a pavilion-style form, comprising a secondary addition connected to the original building by a lower-scale link, to maintain the visual primacy of the original building. Additions to any single storey dwelling house should preferably use pavilion-type forms, with a lower scale link between the original building and any new two storey addition
- Where a pavilion-style form is not feasible or appropriate, an upper floor addition may be acceptable if it is:
- located significantly to the rear of the building
- designed to minimise visual impact on the principal roof form
- discreet or not visible when viewed from the public domain
- Unless site-specific controls provide otherwise, within a Heritage Conservation Area, an upper-level addition must not be visible above the ridge line or parapet of the existing building when viewed from the opposite side of the primary street
- Where rear lanes exist, additional floor space should be provided in a rear outbuilding, rather than an upper-level addition to the principal dwelling
- Rear additions to semi-detached dwellings must not compromise the symmetry or integrity of the front elevation, and must not visually dominate the adjoining dwelling in the pair, including but not limited to its form, massing original roof form
![page 16 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 17 -->

- Rear additions to attached dwellings (e.g. terrace houses) must not compromise the integrity of the front elevation or the form of intact rear wings, including but not limited to original roof forms
- Development must not compromise the integrity of an intact or original roof form of heritage or contributory items.

## Non-contributory buildings

- The scale and form of new buildings must be compatible with the streetscape character, typically single storey, or single storey at the front with two storeys to the rear. The roof form and articulation must also be sympathetic and enhance the heritage and streetscape character.

# 2.5. Siting and setbacks


## Explanation

The setting of a place comprises its immediate and wider environment, which contributes to its cultural significance and distinctive character. This includes built structures, open spaces, landforms, waterbodies, the sky, and views to and from the place, including along cultural routes. The setting also encompasses historical and contemporary relationships - both tangible and intangible that shape and inform the identity and meaning of the place.

Front and side boundary setbacks are key elements of the setting and make a significant contribution to the character and significance of heritage items and Heritage Conversation Area. New development should respect and maintain the original setback patterns in order to preserve the established rhythm and spatial relationships between buildings and spaces.


## Objectives

- Conserve and maintain established historic street setback patterns
- Ensure heritage items retain an adequate curtilage and landscape setting that supports their significance
- Retain the integrity and significance of heritage items, contributory buildings and their settings, and heritage conservation areas, by ensuring the careful siting of new development, including alterations or additions to existing buildings.
![page 17 img 6 (353x245)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0017-eadf343bdd46.png)
![page 17 img 7 (76x88)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0017-31b851281387.png)
![page 17 img 8 (76x88)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0017-31b851281387.png)
![page 17 img 9 (88x78)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0017-0e5c546e34df.png)
![page 17 img 10 (68x78)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0017-ffe7747f3e58.png)
![page 17 img 11 (86x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0017-d7aeab707ec4.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 18 -->


## Controls


## All development

- Development must align with the predominant front setbacks of the streetscape
- Side setbacks and rear alignments/setbacks must be consistent with those of adjacent and nearby properties to maintain the established spatial pattern and relationships between buildings and spaces
- Front and rear setbacks must be sufficient to preserve the existing landscape character of the heritage item or conservation area, including significant landscape features
- Significant historic subdivision patterns and lot sizes must be retained. Subdivision or site amalgamation involving heritage items or contributory buildings must not compromise the setting or curtilage of buildings on or adjoining the site.
Heritage items and contributory buildings

No additional requirements.

Non-contributory buildings

No additional requirements.

![page 18 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


*Figure 7: Maintain the established pattern of setback and building siting.*

![page 18 img 2 (925x1490)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0018-d6d0aee16338.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 19 -->


# 2.6. Detailing


## Explanation

The significant features and elements of a heritage item or heritage conservation area are often expressed through fine details such as windows, doors, decorative timberwork, metalwork, brickwork, stonework and cement render. These elements contribute to the cultural significance and distinctive character of the place and are to be carefully conserved.


## Objectives

- Ensure that significant fabric, and both internal and external features and detailing, are retained and maintained in good repair
- Ensure the reinstatement of original architectural elements and detailing where these have been lost
- Ensure alterations, additions and new development incorporate detailing that is appropriate to the architectural character and style of the heritage item or heritage conservation area setting
- Ensure the pattern, proportions, and scale of door and window openings are consistent with original fenestration and detailing of the original heritage fabric
- Ensure that the alteration to, and addition of, window and door grilles, bars and shutters are visually discreet and do not detract from the character of the building.

## Controls


## All development

- Only detailing that is known to have been part of the original building is acceptable. Decorative elements that were never part of the original design are not to be introduced
- Roller shutters will not be permitted to windows or doors
- External security bars/ grilles and shutters on front doors and windows are discouraged. Where there is no alternative, the installation of external security bars is permitted provided they consist of simple unembellished rectangular bars in a vertical pattern or a pattern that reflects the configuration of the glazing bars of the window or door frame. They should be painted a dark recessive colour or preferably the same colour as the door to reduce visibility
- Clear plastic security film may be attached to the internal face of glazing.

## Heritage items and contributory buildings

- Retain and repair significant fabric and internal and external features. This included but is not limited to chimneys, hearth and fireplaces, mantels, ceilings, staircases, balustrade, doors, windows, original sunhoods, awnings, gable detailing, verandahs and balconies, and other decorative elements to principal elevations. Original leadlight and coloured glass panes should also be retained and repaired
- Where original windows, doors and façade detailing have been removed and replaced with modern materials, consideration should be given to reconstructing these original features based on available evidence
- Authentic reconstruction of lost elements is encouraged. Decorative elements must not be introduced unless documentary or physical evidence indicates the decorative elements previously existed. Thorough research should be undertaken before attempting to reconstruct lost detail and elements
- Alterations and additions should incorporate new doors and windows which are compatible with the position, size, and proportions and detailing with original windows and doors
![page 19 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 20 -->

- Alterations and additions should complement the significant fabric and generally be less elaborate than the original, to ensure that the primacy of the original design is maintained.

## Non-Contributory Buildings

- Decorative elements, detailing, or features should be restrained and not replicate or imitate inappropriate or inauthentic heritage architectural/design style. Any new detailing must be clearly distinguishable from that of heritage items and contributory buildings.

# 2.7. Materials, finishes and colour schemes


## Explanation

In some cases, the replication of original materials may not be feasible due to limited or no availability. In such instances, replacement materials and colour schemes should be selected to visually relate to or approximate the original building elements in terms of scale, size, style, form and finish. Thoughtful use of colour, particularly in the painting of heritage items and contributory buildings, can enhance their visibility and reinforce their historic character.

Original face brickwork is a significant heritage feature and must not be rendered, bagged or painted, as such treatments will detract from and diminish the heritage significance of the building.


## Objectives

- Ensure the selection of materials and colours is informed by the significant fabric and original finishes, and is consistent with those of the heritage item or Heritage Conservation Area
- Enhance and maintain the visual quality of heritage items and Heritage Conservation Areas by encouraging the use of colour schemes that are appropriate to their character in all development on or within the vicinity of heritage items and Heritage Conservation Areas.

## Controls


## All development

- Materials and finishes for external surfaces and for pathways and driveways must be consistent with the character and setting of heritage items or HCAs.

## Heritage items and contributory buildings

- Changes to materials (including roofs and walls) on elevations visible from a public place are discouraged. Original face brickwork or sandstone must not be rendered, bagged or painted. The removal of external brickwork skin is not supported
- Repairs to external surfaces must use matching materials. For new face brickwork, materials must match the existing colour and texture of the brick, the type of jointing, and mortar colour
- New or replacement roof materials must match existing materials. Alternative materials may be considered where they are appropriate and sympathetic to the architectural style of the building and the streetscape character
- Alterations and additions must use materials and colours that are consistent with, or complementary to the original material or colours of the building.

## Non-Contributory Buildings

- New development should consider the original colour schemes of the heritage conservation area to ensure visual cohesion.
![page 20 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 21 -->


## Note

Researching the original colour scheme may involve stripping existing layers of paint as well as documentary research. Guidelines on materials and colour schemes typical of different periods of development are available on Council's website

www.randwick.nsw.gov.au

Where possible, second-hand materials or bricks may be sourced to match the original, or new materials that closely replicate the original may be used.


# 2.8. Roofs and chimneys


## Explanation

Roof forms and detailing of heritage items and buildings within a Heritage Conservation Area vary according to building type and architectural style. This diversity contributes significantly to the aesthetic value and visual richness and complexity of heritage items and Heritage Conservation Areas. Fireplaces and chimneys are prominent architectural elements particularly in buildings constructed up to the mid-20th century, and contribute to structural expression and integrity, local character, and rhythm of the roofscape/skyline.


## Objectives

- Retain the characteristic roof forms of heritage items and buildings within Heritage Conservation Areas.

## Controls


## All development

- Attic rooms must be contained within the existing roof form and must not dominate the street elevation or visible side elevation.

## Heritage items and contributory buildings

- Roofs must not be re-pitched or have their eave lines raised to accommodate attic rooms
- Chimneys and associated elements, including but not limited to fireplaces, must be retained.

## Non-contributory buildings

- Roofs of new development must reflect the predominant roof type (i.e. gabled, hipped), pitch, eaves, and ridge height of the Heritage Conservation Area.

## Note

Where roofing materials such as tiles or slate, are difficult to source, consider relocating intact materials from less visible areas. For example, good quality tiles or slates from the rear or sides of the building can replace missing or damaged ones in the front. New materials used at the rear should match the original appearance as close as possible.

![page 21 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 21 img 2 (2690x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0021-357a9f17a965.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 22 -->


# 2.9. Verandahs and balconies


## Explanation

Verandahs and balconies on street frontages are characteristic features of Australian architecture that provide a transitional space between the building and the street or public domain. They contribute to shading, visual interest and the depth and articulation of the front façade, and are important to the heritage character of the streetscape.


## Objectives

- Ensure original verandah and balcony forms are retained, and encourage their reinstatement where removed
- Ensure alterations and additions do not result in the demolition, removal, obscuring or diminution of the significance of original verandahs and balconies.

## Controls


## All development

- Where verandahs and balconies are characteristic of the Heritage Conservation Area, new development must incorporate these elements in a manner that is compatible in scale and form with the established streetscape character.

## Heritage items and contributory buildings

- Original front verandahs and balconies must be retained and conserved. This includes elements such as verandah posts and bases, joinery and bargeboards, tiling, cast iron lace, brackets, decorative features and glass panes
- Verandahs must not be demolished or altered to facilitate, or allow for, car parking
- Enclosure or infill of front verandahs and balconies is not supported. Original enclosed verandahs and balconies must be reinstated. The enclosure or infill of front verandahs and balconies is not supported. Where original verandahs and balconies have been enclosed, their reinstatement is required
- New verandahs and balconies must not be sympathetic to original design of the building, and must not compete with its architectural form. Their design should be informed by existing detailing or an understanding of appropriate styles for the building's period.

## Non-Contributory Buildings

No additional controls apply beyond those set above.


# 2.10. Garages, carports, carspaces and driveways


## Explanation

Early residential buildings in the Randwick Local Government Area were typically designed without garages or carports forward of the building line. The architectural character of this period prioritised a cohesive streetscape with front gardens and building facades forming the primary visual elements when viewed from the public domain. In later periods, driveways and garages were introduced as ancillary structures, often discreetly located to the side and rear of properties to minimise their visual impact in the streetscape.

The introduction of hardstand car parking spaces, driveway crossings, and garages, within the front setback is visually intrusive and incompatible with the established heritage character of the Local Government Area. These elements disrupt the rhythm and continuity of landscaped/garden settings, obscure significant architectural and heritage features, and erode the traditional relationship between buildings and the street. Physical constraints such as narrow lot widths and shallow front setbacks further limit the feasibility of off-street carparking without compromising heritage significance.

![page 22 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 22 img 2 (1263x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0022-cbcf55fda58a.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 23 -->

Accordingly, the provision of off-street carparking must be carefully managed to avoid detracting from the heritage significance of the building, the integrity of the Heritage Conservation Area, and character of the streetscape. Alternative solutions, such as locating carparking to the side or rear of dwellings are strongly encouraged to preserve the visual prominence of the dwelling and its landscaped/garden setting.

While some heritage streetscapes within Randwick Local Government Area have been compromised by the introduction of visually intrusive garages and hardstand carparking areas, intact front gardens and yards remain as important evidence of the original character and subdivision pattern and planning of these areas. These surviving elements must be actively protected and retained, as they provide tangible evidence of the historic development and streetscape patterns and contribute to the cultural significance of the locality.


## Objectives

- Minimise the visual impact of car parking on heritage items, Heritage Conservation Areas and the streetscape
- Ensure carparking structures and paved areas are visually discreet, subordinate, and do not dominate or compete with heritage items or buildings within the Heritage Conservation Areas.

## Controls


## All development

- Driveways, garages, carports, and car spaces must not be located forward of the front building line or within the front setback
- Where available, rear lane access or side street access must be used to accommodate carparking structures
- Existing building fabric, including verandahs and balconies, must not be altered or removed to accommodate carparking structures or open hardstand car parking spaces
- Open hardstand carspaces must not visually dominate the setting of the building and must not result in the loss of deep soil planting, opportunities for landscaping, or significant features such as fencing or retaining walls
- Carparking structures must be located behind the main building line and remain visually subordinate to the principal building
- Where an existing vehicular crossover is present and a minimum side setback of 3m is provided carparking structures may be located to the side of the principal building
- The form and materials of carparking structures must complement those of the principal building. Contemporary design is supported where it is of a high quality and must not imitate historic style and design. Bulky pitched roofs and other design elements that increase the visual prominence of these structures are not supported
- Existing driveways comprising two separate wheel strips must be retained as they contribute to the character of the streetscape
- Extensive areas of concrete must be avoided. Alternative materials such as dry laid brick pavers, gravel, two separate wheel strips, or permeable paving must be used to maintain and enhance the landscape and streetscape character
- Structures originally constructed as stables, coach houses or interwar motor garages should be retained and conserved wherever feasible as they contribute to the historical narrative, historic character and built form of the area
- Where carparking proposals involve works to public assets and traffic and pedestrian management, the development must respect the established streetscape character and landscape character elements. Any proposed work must not result in the loss of such
![page 23 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 24 -->

character elements. In particular, this applies to elements such as split footpaths, road cuttings and embankments, steps and stairways, retaining walls (including sandstone and/or brick), established fencing and railing arrangements, stone trim/base elements, stone or brick kerbing and guttering, and natural stone and rock outcrops

- Vehicle entries and exits must not adversely impact pedestrian safety and movement, traffic flow, Council infrastructure, utility services infrastructure, or result in the loss of existing or potential urban tree canopy
- Sandstone street kerbing and gutters must be retained in situ. Where removal is unavoidable or there is risk of damage or demolition, they must be carefully dismantled and salvaged for reuse
- Carparking structures on rear lanes must be sympathetic to the historic scale, form, streetscape character and architectural style and materials of the principal building on the site.
Heritage items and contributory buildings

No additional controls apply beyond those set above.

Non-contributory buildings

No additional controls apply beyond those set above.


# 2.11. Fences


## Explanation

Front fences are a highly significant element of the streetscape in Heritage Conservation Areas with each architectural style typically associated with a distinctive fence type. These fences contribute to the visual rhythm, character, and historical integrity of the streetscape and form an important element of its heritage significance.


## Objectives

- Ensure the retention, repair and reconstruction of original fencing
- Promote fencing that is consistent with and complements the character of original buildings
- Support and maintain consistent fencing where these are a defining characteristic/feature of the Heritage Conservation Area
- Encourage side and rear boundary fencing that reflects the scale, height and materials of original fencing.

## Controls


## All development

- New and replacement front fences must not obscure building facades. High solid front fences are not permitted
- The height and form of new fencing must be appropriate to the character of the heritage item, or the Heritage Conservation Area
- Lych gates must not be introduced unless there is evidence that they originally and/or historically existed on the site
- Side fencing forward of the building line must be simple in design, and its level of detailing, materials, and height must be compatible with the heritage item, contributory building or Heritage Conservation Area
- Side and rear boundary fences should be of traditional timber construction, or where appropriate, masonry. Colorbond or similar metal sheet fencing is not appropriate.
![page 24 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 25 -->


## Heritage items and contributory buildings

- Original fences and retaining walls should be retained, repaired or reconstructed where possible
- Where an original fencing has been lost, new fencing should be designed to reflect or replicate the original style based on available evidence.

## Non-contributory buildings

No additional controls apply beyond those set above.


## Note

Researching the original fence style may involve reviewing old photographs, architectural drawings, or examining fencing on houses of similar age and style.


# 2.12. Gardens, garden elements and swimming pools


## Explanation

Period gardens and landscaped front setbacks enhance the relationship between a dwelling house and its setting, contributing to the streetscape character of Heritage Conservation Areas. These landscaped areas soften views of buildings, highlight architectural features and help screen unsympathetic buildings, including alterations and additions.


## Objectives

- Retain or reinstate landscaped settings and elements, including pathway location and materials, for heritage items and buildings within Heritage Conservation Areas
- Encourage front garden areas that are attractive and reflect the character of original houses
- Enhance the streetscape character setting of all buildings in the Heritage Conservation Areas and development within the vicinity of heritage items or Heritage Conservation Areas.

## Controls


## All development

- Significant trees and landscape elements such as pathways, garden beds and structures must be retained
- Large areas/expanses of hard paving are not permitted. Hard paved areas must be minimised to preserve soft landscaping
- Garden and ancillary structures must be appropriate in scale, form, style, materials and design to the principal building
- Swimming pools must be located at the rear of the property and designed to retain significant trees and areas of soft landscaping. Swimming pools must not result in substantial changes to ground levels or loss of tree canopy or urban greenery on the site.

## Heritage items and contributory buildings

No additional controls apply beyond those set above.


## Non-contributory buildings

No additional controls apply beyond those set above.

![page 25 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 26 -->


## Note

Guidelines on garden styles and elements typical of different architectural periods are available on Council's website


# 2.13. Access and mobility


## Explanation

Heritage places should be accessible to all members of the community including people with disabilities, older persons, and families with young children. Developments should support inclusive access while respecting the heritage significance of the place. Access solutions should be tailored to the specific characteristics of each heritage building to minimise impact on significant fabric.


## Objectives

- Ensure that development facilitating access, adaptable dwellings or universal housing does not adversely affect the heritage fabric or significance of heritage items or Heritage Conservation Areas.

## Controls


## All development

- Modifications and alterations to improve access and mobility must be sympathetic to the heritage significance and heritage fabric
- Alterations and additions to facilitate access and mobility must be reversible, so that future restoration of heritage elements is possible
- Where compromises are necessary, priority must be given to preserving heritage items and elements of heritage significance.
Heritage items and contributory buildings

No additional controls apply beyond those set above.


## Non-contributory buildings

No additional controls apply beyond those set above.


# 2.14. Commercial properties


## Explanation

Randwick City contains a number of heritage-listed commercial buildings, as well as Heritage Conservation Areas that include traditional commercial buildings, such as corner stores. These building types reflect historic land use patterns and contribute to diversity and character of the built environment.


## Objectives

- Ensure that original form, detailing, and character of traditional/historic neighbourhood and retail/commercial buildings are retained and enhanced.

## Controls


## All development

No additional controls apply beyond those set out in this section.

![page 26 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 26 img 2 (1221x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0026-6d48da606add.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 27 -->


## Heritage items and contributory buildings

- Original forms, architectural detailing, materials, and finishes must be retained or reinstated where feasible. This includes original shopfronts, original suspended awnings and open first floor balconies
- Where the property forms part of a single larger building or unified composition, changes to ground level shopfronts and upper-level facades must not compromise the integrity and collective value of the group.

## Non-contributory buildings

No additional apply beyond those set out in this section.


# 2.15. Services, security, and new technologies


## Explanation

Council supports the installation of technologies that improve water conservation and energy efficiency. For heritage items and buildings in Heritage Conservation Areas such technologies (including solar energy systems and telecommunications infrastructure) must be discreetly located and designed to avoid visual intrusion when viewed from the public domain or neighbouring properties. Their siting and appearance must respect the heritage significance of the building and its setting.


## Objectives

- Minimise the visual impact of new building services and technical equipment on heritage items and Heritage Conservation Areas.

## Controls


## All development

- Air exhausts, ventilation systems, skylights, air conditioning systems, solar energy panels, TV antennae, surveillance systems, and satellite dishes must not be located on principal elevations or be visible from the public domain. They must not attached be to chimneys. These elements are to be located to the rear, within the roof spaces, or integrated/flush with the roof cladding, and must match the pitch of the roof. All equipment must be modest in scale/size and not visually prominent from the public domain/street
- Skylights, solar panels, and other roof mounted structures must be located away from visually prominent roof planes and front elevations
- Where solar energy panels are proposed on the rear principal roof plane of a heritage item or contributory building in a HCA, they must be reversible/removable, aligned parallel to the pitch of roof, and preferably integrated with the roof. The panels must make minimal intrusive change to significant roof fabric
- Alterations to accommodate electrical, telecommunications, plumbing, or other services must be limited to what is essential for the proposed use and must minimise impacts on heritage fabric
- Rainwater tanks must be located at the rear or side of the dwelling and suitably screened so as not to be visible from the public domain/street.

## Heritage items and contributory buildings

No additional apply beyond those set out in this section.


## Non-contributory buildings

No additional apply beyond those set out in this section.

![page 27 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 28 -->


# 2.16. Signage


## Explanation

This section provides guidelines for signs and advertisements (signage) that contribute positively to the public domain through high quality design. Signage must be appropriately located and designed to protect the architectural character of buildings, the streetscape, and the city skyline. Within Heritage Conservation Areas and on heritage items, signage must enhance, rather than detract from, the visual and cultural significance of the place.


## Objectives

- Ensure signage is compatible with the architecture, materials, finishes, and colours of heritage items and Heritage Conservation Areas
- Ensure signage does not detract from the amenity or visual quality of heritage items and Heritage Conservation Areas
- Prevent visual clutter having regard to existing signage, neighbouring buildings, streetscape character, and the cumulative impact of signage.

## Controls


## All development

- A detailed signage plan or strategy must be submitted with all new signage applications within a Heritage Conservation Area
- Existing signage that has heritage significance must be retained and conserved in its original location
- Signage must not obscure architectural features, including fenestration, or detract from the architectural quality of heritage items or buildings within Heritage Conservation Areas
- Shopfront windows must remain unobstructed to allow clear views into the premises from the public domain
- A maximum of two signs is permitted per elevation visible from the public domain.
- Signage located above the awning line, or the first-floor level and parapet for any building is not permitted
- Where appropriate to the heritage style and period, traditional style hand painted signage on window glazing at ground floor level may be permitted subject to consent where the area of lettering/text does not exceed 0.1 sqm, to maintain a high level of visual transparency into the premises
- Signage must be designed and located, to ensure the character of the building and streetscape or HCA remain the dominant visual element
- The design, style, materials, colours, images, finishes and lettering of signage must be of high quality and consistent with the relevant heritage style and period. Preferred materials include bronze, brass, and stainless steel. Plastic material, including coloured or clear acrylic, are not supported except as ancillary components/materials
- Corporate branding and colour schemes are not encouraged and must be adapted to suit and respond to the character and significance of the heritage item and/or Heritage Conservation Area
- New internally illuminated signage is only permitted where:
- it reconstructs an original significant sign
- it can be demonstrated that internally illuminated signage is integral to the significance of the Heritage Conservation Area or heritage item; or
- the illumination is low voltage and visible through cut out lettering in high quality metal consistent with the heritage character.
- Externally illuminated signage is only permitted where:
- the design of the signage achieves a high degree of compatibility with the significance of the HCA or heritage item
- lighting is provided from concealed or energy efficient source; and
![page 28 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 29 -->

- all cabling and conduits are fully concealed.

## Heritage items and contributory buildings

- A signage plan must accompany any development application for signage on a heritage item or in an HCA prior to the granting of development consent
- Council may require a SOHI to accompany a development application for signage on a heritage item or in an HCA
- New signage must have minimal impact on the character of the heritage item or HCA
- Original and early signs must be conserved and not be covered or painted over by a new signage
- Building name signs on the pediments and parapets of the facades are encouraged where historically accurate and appropriate
- Signage design must incorporate traditional materials, colours, fonts and size, that are appropriate to the building's architectural style and period, and be of a high standard of materials, design, construction and graphic quality
- Signage must be installed in a reversible manner that does not damage significant fabric of heritage items and must be designed to be of high quality. Where signage is attached to stone or brick walls, it is to be attached with non-corrosive fixings to mortar joints rather than to the stone or brickwork. Projecting and cantilevered signage must use a bracketed system that avoids bulky structural components attached to heritage fabric.

## Non-contributory buildings

No additional controls apply beyond those set out in this section.


# 2.17. Aboriginal cultural heritage


## Explanation

This section provides guidance for development of land that may contain an Aboriginal objects, relics or places of cultural significance. The level of assessment required will depend on the nature of the proposal and the findings of a 'Due Diligence Assessment Report ' and an 'Aboriginal Cultural Heritage Assessment Report' (ACHAR) as outlined below.

Due Diligence Assessment Report is required for -

- subdivision of land where work is required
- developments involving excavation or ground disturbance
- development on land identified by Council as containing, or being in proximity to, land which has been identified as Aboriginal Cultural Heritage place or contains Aboriginal Cultural Heritage objects.
Aboriginal Cultural Heritage Assessment Report (ACHAR) is required for the following types of development:

- subdivision of undeveloped or undisturbed land where the scale of the development is likely to result in significant ground disturbance
- sites containing rock outcrops, caves, platforms or cliffs
- Development where otherwise required by Council or relevant authorities.
Applicant must undertake assessments and prepare documentation in accordance with the Due Diligence Code of Practice for the Protection of Aboriginal Objects in New South Wales (Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW)) or its most current amendment/version. This should include documented research of the Aboriginal Heritage Information Management System (AHIMS) for known/registered Aboriginal objects and places within or in the immediate vicinity of the development application site.

On certain sites, an assessment under the Due Diligence Code of Practice for the Protection of Aboriginal Objects in NSW is not considered to be a substitute for an ACHAR. The Due Diligence process does not include Aboriginal community consultation or detailed archaeological assessment and may not adequately assess impacts on Aboriginal cultural heritage. In such circumstances, an ACHAR will be required.

![page 29 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 29 img 2 (2793x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0029-d2cc1135ddc3.png)
![page 29 img 3 (1399x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0029-4ed8b919b94d.png)
![page 29 img 4 (235x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0029-c7c1fcf49730.png)
![page 29 img 5 (454x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0029-fb1ac0b2b86a.png)
![page 29 img 6 (1537x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0029-ceb51e1bdbfb.png)
![page 29 img 7 (86x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0029-ab42c046b1ad.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 30 -->


## Objectives

- Ensure compliance with the requirements of the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1974 and associated regulations and guidelines relating to Aboriginal objects and Aboriginal places of cultural significance
- Conserve and manage Aboriginal cultural heritage in consultation with the Aboriginal community
- Ensure Aboriginal objects and places are identified and appropriately managed through the development application process, with impacts avoided or, where avoidance is not possible, appropriately minimised and mitigated
- Ensure that new development respects and responds appropriately to the cultural significance of Aboriginal cultural heritage.

## Controls


## All development

- An assessment of Aboriginal Cultural Heritage must accompany any development application on lands that contain, or is likely to contain, Aboriginal objects or place of cultural significance. The assessment report must be prepared by a suitably qualified archaeologist or heritage consultant
- A Due Diligence Assessment Report and/or an assessment of Aboriginal Cultural Heritage must accompany any development application involving undisturbed land where:
- the proposal involves excavation or ground disturbance
- ii) the site is within 200 metres of a known or recorded Aboriginal object or Aboriginal place of cultural significance or
- iii) the site is within 200 metres of a previously recorded or known Aboriginal object or Aboriginal place including but not limited to cultural landscapes, existing or former ceremonial grounds, burial sites or cemetery, story places or mythological sites, former Aboriginal reserves or historic encampments, or archaeological sites of significance.
- Developments, including landscaping and associated works, should be designed and located away to avoid impacts on known or potential Aboriginal cultural heritage values.

## Non-contributory buildings

No additional controls apply beyond those set out in this section.


## Note

In preparing reports, consultation will be required with the Aboriginal community, as advised by Council and/or Heritage NSW.

For further information on Due Diligence Code of Practice refer to Heritage NSW website - https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/publications/due-diligence-code-practice-protectionaboriginal-objects-new-south-wales

For further information on disturbed land refer to Due Diligence Cod of Practice.

It is recommended that a 200-metre buffer be applied to AHIMS searches to account for potential location inaccuracies and to provide a broader understanding of Aboriginal heritage in the area, the nature and distribution of Aboriginal objects and places within the immediate area.

![page 30 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 31 -->


# 3. Landscape elements


## Explanation

Randwick City's physical environment comprises a unique and complex pattern of natural and man-made elements. Some of the most identifiable features are the result of the adaptation of buildings and infrastructure to dramatic coastal topography, and of the powerful influence of the sandstone and the sand on which the City is founded and built. These elements include sandstone and brick retaining walls, stairs, embankments, and road cuttings.

A number of significant landscape elements are listed as heritage items in Schedule 5 of the RLEP due to their cultural significance. In addition, many landscape elements located within or in the vicinity of, heritage items and Heritage Conservation Areas contribute to the heritage significance of these places, even where they are not individually listed.

While many landscape elements are located on Council owned land, both public and private works can impact their heritage value. The following objectives and controls are applicable to all such landscape elements including those that are not individually listed but collectively contribute to the character and identity of Randwick City.


## Note

RLEP Schedule 5 provide item numbers with an 'L' prefix for landscape elements


## Objectives

- Ensure significant retaining walls and associated landscape elements, including but not limited to individually listed heritage items, are retained and conserved
- Ensure contributory landscape elements, including but not limited to individually listed heritage items, are retained and conserved to the greatest extent practicable
- Ensure that private works, including the provision of vehicular access, modifications and repairs, do not adversely impact the significance of landscape elements, including but not limited to individually listed heritage items
- Ensure infrastructure works do not adversely affect the significance of landscape elements, including but not limited to individually listed heritage items
- Ensure repair and maintenance works are undertaken in a timely manner using appropriate materials, methods and techniques
- Ensure hilltop landforms, including terracing and retaining walls above road or footpath level, are retained and conserved including but not limited to individually listed heritage items.

## Controls

- Sandstone and brick retaining walls must not be removed or replaced
- Sandstone and brick retaining walls and natural rock faces must not be modified to accommodate vehicular access
![page 31 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 31 img 2 (3740x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0031-050ff33b38e8.png)
![page 31 img 3 (2503x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0031-8c694306fefe.png)


<!-- SRC: b2-heritage.pdf | PAGE: 32 -->

- Surface mounted infrastructure including water and gas supply pipes, storm water and sewerage pipes, service conduits and other fixings, must be minimised particularly on sandstone and brick retaining walls
- Maintenance and repairs must use the same materials and techniques consistent with the original construction, and should be undertaken by suitably experienced tradespeople
- Reconstruction works must match the existing retaining wall in terms of block size, texture, bond pattern, alignment of blocks, mortar joint colour and capping detail
- Replacement of associated elements such as handrails, should match existing materials and details
- Cyclical maintenance programs, including regular inspections, should be established to ensure the ongoing conservation of significant and contributory landscape elements
- New plantings associated with retaining walls and landscape elements should be consistent with Council's Street Tree Masterplan and must avoid species that may cause structural damage
- Retaining walls and natural rock faces on public or private land must not be modified or altered, including but not limited to partial demolition, rendering and painting, or addition of stairs or handrails, without Council advice and approval
- Landscape elements which are not heritage listed including but not limited to hilltop land formation (such as terracing) and retaining walls above the road/footpath level must be carefully assessed for their contributory heritage value where they may be impacted
- Traffic, pedestrian management and development works for individual property development at the public-private interface must respect established local character and landscape character elements. Any proposed work should not result in the loss of such character elements. In particular, this applies to such elements as split footpaths, road cuttings and embankments, steps/stairways, retaining walls, established fencing and railing arrangements, stone trim/base elements, stone or brick kerbing and guttering, and natural stone and rock outcrops
- Sandstone and brick street kerbing and guttering must be retained and maintained in situ, and, where at risk, salvaged for reuse
- Inlaid concrete footpath signage must be protected, retained and maintained. Opportunities to e incorporate street names embedded in footpaths should be supported.

# 4. Heritage Conservation Areas

This subsection provides an overview of Heritage Conservation Areas (HCAs), including their key character values, and guidelines for managing change. These key values and characteristics, and the guidelines for change that follow, are to be considered in conjunction with:

- the heritage conservation requirements, principles and practices contained in the Burra Charter
- Clause 5.10 of the Randwick Local Environmental Plan
- Heritage Inventory Assessment Reports (State Heritage Inventory) available online via the Heritage NSW website and database, and
- the general guidelines and controls contained in this DCP including but not limited to Part B1 Local Character Statements.
Heritage Conservation Areas exhibit distinctive historic and streetscape qualities that reflect particular phases in the development of Randwick City. Elements that contribute to this special character of HCAs must be retained, and new development must respond to and reinforce/enhance, this established character.

Buildings and sites within HCAs are identified on the relevant Council maps as being contributory, neutral, or detracting to the character and significance of the HCA.


## General objectives

- Development in the vicinity or within the heritage curtilage of a heritage item or an HCA must
- be consistent with policy guidelines contained in the Heritage Inventory Assessment Report (State Heritage Inventory) for individual HCAs in addition to the l guidelines and controls contained in this DCP
- maintain and enhance the key values and characteristics identified in the HCA 's statement of significance
- respect and be compatible with the local character, including architectural style, built form and scale, and subdivision pattern, streetscape character, setbacks, landscape elements, front gardens, fencing, and roofscapes
- achieve a high standard of architectural design, materials and finishes, and detailing, that complements and reinforces the existing character without replicating historic/heritage styles
- avoid the introduction of new driveways, garages, carports, or carspaces across the front boundary, forward of the front building line, where such elements are inconsistent with the established character, and historic streetscape, of the area
- provide appropriate transitions in height and scale, and greater setbacks, between new development and heritage and contributory items and HCAs
- respond to the prevailing/significant roofscape character, including the use of pitched or gabled roof forms where these are characteristic of the area
- use materials that are sympathetic to those traditionally used in the HCA including facebrick, sandstone, brick pavers, timber, slate, and corrugated metal roof
- retain and enhance significant landscape elements, including front gardens, urban/tree canopies, and original landscape features and land formations such as sandstone or brick retaining walls, that contribute to the historic/significant streetscape character.
- Any development under SEPP (Housing) within, adjoining, or in the vicinity of an HCA must comply with the objectives and controls in this DCP (Part B2 Heritage) to ensure the significance and character of Randwick's HCAs are conserved. In particular, development must:
- Respond to, reinforce, incorporate and enhance the established significant character of the HCA including its architectural style, built form and scale, and
