# Controls

- The controls in this section apply to:
- Major development proposals valued over $10M located within E2 Commercial Centres and the selected E1 Local Centre zones shown in Figure 7; or
- Any other development or masterplan sites across Randwick City valued over $15M
- Development specified in a) must deliver artwork as part of the development.

## Note

A minimum allocation of 1% of the estimated development cost should be allocated toward a public art budget. This includes artist and community engagement fees, engineering and manufacture of the artwork but excludes public art consultant fees and installation of the artwork.

- Public art is to be provided on identified sites, plazas and mid-block links as per the block-by-block controls in Section B of DCP Part D1 Kensington and Kingsford
- In accordance with the Randwick Public Art Guidelines, a detailed Public Art Proposal is to be prepared by a public art consultant and submitted with the DA. The Public Art Proposal must include:
- Site analysis, curatorial framework, treatment options, project parameters, community consultation plan, proposed artists, project team, budget allocations
- A commitment to submitting to Council key milestone documentation at detailed project phases, in alignment with Council's review and approval timelines

## Note

To ensure the delivery of public art is appropriate in its context, applicants and developers are encouraged to engage with Council early in the design development phase of a project (as part of pre-DA discussions), to develop a Public Art Proposal in line with the Public Art Guidelines.

- Artwork must demonstrate alignment with the Randwick Public Art Guidelines. This may include a reflection of Randwick's history, culture, and connection to Country
- Where delivered on private land, artwork must be:
- Located in a publicly accessible and visible part of the site in order to provide an unobstructed sensory experience of the work
- Designed to be integrated into the overall layout of the development
- To enhance visual amenity and contribute to the public realm, artwork is to be incorporated onto common/ side boundary walls where developments would otherwise result in large, unarticulated facades
- Where provided in accordance with the Randwick Public Art Guidelines, advice from the Randwick Public Art Advisory Panel (PAAP) must be considered and addressed in the design of the artwork. Documentation of this advice, and response, must be provided in the supporting Public Art Proposal
- Public art must be entirely free from commercial influence and cannot include any marketing, advertising, or brand alignment, including identifiable brand elements such as logos, trademarks, proprietary typefaces, colour schemes, or imagery associated with commercial entities.

# 3. Creative hoardings


# Introduction

Consent is required under the Roads Act 1993 and Local Government Act 1993 to erect a hoarding in a public place. Council is responsible for issuing this consent.

Hoardings serve as a platform for presenting diverse artwork, graphics, and imagery within the public domain. Figures 8 and 9 provide examples of Creative Hoardings within the City of Sydney. The Creative Hoardings program is a creative response to improving our urban environment during periods of growth and development, facilitating and engaging a sense of place and local identity.

![page 10 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


*Figure 8: 'Fantastical Fabulous Fun', Rosie Deacon, Eveleigh Street Redfern, 2020*

![page 10 img 2 (1596x88)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0010-3f76a146e511.png)


*Figure 9: Historic images hoarding display*

Source: Photographer: Katherine Griffiths. City of Sydney

Source: City of Sydney

Artwork, or images on hoardings (i.e., creative hoarding) will be required if the proposal meets criteria based on the location of the proposed hoarding, site width, capital investment value (CIV), and the period which the hoarding will be erected. A condition of consent will be included for developments that trigger the requirements for creative hoardings.

When a condition of consent triggers a requirement for creative hoardings, the applicant can choose from the following options for selecting artwork:

- Council commissioned artwork - artwork that has been licensed by Council and is free of copyright charge for use
- Historic images - local historic photographic images that have been pre-approved and sourced from Council archives, relevant to the ward in which the development is taking place. Free of copyright charge for use
- From the collection - photographic images of special objects held in La Perouse Museum
- Bespoke artwork - a unique artwork that has been commissioned directly by the applicant for their own hoardings. Bespoke commissions are to follow set criteria which outline minimum fees for the artist, reasonable licence terms and conditions, and ensure commissioned artworks meet a high artistic quality. Bespoke artworks must not, in any way, be perceivable as advertising. They must be entirely free from commercial influence and cannot include any marketing, advertising, or brand alignment, including identifiable brand elements such as logos, trademarks, proprietary typefaces, colour schemes, or imagery associated with commercial entities.

Further details and the step-by-step process can be found in the Public Art Guidelines. Details of Council commissioned artwork and historic images can be viewed on Council's website .


## Objectives

- Specify requirements for the provision of public art on hoardings through the Creative Hoardings program
- Achieve and reflect a distinct character and identity for town centres and neighbourhoods in the LGA through site specific artwork and creative treatments
- To contribute to the visual amenity of the public domain and streetscape during construction phase of development
- To discourage bill posters and graffiti at construction sites
- To ensure proposals for Creative Hoardings have endorsement from Council Staff regarding placement, quality, artistic vision and compliant installation.

# Controls

- Where an application for a Type A or Type B hoarding is required under the Roads Act 1993, Local Government Act 1993, and by condition of consent, creative hoardings will be required on sites:
- Zoned E1 Local Centre and E2 Commercial Centre where erected for 8 weeks or more, or
- Located along a State classified road where erected for 8 weeks or more, or
- In any other location, with a frontage of 12m wide or greater, and erected for 12 weeks or more, except where:
- The capital investment value (CIV) of the work to which the hoarding relates is less than $1 million, or
- The land is zoned R2 Low Density Residential, or
- Hoarding installations are proposed on minor or secondary roadways such as laneways used primarily for local traffic and where the prevailing from of the laneway consists of rear fences, garages, gates, roller doors and the like.
- Applications for creative hoardings are to demonstrate compliance with the requirements of Council's Public Art Guidelines, including the Terms and Conditions listed therein.

## Note

Notwithstanding the above requirements, Council may determine that the provision of creative hoardings is required on sites with a street frontage of less than 12m where the scale, duration or nature of construction works is likely to result in a level of impact on the public domain comparable to development on wider sites.


## Note

In cases where a hoarding is installed on a main frontage of a corner block and the hoarding extends along the side laneway having a width of less than 6m, measured from the property boundaries, graphics must be displayed for the length of at last 5m within the laneway measured from the corner intersection. Where a side laneway width exceeds 6m, graphics must be displayed the full length of the hoarding.


## Note

Notwithstanding the above requirements, Council may determine that creative hoardings may be unnecessary in particular circumstances.

This section applies to all new development and alterations and additions for low density forms of housing in the Randwick Local Government Area (LGA), being:

- Dwelling houses
- Dual occupancies (attached)
- Dual occupancies (detached)
- Semi-detached dwellings
- Secondary dwellings
And ancillary facilities relating to the above dwelling types.

# 2. Site planning


# 2.1. Minimum lot size


## Explanation

The lot size controls for properties in the Randwick Local Government Area (LGA) are contained in the Randwick Local Environment Plan (RLEP) Lot Size Map.


# 2.2. Lot frontage


## Explanation

The minimum lot frontage controls in this DCP supplement the RLEP provisions on lot size and aim to maintain the established and desired future character of low-density neighbourhoods occupied by dwelling houses, semi-detached dwellings, dual occupancies or a mixture of these housing types.

The frontage control serves to ensure suitable subdivision configuration, which will in turn enable dwellings of adequate dimensions, configuration, and amenity. It also functions to ensure that suitable space for open space and visually acceptable and efficient parking and access arrangements can be achieved.


## Objectives

- To ensure land subdivision respects the predominant existing or planned future subdivision and development pattern of the locality
- To ensure land subdivision creates allotments that have adequate width and configuration, to deliver suitable building design and to maintain the amenity of the neighbouring properties
- To ensure dwellings have suitable scale and built form proportional to their allotment to complement the streetscape
- To ensure dual occupancy dwellings do not result in unreasonable impacts on the surrounding properties in terms of visual amenity, solar access and privacy.

## Controls

- The minimum frontage widths for subdivision of lots must meet the following:
| Minimum lot primary street frontage widths for subdivision   | Minimum lot primary street frontage widths for subdivision   | Minimum lot primary street frontage widths for subdivision   | Minimum lot primary street frontage widths for subdivision   |
|--------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Low density housing type                                     | Zone                                                         | Parent lot                                                   | Resulting lot following subdivision                          |
| Dwelling houses                                              | R2                                                           | 24m                                                          | 12m per dwelling                                             |
| Dwelling houses                                              | R3                                                           | 18m                                                          | 9m per dwelling                                              |
| Semi-detached dwellings                                      | R2, R3 and where permissible                                 | 15m                                                          | 7.5m per dwelling                                            |

![page 8 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 9 -->

- The minimum frontage widths for development of lots where dual occupancy development is proposed must meet the following:
- Any subdivision of land must not create battle-axe or hatchet shaped allotments for the purposes of dwelling houses, semi-detached dwellings or dual occupancies (attached).
| Minimum lot primary street frontage widths for dual occupancy development                                                       | Minimum lot primary street frontage widths for dual occupancy development   | Minimum lot primary street frontage widths for dual occupancy development   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Low density housing type                                                                                                        | Zone                                                                        | Parent lot                                                                  |
| Dual occupancy (attached)                                                                                                       | R2, R3 and where permissible                                                | 15m                                                                         |
| Dual occupancy (detached), where the allotment has dual frontages with either rear lane or secondary street access (corner lot) | R3 and where permissible                                                    | 9m                                                                          |
| Dual occupancy (detached), where dwellings front primary street in a side-by-side arrangement                                   | R3 and where permissible                                                    | 18m                                                                         |

# 2.3. Dual occupancy (detached) site layout


## Explanation

Building layout plays an important role in ensuring adequate levels of amenity for the occupants of dual occupancy (detached) dwellings and adjoining properties, and to avoid adverse visual impacts on the streetscape.

Ensuring appropriate building layout of dual occupancy (detached) that achieves adequate levels of privacy at the time of construction also is also a key consideration in the instance that future subdivision is sought.


## Objectives

- To ensure each dwelling in a dual occupancy (detached) development achieves adequate levels of living amenity in terms of private open space provision, solar access, privacy and accessibility.

## Controls

- The dwellings in a dual occupancy (detached) must be sited in the following manner:
- One dwelling fronting the primary street and the other fronting the rear lane
- One dwelling fronting the primary street and the other fronting the secondary street
- Both dwellings fronting the primary street in a side-by-side arrangement for sites without rear lane or secondary street access
- Pedestrian access of not less than 900mm in width must be provided to link any rear lane dwelling with the street frontage
- Minimum building separation between the two dwellings in a dual occupancy (detached) must satisfy the following:
| Minimum Building Separation          | Minimum Building Separation                                                            | Minimum Building Separation   |
|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Site characteristics                 | Building layout                                                                        | Minimum building separation   |
| Dual frontages with rear lane access | One dwelling fronting the street, with the other fronting the rear lane                | 10m                           |
| Corner allotment                     | One dwelling fronting the primary street, with the other fronting the secondary street | Merit assessment              |
| Single frontage                      | Both dwellings fronting the street in a side-by-side arrangement                       | 1.8m                          |


## Definition

Building separation is the distance between the nearest external walls of two buildings, excluding eaves, gutters, unroofed terraces, decks or landings not more than 1m above ground level (finished), and minor projecting features, such as awnings, sun hoods, screening devices and the like.

# 2.4. Site coverage


## Explanation

The site coverage control, in conjunction with setback controls, determines the extent and location within the property that a building may be constructed. The control ensures that there is sufficient unbuilt upon areas on a property to accommodate private open space, deep soil planting, permeable surfaces, recreational area and for services.

Site coverage is expressed as a percentage to describe the proportion of a site that could be built upon. The allowable site coverage percentage decreases as allotment size increases, so that the mass and scale of any building will not detract from the character of the street.


## Definition

( RLEP) Site coverage means the proportion of a site area covered by buildings. However, the following are not included for the purpose of calculating site coverage -

- (a) any basement,
- (b) any part of an awning that is outside the outer walls of a building and that adjoins the street frontage or other site boundary,
- (c) any eaves,
- (d) unenclosed balconies, decks, pergolas and the like.
Further to the LEP definition above, the following guidance is provided:

- The following are not included for the purpose of calculating site coverage:
- (a) an access ramp
- (b) a driveway
- (c) carports
- (d) a fence or screen
- (e) a pathway or paving
- (f) a rainwater tank attached to the principal or secondary dwelling
- (g) a swimming pool or spa pool.
- Unenclosed balconies, decks, pergolas and the like are those that do not have walls higher than 1.4m above floor level or are those not elevated more than 1.4m above ground level.

## Objectives

- To ensure new development and alterations and additions to existing dwellings reserve adequate unbuilt upon areas for the purpose of private open space, deep soil planting, permeable surfaces and ancillary development
- To ensure a high level of environmental amenity for residents of low density dwellings in the LGA.

## Controls

- The maximum site coverage of a building must not exceed the following based on site area:
| Site area        | Maximum Site Coverage- (% of site area)   |
|------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Up to 300 sqm    | 60%                                       |
| 301 to 450 sqm   | 55%                                       |
| 451 to 600 sqm   | 50%                                       |
| 601 sqm or above | 45%                                       |

![page 12 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)
![page 12 img 2 (173x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0012-cc62aad42f81.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 13 -->

![page 13 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


*Figure 4: Calculating site coverage*

Source: Randwick City Council, 2025


## Notes

Site area is measured according to the RLEP definition, being the area of any land on which development is, or is to be carried out. It is not measured against any proposed allotments / subdivision,

Development applications must be supported by a site coverage calculation and deep soil permeable surface diagram see Figure 7 for an example.


# 2.5. Deep soil permeable surfaces


## Explanation

Deep soil planting moderates local climatic conditions and enhances permeability of surface water and infiltration of stormwater, thus improving the environmental performance of development. It also provides areas for vegetation, tree planting and shade, and plays a screening function that improves mutual privacy and visual amenity between a development and its neighbours.


## Definition

Deep soil permeable surfaces include areas used for the growing of plants (including grasses, shrubs and trees) and areas occupied by loose gravels upon soil at the ground level of the site. However, the following are not included for the purpose of calculating deep soil permeable surfaces:

swimming and spa pools

- paved areas including step ping stone pavers
- artificial turf
- planter boxes, or planted areas above basements, podiums, roofs, or slabs.
![page 13 img 2 (1384x621)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0013-571848ae9e42.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 14 -->


## Objectives

- To retain and provide planting area for canopy trees and general vegetation to contribute to the overall tree canopy cover of the LGA and to the establishment of landscaped corridors across the locality
- To assist with stormwater infiltration and reduction of overland flow
- To improve climate resilience of the site.

## Controls

- New development, or alterations and additions that change the existing site coverage by more than 10%, must provide the minimum area of deep soil permeable surfaces as specified in the table below:
- Where new development, or alterations and additions do not change the existing site coverage by more than 10%, there must be no net loss of deep soil permeable surfaces.
- Deep soil permeable surfaces must have a width of not less than 900mm
- Deep soil permeable surfaces should be located to support the retention of existing significant trees on site or those on adjoining sites
- A minimum of 25% of the front setback area of a property must comprise deep soil permeable surfaces.
- Permeable pavement and the like must not comprise more than 50% of deep soil permeable surfaces of the front setback area and no more than 20% of overall deep soil permeable surfaces required.
| Site area        | Minimum Deep Soil Permeable Surfaces (% of site area)   |
|------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| Up to 300 sqm    | 30%                                                     |
| 301 to 450 sqm   | 35%                                                     |
| 451 to 600 sqm   | 40%                                                     |
| 601 sqm or above | 45%                                                     |


## Dual occupancies and semi-detached dwellings

- For new development, deep soil permeable surfaces are calculated on the overall site area and must be evenly distributed between the pair of dwellings.

## Note

When calculating changes in site coverage for alterations and additions, these are to be calculated as a percentage, not as percentage points.

For example, if a development application proposes increasing site coverage from 40 percent to 45 percent, this is a 12.5% increase in site coverage and would trigger requirements within this DCP for minimum areas of deep soil permeable surfaces (2.5) and canopy cover (2.6) to be achieved.

# 2.6. Landscaping and tree canopy cover


## Explanation

Landscaping assists in visually integrating development with the streetscape and the wider neighbourhood and provides an attractive and useable outdoor environment for residents.

Tree canopy cover in urban areas provides numerous benefits including reduced building energy use, air pollution removal and carbon sequestration. In addition, areas with higher tree canopy cover provide increased amenity through shading, softening of built form and habitat for wildlife.


## Objectives

- To ensure landscaped areas are effectively distributed on the site to achieve a visual balance between building structures and open space
- To provide privacy screening between dwellings
- To retain and provide for canopy trees and large shrubs to contribute to the overall tree canopy cover of the locality
- To encourage urban greening that contributes positively to the existing and desired future character of the locality
- To establish vegetation corridors across the locality
- To reduce the impacts of urban heat island effect.

## Controls

- New ancillary development, or alterations and additions that changes the existing site coverage by more than 10%, must demonstrate that a minimum of 25% canopy coverage as a proportion of the site area can be achieved within 10 years from the completion of development based on maturity of trees selected
- In the circumstances where the consent authority is satisfied that there are sufficient environmental constraints on a site (such as significant slope) to limit the ability to achieve a 25% tree canopy cover on a site, a street tree planting fee may be considered to enable Council to plant trees in the public domain
- To achieve the minimum canopy coverage requirement, the number of large canopy trees should be provided is in accordance with the table below:
- Despite c), a combination of canopy tree sizes can be used to achieve the minimum tree canopy cover area
| Site area        |   Minimum number of large canopy trees |
|------------------|----------------------------------------|
| Up to 300 sqm    |                                      2 |
| 301 to 450 sqm   |                                      3 |
| 451 to 600 sqm   |                                      4 |
| 601 sqm or above |                                      4 |

![page 16 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 17 -->

- Canopy trees must achieve a minimum mature height of 5m. For allotments with constrained dimensions or site conditions, smaller trees with minimum mature height of 4m may be accepted by Council subject to achieving the minimum 25% canopy cover as per sub-clause b)
- The trunk of canopy trees should be planted a minimum of 2.5m from any existing or proposed building
- A minimum of 25% of the front setback area of a property must be landscaped with trees, shrubs and groundcover planting
- Native species must comprise at least 60% of the plant schedule, incorporating a mix of locally indigenous trees, shrubs and groundcovers appropriate to the area and surrounds
- Existing mature native trees on the site must be retained and incorporated in the landscape design whenever possible. Where a development involves removal of such existing trees, suitable replacement planting of equivalent or larger size must be provided
- Suitable soil depth and volume must be provided on the site to support the healthy, sustained growth of trees
- Proposed and existing retained trees must be protected by locating paved areas, underground services and rainwater tanks and building structures away from their root zones
- Provide adequate sight lines for vehicles and pedestrians, especially near corners and intersections.

## Dual occupancies and semi-detached dwellings

- The minimum canopy coverage and number of canopy trees are calculated on the overall site area and must be evenly distributed between the pair of dwellings
- For dual occupancies (attached) and semi-detached dwellings the front setback must contain at least one (1) tree per dwelling.
![page 17 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 18 -->


## Notes

Landscape requirements, plans and details are to be provided as per the requirements outlined in Section B4 of the RDCP.

A street tree planting fee may be imposed on sites that cannot meet the tree canopy coverage targets outlined within this DCP due to site constraints. The funds accumulated from the street planting fee are utilised for street and public open space tree planting throughout the LGA.

Tree species guidance and average mature dimensions for canopy calculations can be found in Council's Street Tree Master Plan. It can be downloaded from the following link -

https://www.randwick.nsw.gov.au/environment-and-sustainability/trees/preserving-our-trees

An interactive version of the Precincts and Precinct Palette Species list contained within the Street Tree Master Plan can be accessed here - https://randwick-

council.maps.arcgis.com/apps/webappviewer/index.html?id=5343844065dd44b0adc4d4ea5 37816d5

Native / indigenous plant species are required to be provided as they are better suited to the local soils and climate, they support native fauna (through providing food and habitat) and they require less water and are more drought tolerant.

A tree is located within the site area if the majority of its trunk is located within the site area boundary.

Street verges - commercial, coastal and special precincts

Council's Urban Design Elements Manual (UDEM) applies to public domain upgrades in commercial centres, coastal areas, parks and special precincts. This Manual is available on Council's website.

Conditions of consent may require applicants to prepare, submit, and have approved by Council's Officers, detailed landscape plans which include plant schedules, planting plans, sample/materials boards and sections/elevations.

Where a contributions plan or a VPA agreement with Council applies (such as a Community Infrastructure Plan or a s.7.12 Development Contributions Plan), Council may consider public domain improvement works are delivered as 'works in kind' by a developer or through a monetary contribution to Council to undertake the work.


## Street verges - residential areas

Council encourages the establishment of street gardens in residential street verges as part of development proposals rather than providing a standard turfed verge. Street gardens must be designed in accordance with Council's Street Garden Guidelines.

For larger developments, Council may require the applicant to upgrade the public verge with mass-planted, low growing, low maintenance species, consistent with the Street Garden Guidelines to support high-quality presentation and integration of new development into a residential streetscape. Such treatments improve landscape cohesion, increase shade potential and support Council's broader environmental, walkability and liveability objectives.

Artificial or synthetic turf is not permitted within nature strips or street verges. Nature strips and verges must be landscaped using natural turf, groundcovers or planting that supports streetscape outcomes, urban cooling, stormwater infiltration, and the protection of public utility infrastructure.

All public domain works are at the applicant's cost.

# 2.7. Private open space


## Explanation

Private open space provides outdoor living areas for recreational activities of residents and should be located and designed to maximise solar access, privacy, accessibility, and useability.


## Objectives

- To ensure an adequate level of private open space is provided for dwellings to enable passive recreational activities by residents
- To ensure private open space is designed for useability, solar access, privacy and accessibility
- To ensure semi detached dwelling and dual occupancy development provides a suitable level of functional private open space for each dwelling that offers high amenity for residents.

## Controls

- Provide at least one (1) contiguous area of private open space satisfying the following dimensions based on site area:
| Minimum Dimensions for Contiguous Private Open Space   | Minimum Dimensions for Contiguous Private Open Space   |
|--------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| Dwelling Houses and Semi-detached Dwellings            | Dwelling Houses and Semi-detached Dwellings            |
| Site area                                              | Minimum dimensions                                     |
| Up to 300 sqm                                          | 5m x 5m                                                |
| 301 to 450 sqm                                         | 6m x 6m                                                |
| 451 to 600 sqm                                         | 7m x 7m                                                |
| 601 sqm or above                                       | 8m x 8m                                                |
| Dual occupancy (attached and detached)                 | Dual occupancy (attached and detached)                 |
| Site area                                              | Minimum dimensions                                     |
| 451 to 600 sqm                                         | 5m x 5m for each dwelling following development        |
| 601sqm or above                                        | 6m x 6m for each dwelling following development        |

b) The contiguous private open space must:

- Be situated at ground level (except for dual occupancy (attached) development where one dwelling is situated above another)
- Be adjacent to and directly accessible from the primary living or dining room of the dwelling
- Be oriented and configured to maximise solar access
- Be located to the rear of the allotment behind the dwelling where possible
- Have minimal change in gradient
- Include landscaped areas, terraces, decks, paved surfaces and the like
- Not include any open space on podiums or roofs.
![page 20 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)

# 3. Building envelope

The building envelope is the maximum theoretical three-dimensional space within which a development may occur, and is established by the parameters of Floor Space Ratio (FSR), maximum Height of Building (HoB) and front, side and rear setbacks.


# 3.1. Floor Space Ratio


## Explanation

Floor Space Ratio (FSR) is a measure that assists in controlling the mass and bulk of a development. FSR operates in conjunction with building height, wall height and setback controls to define the three-dimensional space within which a development may occur, that is, the building envelope. FSR is expressed as a ratio of the permissible Gross Floor Area (GFA) to the site area.

The maximum permissible FSR for any development is prescribed and defined in the Randwick LEP Floor Space Ratio Map.


## Note

Further to the RLEP definition of Gross Floor Area, the following are included for the purpose of calculating GFA:

- Lifts (where not common) at all floor levels
- Stairs (where not common) at all floor levels other than the uppermost level.

# 3.2. Building height


## Explanation

Building height is a major factor affecting the visual presence of a development and the degree of overshadowing of neighbouring property.

The maximum building height control is stipulated in the RLEP Height of Buildings Map (HoB), which varies across different residential zones. The maximum building height under the Randwick LEP Height of Building Map is 9.5m for low density housing, and is measured from ground level (existing) to the topmost point of a building.


## Objectives

- To limit the bulk, scale and visual impact of buildings as viewed from the street and from neighbouring dwellings
- To ensure low density residential development maintains a two-storey height and street frontage
- To ensure that floor to floor and ceiling heights allow for adequate internal amenity for current and future occupants
- To position any habitable space above the first floor level within the roof of the dwelling
- To ensure development height does not cause unreasonable impacts upon the neighbouring dwellings in terms of overshadowing, view loss, privacy and visual amenity
- To ensure the form and massing of development is respectful of site topography.
![page 21 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 22 -->


## Controls

- Any habitable space located above the first floor level must be integrated into a pitched roof form
- The minimum floor-to-ceiling height for living areas, such as living/lounge, dining and bedrooms is 2.7m
- The minimum floor-to-floor height for building stories, excluding those above the first floor level within the building roofline, is 3.1m
- An alternative design that varies from the two-storey height and street frontage in the Zone R2 may be acceptable having regard to the following considerations:
- Site topography
- Site orientation
- Allotment configuration
- Flooding requirements
- Allotment dimensions
- Potential impacts on the visual amenity, solar access, privacy and views of the adjoining properties.

## Notes

Refer to Section 9 for building height controls for Secondary Dwellings, Outbuildings and development in Laneways.

Any floorspace within a roof must comply with the National Construction Code (NCC) roof height requirements as outlined in Part 10.3 Room height of the NCC linked here - Part 10.3 Room heights | NCC (abcb.gov.au)

Part 10.3 Room heights | NCC (abcb.gov.au)


# 3.3. Setbacks


## Explanation

Setbacks define the outer extremities of a building in relation to the front, side and rear boundaries. The front setback control is formulated to maintain any established building alignment along the street. Side and rear setbacks are established to ensure an adequate level of building separation, and to provide for access, landscaping, privacy, natural lighting and ventilation.


## Objectives

- To maintain or establish a consistent rhythm of setbacks that contributes to the lowdensity, one to two storey character of the neighbourhood
- To minimise visual bulk and to avoid creating overbearing massing of development when viewed from neighbouring dwellings and the public domain
- To ensure adequate separation between neighbouring buildings for visual and acoustic privacy and solar access
- To reserve adequate ground level areas for deep soil planting at the front and rear of dwellings and appropriately located private open space
- To enable a reasonable level of view sharing between a development and the neighbouring dwellings and the public domain.
![page 22 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 23 -->


## Note

Setback distances are measured perpendicular (that is, at a 90-degree angle) from the boundary to the outer face of the building elevation, excluding eaves, gutters, unroofed terraces, decks or landings not more than 1m above ground level (finished) and minor projecting features, such as awnings, sun hoods, screening devices and the like.

Any basement or semi-basement protruding less than 1.2m above finished ground level is not counted as a building storey.


## Note

Setbacks are to be in accordance with TfNSW requirements in relation to classified roads and signalised intersections.


## 3.3.1. Front setbacks


### Controls

- The front setback must be consistent with the average setbacks of the adjoining dwellings. Where there are no adjoining dwellings, the setback must be no less than 6m. Where a development is proposed in an area identified in the site analysis as being an area undergoing transition, the front setback will be determined on a merit basis
- For corner allotments, the setback from the secondary street frontage must be in accordance with the following minimum requirements:
- 900mm for allotments with a primary frontage width of less than 7m
- 1.5m for all other sites.
- The sitting of dwellings on corner lots should generally align with the setbacks of dwellings on adjacent sites
- The front setback areas must be free of structures, such as swimming pools, aboveground rainwater tanks and outbuildings
- Any habitable space located above the first-floor level must be integrated into the building roofline.

### Note

Transitional areas can be areas of mixed character, without clearly prevailing characteristics or features. They can also be precincts or localities in the process of undergoing change in terms of character or built form.


## 3.3.2. Side setbacks


### Controls

- New buildings and alterations and additions must comply with the following minimum side setbacks based on the primary frontage width:
![page 23 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 24 -->

| Less than 6m                    | Merit assessment                                | Merit assessment                                        | Merit assessment                              |

- Despite control a), side setbacks on sites with a significant slope may be subject to a merit assessment. In such cases, applicants must demonstrate that side setbacks:
- Minimise visual bulk and avoid creating overbearing massing of development when viewed from neighbouring dwellings and the public domain
- Ensure adequate separation between neighbouring buildings for visual and acoustic privacy and solar access
- Maintains a consistent rhythm of setbacks that contributes to the low-density, one to two storey character of the neighbourhood

### Note:

Refer to Sub-Section 6. Car Parking and Access for further information relating to side setback requirements for parking facilities.

![page 24 img 2 (814x505)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0024-eb9212a7389e.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 25 -->


## 3.3.3. Rear setbacks


### Controls

- The minimum rear setback must be 25% of the allotment depth or 8m, whichever is the lesser.
- Irrespective of control a) all rear setbacks must demonstrate that the proposed rear setback provides:
- Retention of the existing predominant rear setback line in the subject urban block
- Achieving a reasonable view sharing with the neighbouring dwellings and the public domain
- Adequately protect the privacy and solar access to the neighbouring dwellings.
- Garages, carports, outbuildings, swimming or spa pools, above-ground water tanks, and unroofed decks and terraces attached to the dwelling may encroach upon the required rear setback, in so far as they comply with other relevant provisions of this DCP.
- For irregularly shaped allotments, or allotments with the longest boundary abutting the street or the rear adjoining neighbour (that is, the frontage width being longer than the site depth), the rear setback will be assessed on merit having regard to demonstration of the following:
- Compatibility with the existing development pattern in the subject and adjoining urban blocks
- Provision of adequate private open space with dimensions compliant with the requirements of this DCP
- Potential impacts on the neighbouring dwellings in terms of solar access, privacy and view sharing.

### Definition

The predominant rear setback is defined as the average of adjacent dwellings on either side of the allotment and is determined separately for each storey.


### Note

Rear setback controls do not apply to corner allotments.

![page 25 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)

# 4. Building design


# 4.1. General


## Explanation

Following the establishment of the permissible building envelope (defined by site coverage, setbacks, FSR, Height of Building and external wall height), the form and mass of the development needs to be modelled to respond specifically to the site characteristics and the surrounding natural and built context.

Façade treatment and detailing affect the visual presentation of buildings and play a pivotal role in enhancing the character and continuity of streetscapes. Façade composition has an impact on the perceivable bulk and scale of a building and should be carefully designed to achieve an appropriate streetscape outcome.


## Objectives

- To ensure the form, scale, massing and proportions of dwellings recognise and adapt to the characteristics of a site in terms of topography, configuration, orientation and surrounding natural and built context
- To ensure building facades are articulated to complement or enhance the existing streetscape and neighbourhood character
- To ensure that internal rooms are well proportioned, functional and provide a high standard of amenity
- To encourage contemporary and innovative designs that contribute to neighbourhood character in new and transitional residential areas.

## Controls

- A dwelling's overall built form must respect and follow the natural topography of the site. On sloping sites, the building mass must be modelled or stepped in response to the prevailing slope of the land and avoid concentrating the structural bulk on the uphill or downhill side of the allotment
- When arranging the built form on the site , avoid the creation of 'wedding cake' or 'pyramid' type buildings which due to their visual dominance are generally unsympathetic in their relationship to the natural landform
- External facades of the dwelling must be articulated to reduce the apparent mass and to present a human scale to adjoining properties, public areas and from key vantage points.
This must be achieved by at least two of the following design measures:

- Window openings
- Balconies or terraces
- Entry porches
- Staggered wall planes
- Varied materials and finishes
- Decorative architectural elements.
![page 26 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)
![page 26 img 2 (980x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0026-f6f735c8df66.png)
![page 26 img 3 (1633x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0026-3192ddd37fc2.png)
![page 26 img 4 (1001x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0026-63464e762b40.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 27 -->

![page 27 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


*Figure 11: Design measures for modelling and articulating a building*


## Source: Randwick City Council

- Divide side elevations into sections, bays or modules of not more than 12m length, separated by measures, such as recesses or side courtyards, in order to avoid massive or unrelieved walls
- Articulation zones and recesses are to be a minimum of 0.5m in depth and 1m in width.
- Articulate all street elevations for development on corner allotments
- Alterations and additions to an existing dwelling must present an integrated design with suitable configuration, materials and detailing, so that the new and retained structures provide an integrated composition

## Note

For heritage items or buildings within Heritage Conservation Areas (HCA), it may be desirable to distinguish between old and new works. Refer to Section B2 Heritage of this DCP for further details.

- Balconies, terraces and decks must be of a size and configuration that are appropriate to the proportions of the building without excessively increasing its visual bulk
- Master bedrooms must have a minimum area of 10m 2 and other bedrooms 9m 2 , both with a minimum dimension of 3m (excluding wardrobe space).
![page 27 img 2 (825x672)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0027-d8509e690210.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 28 -->


# 4.2. New semi-detached and dual occupancy (attached) dwellings


## Explanation

Dual occupancies (attached) sharing a single allotment and semi-detached dwellings, provide an alternative form of low-density housing choice.

They have the potential for more significant environmental impacts than single dwellings due to the additional parking and access requirements and associated hard paved surfaces. Dual occupancies (attached) and semi-detached dwellings should aim to present a similar bulk and scale as a large single dwelling to integrate with existing streetscapes.

The following are additional provisions which must be addressed in the design of new dual occupancies (attached) and semi-detached dwellings.


## Definition

RLEP dual occupancy (attached) means 2 dwellings on one lot of land that are attached to each other, but does not include a secondary dwelling.

Further to the RLEP definition above, for the buildings to be attached, they must share a common wall.


## Objectives

- To ensure the configuration, scale, massing and proportions of attached dual occupancies are compatible with other dwellings in the street
- To ensure parking facilities do not dominate the street elevations of dual occupancy dwellings, and instead present as an integrated element of the overall architectural composition
- To encourage the design of buildings that go beyond current minimum sustainable standards to benefit residents and the broader Randwick community.

## Controls

- The architectural design of dwellings must respect and enhance the architectural character of the streetscape
- The front facade of dwellings must be designed to soften the visual dominance of parking facilities. This may include the following measures:
- Place balconies or verandahs above garages
- Provide windows and/or doorways on the front elevation of the parking level, so that garage entries are not the sole façade elements
- Recess garage entries below cantilevered or projecting architectural elements.
- The predominant built form of dwellings should be positioned towards the shared boundary to reduce visual bulk
- The main entrance to dwellings must not be recessed behind the front facade alignment by more than 2m
- Where garages face the primary street dwellings must only have a single car width garage
- Where a dual occupancy or semi-detached dwellings are proposed on a corner allotment, each dwelling, and any associated garaging, should independently address a
![page 28 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 29 -->

street frontage. If both dwellings are proposed to be accessed from one street, car parking and driveways should not dominate the streetscape

- Landscape planting or deep soil permeable surfaces should be maximised in between, or adjacent to driveways to improve visual presentation to the street
- Dwellings are encouraged to incorporate PV rooftop solar and battery storage for the capture and use of energy for lighting, ventilation and services
- Dwellings are encouraged to be 100% electric (no natural gas).

## Notes

Council provides sustainability rebates for electric vehicle charging, hot water systems, insulation, lighting, pool pumps, rainwater tanks, rooftop solar, solar batteries, solar health checks, sustainability checks and waterfix. Refer to:

https://www.randwick.nsw.gov.au/environment-and-sustainability/get-involved/sustainabilityrebates for further details.

Council supports the implementation of green building certifications schemes for new development that demonstrates industry excellence to meet sustainability goals, such as Passive House, Australian Green Building Council and WELL ratings.

Guidance and details on gaining carbon neutral certification can be obtained from the Australian Government Department of Environment and Energy website:

http://www.environment.gov.au/climate-change/government/climate-active/certification

All new development must have regard to the 'Better Practice Guide for Resource Recovery in Residential Developments' (NSW EPA) .

The Australian Government requires a NatHERS 7 Star Rating for all new buildings.

![page 29 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)

Source: Randwick City Council 2022

![page 29 img 3 (3647x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0029-37c664ed9047.png)

# 4.3. Alterations and additions to existing semi-detached and dual occupancy (attached) dwellings

![page 30 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


*Figure 13: Typical semi-detached / dual occupancy (attached) development*

Source: Randwick City Council


## Explanation

The following are additional provisions which must be addressed by proposals for symmetrical semi-detached dwellings on separate allotments and dual occupancy (attached) dwellings.


## Objectives

- To ensure that redevelopment, or alteration and addition, to an individual semi-detached and dual occupancy (attached) dwelling recognises it as being half of a pair of symmetrical, similar, or complementary buildings
- To ensure development of semi-detached and dual occupancy (attached) dwellings are carefully integrated with the building to which it is attached, and takes into account any possible future development to the latter.

## Controls

- Alterations and additions must respect and enhance the architectural character of the pair of semi-detached and dual occupancy (attached) dwellings as a coherent entity
- The design of the dwelling must be based on a detailed site and contextual analysis
- Design solutions must respect the existing architectural expression and symmetry between the pair of semi-detached and dual occupancy (attached) dwellings and address:
- Locating the bulk of any first floor level addition, setback from the principal street frontage and accommodated to the rear of the dwelling, with a substantial portion of the existing front roof remaining intact
![page 30 img 2 (389x223)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0030-135aaa0cef4e.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 31 -->


## Notes

The above controls are particularly important when altering or adding to semi-detached and dual occupancy (attached) dwellings in a Heritage Conservation Area (HCA). Refer to Part B2 Heritage of this DCP for further details.

The above design solutions should not be used where the adjoining dwelling contains unsympathetic or poorly configured additions.

- Alterations and additions to semi-detached and dual occupancy (attached) dwellings may be constructed to the common boundary with the adjoining dwelling
- Avoid the exposure of existing blank party walls of the adjoining semi-detached dwelling to the public domain
- Alterations and additions must seek to minimise the creation of exposed party walls at the common boundary. Where this is not feasible, the party walls must be appropriately finished

## Note

The owners of a pair of semi-detached dwellings or dual occupancy (attached) should coordinate with each other and present a consistent and integrated design approach. It is encouraged that a Development Application/s for both dwellings are submitted to Council concurrently.

- Where a development application seeking first floor additions for both dwellings is not submitted concurrently, the later development application must be consistent with the built form massing of any adjoining, approved first floor addition including roof form, pitch and gutter lines
- The selection of materials used for alterations and additions must enhance the character of the pair of semi-detached dwellings and result in a coordinated / holistic design outcome.
- Positioning the addition behind the apex of existing hipped roofed houses. For gable roofs, additions should be setback from the gable end 100% of the height increase and retain any existing gable features and chimneys
- Designing the first floor level addition as a low profile roof form that is visually secondary to the existing front roof. Alternatively, the addition should adopt a roof form that is compatible with the style and period of the existing roof to be retained.
![page 31 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 32 -->

![page 32 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


*Figure 14: Possible design solutions for first floor additions to semi-detached and dual occupancy (attached) dwellings*

Source: Randwick City Council 2022


## Note

When adding a first floor level addition to an existing dwelling, set the first floor extension back behind the existing roof ridge (top), or alternatively create a new unified architectural character for the pair of dwellings (bottom).

![page 32 img 2 (1190x941)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0032-4cba18851c91.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 33 -->


# 4.4. Roof terraces and balconies


## Objectives

- To ensure trafficable roof spaces (eg. balconies or terraces) are integrated with the overall built form and architectural expression of the dwelling and maintain privacy in relation to neighbouring dwellings
- To ensure terraces do not result in adverse visual bulk or present as an additional storey
- To minimise visual and acoustic amenity impacts of trafficable roof spaces on surrounding properties
- To ensure that trafficable roof spaces allow for view sharing so that equitable access to views are provided from private property
- To ensure trafficable roof spaces are not the primary private open space and are not uncharacteristic of the area.

## Controls

- A roof terrace will be considered by Council on the uppermost or main roof of the building (including the principal dwelling and any outbuilding) if it is demonstrated that:
- They are suitably located to prevent direct views to neighbouring habitable windows and private open spaces and will not result in unreasonable amenity impacts such as loss of privacy and acceptable noise
- The terrace does not exceed 12m 2 in area
- They are designed to provide for view sharing, including minimising associated structures and roof top elements and are suitably located to prevent direct views to neighbouring habitable windows and private open spaces
- It is designed as a secondary private open space and does not to include entertainment facilities such as kitchens, BBQs or similar and shall incorporate screen planting where applicable to minimise impacts
- The terrace and all elements of roof terraces shall comply with the maximum building height control and access to the terrace is provided within the envelope of the building.
- For stepped buildings on sloping sites, a rooftop terrace may be provided on the roof other than the uppermost roof above the storeys below, provided the terrace complies with control a) and the additional following requirements:
- The size is to be subservient to the roof form within which it is located
- It is designed as a secondary private open space and does not to include entertainment facilities such as kitchens, BBQs or similar
- Designed to provide for view sharing, including minimising associated structures and roof top elements
- It is to be uncovered, and all elements of roof terraces shall comply with the maximum building height control
- Roof terraces above garages may only be provided on sloping sites, where the garages are located on the downhill side of the sites fronting the street, and are to comply with the controls outlined in this section
![page 33 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 34 -->


## Note

Existing roof terraces in a locality that do not comply with the above controls should not be utilised as precedent in seeking variations to the controls outlined in this section. This is to ensure that the objectives of low density residential development are met.

![page 34 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)

Source: Randwick City Council, 2022

# 4.5. Roof design and features


## Objectives

- To ensure the roof design integrates with the architectural form, proportions and façade composition of the building
- To ensure low density residential development maintains a two-storey height and frontage to the streetscape.

## Controls


## Dormer windows

- Dormer windows must be located and have a size, bulk and scale that do not dominate the roof form or add excessively to the building mass
- The configuration of dormer windows must satisfy the following:
- A maximum height from base to ridge of not more than 1.5m
- The highest point of a dormer must be situated below the ridge of the roof to which it is attached
- Dormers must be setback from the sides of the roof by a minimum of 500mm
- The front face of a dormer must be setback from the external face of the wall immediately below
- The base of a dormer must be positioned above the gutter of the roof in which it is situated.
- Dormers occurring in the same roof plane must be similarly sized, configured, and arranged symmetrically.
- Dormer windows may only be provided on buildings with an architectural character or style that is suitable for dormer features.
![page 35 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


*Figure 16: Dormer window configuration*

Source: Randwick City Council 2022

![page 35 img 2 (1384x761)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0035-eff1c518819c.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 36 -->

![page 36 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


*Figure 17: Positioning of dormer windows on the roof plane*

Source: Randwick City Council 2022


## Clerestory windows and skylights

- The location, size, configuration and layout of clerestory windows and skylights must be sympathetic to the overall design of the dwelling and the streetscape.

## Note

Clerestory windows are defined as a section of high-level windows, located above eye level, that are designed to admit natural light and fresh air. In a dwelling it may be in the form of a band of narrow windows along the top of a wall below the finished ceiling level.


## Mechanical equipment

- Any plant and equipment must be contained within the roof form or screened behind parapet walls, so that they are not readily visible from the public domain and surrounding properties.
![page 36 img 2 (1401x581)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0036-4220aa6a2cd9.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 37 -->


# 4.6. Colours, materials and finishes


## Objectives

- Ensure building colour schemes and material finishes pallets contribute to the articulation of the building and enhance the streetscape character
- Ensure surface materials and finishes are durable and fit for their purpose
- Retain or recycle existing sandstone block works as much as possible
- Reduce the urban heat island effect through material selection
- Ensure external building materials do not result in undesirable or uncomfortable glare to neighbouring properties and public spaces.

## Controls

- The development application must include a schedule detailing the proposed materials and finishes for a new dwelling, alteration or addition in the DA documentation. The selection of colour and material palette must complement the character and style of the building
- The exterior materials (such as wall cladding and roofing materials) of a building must be durable and non-reflective
- External surfaces must be of lighter coloured materials to reduce the impacts of the urban heat island effect
- The use of lighter coloured external materials must consider and mitigate undesirable or uncomfortable glare directed towards neighbouring properties
- Large expanses of rendered masonry must be avoided in street frontages and laneway elevations, except where they are required due to heritage considerations
- A combination of materials and finishes must be selected to articulate long sections of walls and create visual interest
- Select materials and details that are suitable for the local climatic conditions to properly withstand natural weathering, ageing and deterioration
- Sandstone blocks in existing buildings or fences on the site must be recycled and reused
- The extensive use of fixed panel grills, perforated metal, louvres, expanded mesh and the like, as the primary facade finish/material are to be avoided
- Box-like or monolithic forms, that present as large unarticulated cubes, are not supported, as they are institutional or industrial in character, and therefore unsuited to town centre or residential areas.

## Note

Also refer to controls under Part - B10 Foreshore Scenic Protection Areas (FSPA) for dwellings located in the defined coastal area.

![page 37 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 38 -->


# 4.7. Earthworks


## Objectives

- To maintain or minimise change to the natural ground levels, streetscape, and natural environment
- To ensure excavation and backfilling of a site does not result in unreasonable structural, visual, overshadowing and privacy impacts on the adjoining dwellings
- To provide usable private open space for dwellings with adequate gradient
- To ensure earthworks do not result in adverse stormwater impacts on adjoining properties
- To ensure earthworks do not impact upon the ability to achieve deep soil permeability surface areas and canopy tree planting
- To prevent the use of subterranean spaces as habitable areas.

## Definitions

RLEP Ground level (existing) is defined as the existing level of a site at any point

Ground level (natural) is defined as the pre-modified ground level, prior to any alteration, cutting or filling.


## Note

Excavation for basements associated with dwelling houses, dual occupancies, or semidetached dwellings is generally not encouraged. Council may consider basement excavation where:

- It is demonstrated that no reasonable alternative location exists on the site to accommodate parking and storage.
- The proposed works satisfies the objectives and controls of this Section and Part B8 Water Management of the Randwick DCP.
- Excavation does not add to the visual bulk and scale of the building

## Controls

- Any excavation for basements must have an area no greater than the space required to accommodate:
- A maximum of 1 car space for dwellings with up to 2 bedrooms
- A maximum of 2 car spaces for dwellings with 3 or more bedrooms
- A plant room consistent with control g) of this sub section
- The basement does not exceed 3m in depth and is wholly contained within the building footprint
- Any excavation and backfilling within the building footprint on a flat site must be limited to a maximum 1m at any point on the allotment, these requirements do not apply to swimming pool or spa pool structures
- For sites with a significant slope where the site gradient is too steep to reasonably construct a dwelling, a merit assessment may be undertaken considering:
- Site constraints
- Adverse impacts on adjoining properties
- Relevant geotechnical and stormwater management assessments
![page 38 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 39 -->

- For sites with a significant slope, adopt a split-level design for dwellings to minimise excavation and backfilling, and design dwellings to minimise the height and extent of any exposed under croft areas
- The outer edge of any excavation, piling or sub-surface walls must be setback a minimum of 900mm from the side and rear boundaries
- Any excavation undertaken to create subterranean spaces must not be used as habitable space
- The maximum area permitted for a plant room in any development is the minimum required to meet Australian Standards, accommodate typical dimensions of equipment required and the associated circulation space to access the equipment for maintenance. DA plans must show the approximate location and size of equipment within the plant room
- Retaining walls are to be stepped in response to the natural landform to avoid creating monolithic structures, particularly where visible from the neighbouring dwellings and the public domain
- Where it is necessary to construct retaining walls at less than 900mm from the side or rear boundary due to site conditions, retaining walls must be stepped to follow the topography of the land. Each stepping must not exceed a maximum height of 2.2m, as measured from the ground level (existing). In this case, the retaining walls may be incorporated as part of the boundary fence
- For sites that slope upwards to the rear with the dwelling elevated above street level, the surface area of any blank retaining walls fronting the street must be minimised. Use a combination of materials to create articulation, and/or incorporate landscaping to visually soften the wall structures
- Any cut and fill outside the building footprint (for the purposes of creating useable private open space) must not result in additional privacy and amenity impacts and shall consider boundary fencing heights and required retaining walls in response to changes.
- Cut and fill outside the building footprint shall take the form of terracing following the natural landform in order to minimise the height or depth of earthworks at any point on the site. The appropriate extent of site modification will be assessed on a merit basis.
![page 39 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


*Figure 18: Measures for minimising earthworks*

Source: Randwick City Council 2022

![page 39 img 2 (1461x575)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0039-1be2bfdf3ab2.png)


<!-- SRC: c1-low-density-residential.pdf | PAGE: 40 -->
