# 1. Introduction

This DCP section contains objectives and controls to assist in the assessment of late-night trading premises with particular regard to strengthening and diversifying the night time economy and maintaining residential amenity and public safety.

Randwick City's night time economy plays an important role in meeting the social and cultural needs of the community, while also contributing to the local economy and enhancing the vibrancy of our business centres.

Late night trading premises are an important part of the night time economy and comprise business, retail and entertainment uses which operate at night. These can include (but are not limited to) licensed and/or unlicensed establishments such as pubs, small bars, restaurants and cafes, take away food and drink premises and other such premises which provide late night services such as convenience stores, pharmacies and the like.

Proposals for late night trading premises must demonstrate commitment to good management and ensure that any adverse impacts are minimal and/or capable of being adequately managed.

The following provisions aim to provide greater certainty to the community and proponents of late-night trading premises in respect to appropriate trading hours and location. The provisions do not set out to curb or increase potential trading hours in a blanket fashion throughout Randwick City but rather allow opportunities for late night trading hours in suitable locations with appropriate management actions.

This section of the DCP should be read in conjunction with:

- Part A - Introduction
- Part B - General Controls
- Other sections of the DCP for specific development types, locations or sites, if relevant to the application.
To the extent of any inconsistency between this section and any other DCP sections, this section will prevail.

![page 4 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-ab9eb7eaef76.png)
![page 4 img 2 (3726x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-b083fe5bd589.png)
![page 4 img 3 (87x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-26f8ed734c74.png)


<!-- SRC: c8-night-time-economy.pdf | PAGE: 5 -->


# 2. Objectives, application, trading categories

The following objectives apply to this type of development:


# Objectives

- Strengthen, enhance and diversify the night time economy
- E ncourage a mix of night time uses that provide for the community's diverse s ocial, cultural and retail needs
- Identify appropriate locations and trading hours for late night trading premises
- Protect neighbourhood amenity and property, particularly residential and other sensitive land uses
- Minimise opportunities for anti-social behaviour and crime, through the responsible management of late-night trading premises and their surrounding environment
- Deliver certainty to applicants, operators, and the local community about the planning requirements regarding late night trading premises
- Ensure a consistent approach in the assessment of DAs for late night trading premises.

# Relationship to other documents

Development Applications (DA) for late night trading premises may also be subject to other Council plans, codes and policies. Applicants should check with Council to determine what other documents need to be considered when preparing a DA for a late-night trading premises such as documents relating to the NSW Government's Vibrancy reforms.


# Application

This DCP section applies to all DAs for new or existing late night trading premises that seek approval wholly or in part for:

- A change of use
- New, modified or extended trading hours
- Refurbishment, additions or extensions that are likely to result in an intensification of the current use
- An extension or renewal of trial trading hours or renewable conditions of consent.

## Note

For the purposes of above, an intensification of use includes an increase in:

- Patron capacity
- Amount of floor area.
![page 5 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-ab9eb7eaef76.png)
![page 5 img 2 (3034x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-49482f416610.png)
![page 5 img 3 (2910x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0005-6cc335907882.png)


<!-- SRC: c8-night-time-economy.pdf | PAGE: 6 -->


# Late night trading definition and categories

For the purposes of this DCP, late night trading premises are defined as any retail, business or entertainment use that operates at night. The DCP categorises these as High or Low Impact, as follows:


## High impact

- A pub
- A registered club
- Any premises with a capacity of more than 120 patrons where alcohol is sold and/or consumed on the premises (e.g. restaurant or café)
- Any premises used as a function centre or entertainment facility where alcohol is sold and/or consumed on the premises.

## Low impact

- Any premises with a capacity of 120 patrons or less where alcohol is sold and/or consumed on the premises (e.g. small bar, restaurant or café)
- Any other retail or business premises which operates after 10pm.

## Note

- Outdoor seating is included in the calculation of patron capacity
- High and Low Impact categories do not include sex services premises and restricted premises. See Part C9 Sex services premises for separate controls.
![page 6 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


<!-- SRC: c8-night-time-economy.pdf | PAGE: 7 -->


# 3. Development controls


# Explanation

All DAs for low and high impact late night trading premises must address several matters of consideration. This provides the basis for a consistent approach to determining suitability of proposals, appropriate hours of operation and maximum patron capacity.


# Objective

- Ensure that late night trading proposals are appropriate to the location in terms of nature and scale of operations
- Ensure late night trading applications address the NSW Vibrancy Guidelines:(November 2025).

# Controls

All DAs for late night trading premises must address the following matters:

- Specific nature of the proposal (e.g. pub, nightclub, restaurant etc)
- Proposed layout of the premises
- Current and proposed hours of operation
- Existing trading hours and nature of other late night trading premises operating within a 100m radius
- Current and proposed size of the premises and maximum patron capacity (including the maximum number of patrons that will be standing and/or sitting at the one time)
- Details on whether alcohol is to be sold and/or consumed on the premises and measures for responsible service
- Measures to minimise likely noise or other amenity impacts on adjoining properties
- The likely impact of the premises on the concentration of late night uses in the locality
- Details on any proposed entertainment and likely amenity impacts
- Suitability of the location and context of the proposal, including proximity to residential land uses and other sensitive land uses (e.g. schools, places of worship etc).
Table 1 is a guide to the range of hours of operation that may apply to DAs for late night trading premises in the Randwick City Council LGA. These hours of operation may only be granted following Council's consideration of the matters outlined above and, in those circumstances, where good management can be demonstrated and where adverse impacts on residential amenity and public safety are capable of being minimised.


## Note

Applicants should also refer to the NSW Vibrancy Guidelines: Late night hours of operation of food and drink premises (November 2025) when applying for additional hours of operation.

![page 7 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-ab9eb7eaef76.png)
![page 7 img 2 (2527x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0007-d5296441151a.png)

![page 8 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-ab9eb7eaef76.png)
![page 8 img 2 (84x99)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0008-928c277555dd.png)
![page 8 img 3 (1231x96)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0008-3a70364a1e62.png)


<!-- SRC: c8-night-time-economy.pdf | PAGE: 9 -->


# 4. Management plan


# Explanation

In addition to addressing the relevant development controls, all DAs for high impact late night trading premises must be accompanied by a Management Plan that specifies the operations and measures to be undertaken to ensure that the premises will be responsibly managed.

The purpose of a Management Plan is to ensure that applicants demonstrate an understanding of the local context and address any potential adverse impacts that may arise from the operation of the late-night trading premises. It also enables the Council to effectively assess any impacts of a proposal and forms a base for enforcement action if not suitably implemented. A Management Plan may not be required where it can be demonstrated that a proposal will not result in an intensification of a use.


# Objective

The objective for the management plan is to:

- Ensure that potential adverse impacts from the operation of high impact premises can be suitably addressed through appropriate management practices.

# Controls

- Submit a Management Plan with a DA (for the purposes noted in Section 2. Objectives, application, trading categories, subheading Application) for high impact late night trading premises that addresses the general requirements for Management Plans outlined in Part B9 of the DCP, as well as the following specific requirements:
- Onsite security arrangements including number of licensed security staff, details of any electronic surveillance systems and frequency and areas of security patrols inside and outside the premises
- Measures to minimise noise impacts from the use on residential and sensitive land uses
- Measures to manage large groups of patrons during peak trading periods (e.g. during weekends, special events, etc)
- Measures to assist patrons to wind down before closing (e.g. reducing music volume, increasing lighting levels inside the venue, etc). Provide a copy of the House Policy describing measures to minimise harm, anti-social behaviour and crime through the responsible service of alcohol (e.g. lock out times, etc)
- Measures to monitor and manage patron behaviour within and outside the premises including when entering and leaving the premises late at night
- If queuing outside the premises is to occur, a description of measures that will be taken to ensure that queuing is controlled to minimise adverse amenity impacts (e.g. maximum queue numbers, use of temporary ropes/bollards, actions to be undertaken to minimise loitering, etc)
- An Incident Register is to be always kept with the Management Plan
- Designated smoking areas and measures to increase patron awareness of the responsible disposal of cigarette butts
- Actions to be undertaken to discourage drug use and manage drug related incidents
![page 9 img 1 (60x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-ab9eb7eaef76.png)


<!-- SRC: c8-night-time-economy.pdf | PAGE: 10 -->

- Overview of the accessibility and frequency of public transport and taxis during late night trading hours
- Measures to increase patron awareness and use of public transport and taxis
- Measures to address other likely social impact because of the proposal (see note below)
- Outcomes of preliminary consultation between applicants and the NSW police.

## Note

- Information regarding the issuing of liquor licences should be directed towards the NSW Office of Liquor and Gaming.
- A Social Impact Assessment (SIA) is required for new or significant expansion of licensed premises. Council may also require a SIA for other types of late-night trading proposals as part of a merit assessment. Applicants are to contact Council to determine whether a SIA is required as part of the application. A SIA must address the following:
- Proposed liquor licence type
- Prevalence of proposed liquor license types within the suburb
- Comparative NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR) over the past 10 years for the LGA and suburb
- Community profile for the suburb
- Relevant academic research in alcohol, security, social impact of late-night trading and benefits.
- NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR) is the official source of NSW crime information. More information on statistics per Local Government Area can be found on BOCSAR
- Approvals for late night trading premises including hours of operation and/or patron capacity may be subject to a trial period of operation. This would allow the flexibility to monitor the ongoing management of a premises and its impact on residential amenity and public safety.
- Section 417 (imposition of conditions) of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979 permits the use of reviewable conditions by a Consent Authority to approve hours of operation and/or maximum persons permitted when it is uncertain about the impacts of the proposed development on adjoining land uses.

# 1. Introduction

This section contains objectives and controls describing Council's policy and criteria for the assessment of restricted and sex services premises. These development controls will ensure that premises are well located, designed and managed to avoid adverse impacts on the surrounding area and to maintain a high level of amenity (both inside and outside the premises).

This Part of the DCP should be read in conjunction with:

- Part A - Introduction
- Part B - General Controls
- Other parts of the DCP for specific development types, locations or sites, if relevant to the application.
The following documents should also be considered:

- The Work Health and Safety Act 2011 and the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2017 which sets requirements for health and safety at work and covers every place of work in NSW, including Sexual Services Premises (SSP)
- The NSW Health Department's Health and Hygiene Guidelines for Brothels and Adult Services.
![page 4 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 4 img 2 (1829x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-c593c5ca0f3e.png)
![page 4 img 3 (87x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-26f8ed734c74.png)
![page 4 img 4 (3376x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-90ed0dd08205.png)


<!-- SRC: c9-sex-services-premises.pdf | PAGE: 5 -->


# 2. Matters for consideration


# Explanation

Clause 6.15 - Location of sex services premises in the Randwick Local Environmental Plan (RLEP) provides for a reasonable separation between sex services premises and other sensitive land uses (residential and public recreation) and places regularly frequented by children. The purpose is to minimise land use conflicts and adverse amenity impacts, arising from the location and operation of these premises. These planning issues are to be addressed when submitting a Development Application (DA).


## Notes

In addition to the RLEP, the Restricted Premises Act 1943 provides the statutory framework for the control of sex services premises and restricted premises in NSW.

The NSW Land and Environment Court has developed a planning principle relating to brothels based on the case of Martyn v Hornsby Shire Council [2004] NSWLEC 614.


# Objectives

The objectives are to:

- Suitably locate restricted premises or sex services premises, to minimise impacts and to ensure appropriate hours of operation
- Ensure the design and operation of the premises are discreet, fit within the character of the streetscape and do not adversely impact on the amenity of the neighbourhood.

# Controls

- In employment zones, restricted premises and sex services premises are to be designed with separate entries to any other use and to minimise views from public areas into the premises
- Owners/operators are to consider the impact of the business on existing businesses in the area, the hours of operation, size and use of premises, access, car parking/traffic etc. associated with those premises
- Restricted premises and sex service premises are to be located above the ground floor level or street level of a building, away from shopfronts and arcades or thoroughfares of high pedestrian use. The entrance however should preferably be located at ground level on the primary frontage
- The external design and colour of the premises must be in keeping with the character and appearance of the streetscape, and not be a prominent feature in the street.
![page 5 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 5 img 2 (87x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-26f8ed734c74.png)


<!-- SRC: c9-sex-services-premises.pdf | PAGE: 6 -->


# 3. Privacy and noise


# Objectives

The objectives for privacy and noise are to:

- Ensure that the activities within the premises arising from its operation are not visible from the street or an adjoining property
- To minimise noise and vibration at the boundary of the premises.

# Controls

- A sex services premises must not give rise to:
- A sound level at any point on the boundary of the site greater than the background levels specified in AS 1055 Acoustics - Description and measurement of environmental noise
- ii) An 'offensive noise' as defined in the Protection of the Environment Operations Act 1997
- iii) The transmission of vibration to any place of different occupancy
- Premises should be designed, incorporate building materials and arrange room layouts to minimise noise transmission, and to provide privacy (internal and external) and to prevent activities being visible from outside the premises
- There is to be no display of restricted material, sex-related products, sex workers, performers or semi-dressed staff from windows or external doors, or public areas outside the premises
- Business spruikers for any restricted premises or sex services premises are not permitted.
![page 6 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 6 img 2 (3170x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0006-7e4bdcb0fc72.png)


<!-- SRC: c9-sex-services-premises.pdf | PAGE: 7 -->


# 4. Health and safety


# Objective

The objective for health and safety is to:

- Ensure that the design and operation of restricted premises and sex services premises maximise the comfort, safety and security of visitors/clients, staff, workers and the general public.

# Controls

- All DAs for sex services premises must comply with the requirements of the Public Health Act 2010 and the requirements of the New South Wales Health Department
- Provide internal reception/waiting areas (except for premises providing retail services) for visitors
- Design internal areas to minimise alcoves and entrapment spaces
- Provide suitable safety and surveillance systems (both internal and external) including adequate lighting of accessways and car parking areas
- Design entrances and exits to facilitate the privacy of staff and visitors without compromising personal safety
- Landscaping is not to obstruct visibility from public areas to exits and entrances for the safety of staff and visitors
- Premises are to be clearly numbered, so the number is visible from the street to prevent inadvertent visitors to private homes or businesses in the area
- For sex services premises of three or more rooms, all working rooms and staff areas are to be provided with intercoms and duress alarm systems linked to a central base and always monitored
- Storage spaces are to be provided for both soiled and clean linen, and safe sex equipment.
![page 7 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: c9-sex-services-premises.pdf | PAGE: 8 -->


# 5. Management plan


# Explanation

The safe and efficient operation of a sex services or a restricted premises should effectively minimise any adverse impacts on the amenity of a locality. The preparation of a Management Plan is required to set out clear procedures and responsibilities of owners and operators of premises. The plan is to be an active document (reviewed annually) and will assist business owners and operators, the community and Council in ensuring the suitable ongoing operation and oversight of the premises.


# Objectives

The objectives for the management plan are to:

- Minimise the potential for the operation of sex services or restricted premises to cause disturbance in the surrounding area
- Ensure the safe and adequate storage, handling and disposal of waste, appropriate cleaning procedures and the safety and health of staff and visitors.

# Controls

- A Management Plan is to be submitted for all DAs for new or expanded restricted or sex services premises that addresses the general requirements for Management Plans outlined in Part B9 of this DCP, and is also to address the following specific requirements:
- Procedures appropriate to the nature of the proposed activities; and procedures for where staff are placed under duress
- ii) How access can be provided when required by a client with a disability
- iii) Access arrangements for the attendance of health service providers
- iv) Procedures that support the health and health education needs of staff
- Demonstrate compliance with the SafeWork, Health and Safety Guidelines for Sex Services Premises in NSW.
![page 8 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)

# 1. Introduction

This DCP section applies to applications for new development, redevelopment, alterations, additions and changes of use in E4 General Industrial zoned land under Randwick LEP 2012 and IN1 General Industrial under the Transport and Infrastructure SEPP, that is located within the Randwick Local government area. Figure 1 shows the location of the two zones.

This section of the DCP should be read in conjunction with:

- Part A - Introduction
- Part B - General Controls which include B13 Noise management
- Other sections of the DCP for specific development types, locations or sites, if relevant to the application.
To the extent of any inconsistency between this section, and any other DCP sections, this section will prevail.


## Note

All development within Port Botany and the adjacent IN1 zone is covered by the Transport and Infrastructure SEPP 2021. Accordingly, Randwick LEP 2012 does not apply within these areas.


# 1.1. E4 General Industrial Zone

The NSW Government's Employment Zone reforms which came into effect in April 2023 introduced new zone structures to increase flexibility in the range of permissible land uses in the industrial zones and support employment growth across Sydney. Under the Randwick Local Environment Plan the IN2 Light Industrial zone was translated to E4 General Industrial.

As a result, this new E4 General Industrial zone permits the following additional land use types previously not permissible within the IN2 Light Industrial zone: freight transport facilities, general industries, industrial retail outlets and local distribution premises. Definitions for these land use types can be found in the Randwick LEP 2012 Dictionary https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/RLEP.


## Note

Hours of operation in the E4 zone are controlled under the Exempt and Complying Codes SEPP 2008 - Clause 2.46C of the SEPP permits 24-hour operations.


# 1.2. Delegated Authority for IN1 zoned Land

On 9 May 2025, the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure notified the Council that it had approved the delegation of the Department's planning authority functions relating to Development Control Plans (DCPs) to Council in accordance with Division 3.6 of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979.

This delegation applies to land within Randwick City Council that is subject to Chapter 5 of the State Environmental Planning Policy Transport and Infrastructure 2021 (old Three Ports SEPP). This delegated land is zoned General Industrial IN1 under the SEPP (purple shaded area in Figure 1 below). The delegation does not apply to the Lease Area, Special Activities Zone SP1 (shaded in yellow). This General Industrial IN1 zone within the Randwick LGA comprises 68.94 hectares. By comparison the area of General Industrial E4 zoned area under the Randwick Local Environment Plan 2012 is 12.78 hectares.

Council is the consent authority for land zoned General Industrial (IN1) zone under the Randwick LEP. While the IN1 zone facilitates a range of industrial and employment-generating uses, it is essential that new development is carefully designed and managed to minimise adverse impacts on surrounding land uses, particularly where industrial areas interface with residential zones and the public domain.

The inclusion of Part C10 of the DCP allows Council to apply more detailed non-statutory controls to complement the provisions of the LEP and relevant State Environmental Planning Policies. These controls provide a framework to ensure development applications appropriately address, assess and mitigate potential environmental impacts. In particular development within industrial zones must consider impacts relating to amenity, acoustic, traffic generation, access, parking, loading and unloading, light spill, water and air quality and stormwater management.


# 1.3. Industrial precincts

The industrial land located within the Randwick Local Government Area (LGA) comprises two distinct precincts, each of which exhibits a different urban structure, lot configuration and operational typology, supporting a diversity of industrial uses and business types. These two areas are illustrated in Figure 1.

## Perry Street Area

The Perry Street Area Zoned E4 zone - General Industrial is characterised by small and individual allotments accommodating a range of light industrial and service-based uses, including wholesale food distributors, building supplies, warehouses and distribution centres, and transport related activities that support the broader economy. The desired future character of the precinct is to retain and support a diverse range of small and medium sized tenancies (including strata developments) to ensure ongoing viability of smaller-scale industrial premises. The Matraville industrial precinct will continue to function as a strategically important employment area supporting the Eastern Suburbs and the broader metropolitan economy, particularly through its proximity to Port Botany, Sydney Airport and the arterial road network.

The precinct will consolidate its role as a modern, high - functioning industrial and urban services hub, accommodating a diverse mix of warehousing and logistics operations, light industrial and manufacturing uses, building and trade suppliers, and service-based industries that support the daily needs of the surrounding community.

Given the proximity of residential areas, careful management of the interface between the intensive port operations and sensitive land uses within the surrounding low density residential area is essential. Development should be designed and operated to minimise potential impacts.

Council has implemented a range of local traffic management measures to mitigate the impacts of industrial operations on adjoining residential areas. This includes the designation of Perry Street with a vehicular weight restriction of 3.4 tonnes, limiting access by heavy vehicles.

In addition, the existing traffic arrangement at the Perry Street and McCauley Street intersection incorporates a traffic island that physically restricts turning movements, effectively preventing heavy vehicles from accessing Perry Street.

These measures play an important role in reducing heavy vehicle traffic, improving residential amenity, and enhancing the safety and functionality of the local road network.


## The Botany Road/Military Road area

The Botany Road/Military Road area, zoned IN1 - General Industrial under the Transport and Infrastructure SEPP is characterised by medium to large lots. The desired future character of the precinct is to retain these large allotments that accommodate a range of established industrial and logistics uses. The desired future character of the precinct is to retain and reinforce this larger lot pattern to support the ongoing operation of industrial activities requiring significant floor space, site manoeuvrability and efficient access for freight and servicing. Subdivision that results in small or fragmented lots, including strata subdivision, is discouraged where it would compromise the capacity of the precinct to accommodate larger-scale and port-related industrial uses.


## Port Botany Area

The Port Botany area, zoned SP1 - Special Activities under the State Environmental Planning Policy (Transport and Infrastructure), is a strategic industrial precinct of State significance that supports port operations and associated industries.

The desired future character of the precinct is to maintain and protect land for port and portrelated uses that require large allotments, high-capacity infrastructure, and direct access to major road and rail freight networks. Development within this area must ensure the ongoing efficiency and operational capacity of the port, while avoiding land fragmentation or incompatible uses that may constrain its long-term function.

## Notes

Port Botany

Port Botany is one of Australia's most critical gateways and plays an important role in the NSW economy, contributing $10.7 billion to NSW Gross State Product annually. The port is the second largest container port in Australia and container volumes are forecast to more than triple by 2056. It is estimated that 42% of all goods in a Sydney household are imported in containers through Port Botany. The port manages around onethird of the nation's container volumes and a significant portion of the state's fue l supply.

Port Botany Landside Improvement Strategy 2023


## Objectives

The objectives for this DCP chapter are to:

- Retain and protect the industrial zoned land within the Matraville area to meet the current and future industrial, urban services and employment needs of the Randwick LGA
- Ensure land use compatibility and efficiency by retaining small allotments within the Perry St Area to support small-scale and local industrial businesses and maintaining larger allotments within the Botany Rd/Military Rd and Port Botany areas to accommodate large-scale, logistics and port-related industrial activities
- Encourage light industrial and low impact employment uses in locations adjoining residential areas having regard to noise, traffic generation, hours of operation and environmental performance
- Facilitate industrial development that provides a range of goods and services and employment opportunities, while ensuring the amenity, health and safety of the nearby residential areas are not adversely affected
- Ensure industrial development is well-designed with a high quality streetscape presentation, and operates to minimise adverse impacts on land, water and the environment including through appropriate stormwater management, waste handling and emissions control
- Ensure that new industrial development does not increase the cumulative risk of industrial activities or introduce unacceptable risks including those associated with hazardous materials, heavy vehicle movements noise and vibration
- Allow compatible, small-scale non-industrial uses which support the daily needs of workers within the industrial areas, where they do not compromise the primary industrial function of the land
- Maintain the primacy of industrial activities by ensuring that commercial and office uses, including standalone offices, are only permitted where they are subordinate and directly related to an associated industrial use
- Support existing and encourage new artisan food and drink production, distribution and urban service uses that contribute to the local economy and service the Eastern Suburbs region, where these are compatible with the surrounding land use context.

## Notes

The National Heavy Vehicle Regulator NHVR manages road access and permits for heavy vehicle journeys. It was formed through an agreement between the Australian, New South Wales, Queensland, Victorian, South Australian, Tasmanian and Australian Capital Territory governments. The Heavy Vehicle National Law (HVNL) came into effect in New South Wales in 2014. The NHVR work directly with road managers - state and territory road authorities and local government - to coordinate the application process and issue permits.

They manage access and permits for restricted vehicles including B double Trucks and articulated vehicles.

See the National Heavy Vehicle Regulator National Network Map for approved routes.

Large, restricted access vehicles including B doubles and articulated vehicles must utilise approved B Double approved routes.

# 2. Development Adjoining Residential Zones


## Objectives

The objective for industrial development adjoining residential zones is to:

- Ensure industrial development does not unreasonably impact upon adjoining residential areas in terms of amenity, health and safety.

## Controls

- Development must be sympathetic to the height, scale, siting and character of existing adjoining and/or nearby residential development
- Development must be designed to maintain solar access to the windows of habitable rooms and to the majority of private open space of adjoining residential properties must be substantially maintained or achieved for a minimum period of 3 hours between 9.00am and 3.00pm at the winter solstice (June 22)
- Windows facing residential areas must be treated to avoid overlooking of private open space or private windows
- All mechanical plant and equipment (including air conditioning units, compressors, generators, and similar infrastructure) must be located away from adjoining or nearby residential properties
- Where equipment cannot be fully separated from sensitive land uses, appropriate acoustic insulation and visual screening must be provided
- Development proposing plant or equipment operating outside the hours of 7.00am to 10.00pm must be supported by an Acoustic Report prepared by a suitably qualified acoustic consultant, demonstrating compliance with relevant NSW noise criteria and that impacts on nearby residential receivers are minimised
- Development must be designed and operated to avoid causing nuisance or amenity impacts to surrounding residential areas, including those arising from operating hours, vehicle movements, loading and unloading, parking, headlight glare, external and security lighting.

## Notes:

Reference should also be made to the Industrial Noise Policy (NSW EPA, 1999) which aims to balance the need for industrial activity with the desire for quiet in the community. Noise emissions are to comply with this policy.

# 3. Building design


## Explanation

Good building design and appearance can ensure a high level of amenity and enhance the attractiveness of the streetscape. Through high aesthetic standards, industrial buildings can be designed to provide and maintain a suitable level of visual, acoustic and environmental quality.


## Objectives

The objectives for building design are to:

- Ensure the form and scale of development enhances the streetscape and visual quality of the area
- Achieve high quality, innovative and sustainable design for industrial buildings
- Utilise materials and construction methods to mitigate noise and visual impact to adjoining areas, particularly residential areas.

## Controls

- Building mass and scale should make a positive contribution to the streetscape and compliment the predominant character of the adjoining area
- Building form is to provide visual interest through an articulated façade, such as
- projecting wall elements, shading devices and a variation in texture / finishes / materials
- Building entries should be clear with windows facing the street
- Avoid bulky roof forms or extensive blank facades in a single material or colour, particularly when visible from the public domain
- Roof design must be incorporated in the overall building design
- Any metal roof sheeting should be pre-painted (e.g. Colourbond) to limit the level of reflection and glare
- Building entrances should be clearly defined, well-articulated a through form, materials and colour
- Provide level or ramp access to entrances and waiting areas
- Visible light reflectivity from building materials used on the facades of new buildings should not exceed 20%. The use of non-reflective glass should also be considered
- To promote casual surveillance, office components of an industrial development should be located at the front of the property with windows and entrances facing the street, with the warehousing or industrial use set behind
- Buildings should maximise energy efficiency, through measures such as the use of high efficiency lighting systems, insulation, natural ventilation and lighting, and low embodied energy materials (see ecologically sustainable development (ESD) requirements in Part B4 of this DCP)
![page 10 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: c10-industrial-areas.pdf | PAGE: 11 -->

- Open storage areas shall not be visible from any public place and be clearly defined on plan in the development application.

# 4. Setbacks


# Explanation

This section applies to new buildings only. Building setbacks play an important role in industrial zones by establishing a consistent streetscape, providing space for landscaping, and reducing the visual bulk and scale of development. Front setbacks contribute to the overall character, reinforce the public domain and presentation of industrial streets, ensures space for landscaping, contributes to streetscape consistency, and mitigates the bulk and scale of industrial development. Side Setbacks also provide separation and a transitional area and act as a buffer to adjoining land uses, particularly where sensitive interfaces occur.


# Objectives

The objectives for setbacks are to:

- Minimise the adverse impacts of industrial development on adjoining land uses including noise, air quality and odour by providing building separation and buffering
- Ensure development that responds to and reinforces the streetscape character and ensures a positive well-presented and functional streetscape environment.

# Controls

- The front setback of an industrial building must respond to the dominant street setback. Where there is no clear dominant setback or for sites with large frontages, the front setbacks will be determined on merit, having regard to the desired streetscape character and function
- Front setbacks must be landscaped to provide a high-quality streetscape. Front setbacks must not to be used for storage or display of goods, excessive signage, loading/unloading areas and large areas of car parking
- Where the development adjoins non-industrial uses, a minimum side and/or rear setback of 5m must be provided to provide adequate separation and buffering to
- In all other cases, a minimum side and rear setback of 4m is required
- No buildings, structures, car parking, storage or vehicle manoeuvring areas are permitted within a minimum 6m wide setback area adjoining the Sydney Water heritage listed Bunnerong canal
- Setbacks must be designed to maximise the retention and protection of existing trees and their root systems. Variations to setback dimensions may be considered where this would result in improved tree retention outcomes
Landscaping setbacks must be free from overhangs, hardstand elements such as ramps and driveways and paved areas, except where minor pedestrian access paths are required.

The minimum setback requirements are summarised in the table below:

![page 12 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: c10-industrial-areas.pdf | PAGE: 13 -->

| Boundary                            | Landscape Setback (minimum)   | Building Setback (minimum)   |
|-------------------------------------|-------------------------------|------------------------------|
| Frontage to a classified road       | 4 metres                      | 9 metres                     |
| Frontage to a local road            | 3 metres                      | 9 metres                     |
| Side boundary - residential use     | 5 metres                      | 5 metres                     |
| Side boundary - non-residential use | 4 metres                      | 4 metres                     |
| Rear boundary - residential use     | 5 metres                      | 5 metres                     |
| Rear boundary - any other use       | 4 metres                      | 4 metres                     |
| Canal boundary                      | 6 metres                      | 10 metres                    |


## Note

Bunnerong Stormwater Channel No 11 Sydney Water Heritage Item 4570016

The Bunnerong stormwater drainage canal is listed as a local heritage item under the Sydney Water heritage register (s.170 NSW Heritage Act).

The Bunnerong Stormwater drainage system is of historical significance as it was constructed predominantly by the Public Works Department between 1930-1935 as part of the Depression-era Unemployment Relief Program. The project was funded through the Prevention and Relief of Unemployment Act 1930.

The Bunnerong Stormwater Channel originally drained an area of 674.6 hectares and was one of many channels authorised to improve drainage across Sydney. It is a representative example of Sydney Water's stormwater channels from this period and is substantia lly intact.

The system's operational curtilage covers its bed, walls, and coping, while its visual curtilage varies with surrounding land uses.

https://www.hms.heritage.nsw.gov.au/App/Item/SearchHeritageItems

# 5. Landscaping


## Explanation

Well designed landscaped areas can enhance the visual quality and environmental performance of a development contributing to an attractive and sustainable industrial environment. Landscaping improves the amenity of workplaces for employees and visitors and plays an important role in defining the character of industrial areas. Landscaping also provides effective buffering between industrial development and surrounding land uses and assists in screening and softening the visual impact of industrial buildings, structures and signage particularly where large-scale built form is involved (see Figure 3 below).


## Objectives

The objectives for landscaping are to:

- Improve the environmental and visual amenity of industrial areas
- Integrate building design, car parking and service facilities with landscaping
- Ensure the provision of accessible and useable open space for the use of employees
- Encourage the planting of indigenous, native and low water consuming plants and trees
- Assist stormwater management by maximising permeable areas.

## Controls

- A minimum of 10% of the development site must be provided as landscaped area
- Landscaping must be planned and designed to improve the environmental and visual amenity of industrial areas including the provision of shade, screening, and urban greening
- Building design, car parking and service facilities must be integrated with landscaping
- Ensure the provision of accessible and useable open space for the use of employees
- For sites in excess of 1,000m², an outdoor staff recreation area must be provided with a minimum area of 16m², with a minimum dimension of 3 metres in any direction
- A minimum of 60% of the plantings must comprise indigenous native species as specified in Appendix B4, complemented by drought-tolerant and low water-use plantings
- To assist stormwater management development must comprise hard stand and nonporous surfaces must be minimised Development must incorporate permeable paving, deep soil zones, and other water-sensitive urban design (WSUD) measures to assist stormwater infiltration, reduce runoff, and improve water quality.

# 6. Parking and access


## Explanation

Car parking, access and loading/servicing areas often occupy a substantial proportion of industrial sites. This subsection provides objectives and controls to guide their efficient, functional and well-designed and layout while minimising impacts on site amenity and the surrounding area.


## Objectives

The objectives for parking and access are to:

- Ensure safe and efficient vehicle movements in and out of an industrial development including clear and legible circulation within the site
- Provide sufficient on-site parking to meet operational needs, without adversely impacting the function or amenity of surrounding streets
- Achieve well-designed, safe and functional car parking and circulation areas that contribute to orderly development and safe site layout
- Ensure loading/unloading areas are adequate, accessible and appropriately located, and designed to minimise impacts on adjacent land uses including residential areas
- Provide safe and convenient cyclist and pedestrian access including separation from heavy vehicle movements and service areas.

## Controls

- All vehicles must enter and leave the site in a forward direction
- Vehicle movements within servicing areas must minimise reversing movements. Where reversing is unavoidable development must demonstrate design measures that maximise safety and minimise operational noise impacts including the need for reversing vehicle alarms/beepers
- Where an alternative road access is available, loading and unloading facilities and the majority of car parking must be located along secondary road frontage
- Loading, unloading and services areas must be clearly separated from car parking areas and designed to ensure safe and efficient operation
- Service areas including waste and recycling areas and external storage areas must be located away from primary street frontages and screened from public view
- All loading and unloading operations must occur wholly within the site at all times
- Loading docks, car parking spaces and access driveways must be kept clear and available for their intended use at all times. These areas must be clearly line marked and must not be used for the storage of goods, materials and waste materials.

- Parking rates should be provided in accordance with B7 Transport, Traffic, Parking and Access section of this DCP.
- Traffic Impact Assessments should be completed in accordance with Guide to Transport Impact Assessment (GTIA), TS 00085 v1.1 - published September 23, 2024; effective November 4, 2024.

# 7. Lighting


## Explanation

Lighting is an essential component of industrial development, contributing to safety, security and site functionality. However, if not appropriately designed and managed, lighting can result in adverse impacts on surrounding land uses, including glare, light spill and intrusion into adjoining properties and the public domain.

Lighting must be carefully designed, located and controlled to minimise impacts on nearby development, particularly residential areas and road users. This includes directing light downward, avoiding unnecessary illumination, and incorporating shielding or other design measures to contain light within the site.

Appropriate lighting design ensures adequate illumination for operational and safety purposes, while maintaining the amenity of adjoining land and the surrounding area.


## Notes

- Lighting should also address the principles of Crime Prevention through Environmental Design (CPTED) to ensure safety and security in industrial areas.
- AS/NZS 2293 Series: These standards outline the requirements for emergency lighting and exit signs, ensuring that buildings have adequate illumination during emergencies to facilitate safe evacuation.

## Objectives

The objectives for lighting are to:

- Provide adequate illumination for safety, security and operational requirements within industrial sites
- Ensure external lighting contributes positively to the visual quality of the development and does not adversely affect the amenity of the locality
- Minimise light spill, glare, and sky glow through appropriate design, orientation, and control of lighting systems.

## Controls

- External lighting must be designed and installed to ensure that light sources are directed away from adjoining properties, particularly residential uses and other sensitive receivers
- Lighting must be designed and located to minimise light spill, glare and reflection beyond the site boundary, and must not result in a nuisance to surrounding properties or the public domain
- All external lighting must be shielded, baffled or otherwise designed to prevent upward light spill and unnecessary sky glow
![page 18 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: c10-industrial-areas.pdf | PAGE: 19 -->

- Lighting levels must be appropriate to the intended use of the area and avoid overillumination, particularly in areas adjoining residential zones
- Security and operational lighting must be controlled by timers, motion sensors or similar devices, where appropriate, to minimise unnecessary illumination outside of operational hours
- Development adjacent to residential areas must submit a lighting plan prepared by a suitably qualified professional, demonstrating that lighting impacts are appropriately mitigated.
![page 19 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: c10-industrial-areas.pdf | PAGE: 20 -->


# 8. Water quality


# Explanation

The effective management of stormwater runoff is important to protect the quality Randwick City's natural waterways and receiving environment. Uncontrolled stormwater can transport pollutants, sediments and contaminants from development sites into the drainage network, adversely impacting aquatic ecosystems and environmental health.

Development must incorporate appropriate stormwater management measures to minimise runoff impacts, improve water quality, and support the longterm protection of the City's natural and built water systems.


# Objectives

The objectives for stormwater and water quality are to:

- Manage stormwater quality and quantity and minimise stormwater discharge on adjoining properties
- Minimise surface water runoff through appropriate and integrated site design and water sensitive management measures
- Protect ground water from contamination associated with industrial development
- Encourage on site stormwater collection, treatment and reuse and promote water sensitive urban design (WSUD)
- Maintain natural drainage patterns and minimise unnecessary site disturbance and modification
- To minimise the risk and impact of flooding on development and surrounding land.

# Controls

- Disturbance to the existing drainage pattern should be minimised where possible
- Applicants should demonstrate adequate measures during construction to ensure that erosion/sedimentation during construction is minimised. Revegetation and soil stabilisation measures are to be implemented promptly upon completion of construction
- Development is to a ddress all requirements in Council's Private Stormwater Code
- An emergency stormwater shut-off valve must be installed on all stormwater system outlets discharging to Council infrastructure, natural waterways, or drainage reserves. The valve must be:
- Manually or automatically operable
- Located in an accessible position for emergency response personnel
- Capable of fully stopping the flow of stormwater during pollution events, spillages, or maintenance works
- Have signage indicating the valve location and operation located adjacent to the control point.
![page 20 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 20 img 2 (1191x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0020-1270f3815629.png)
![page 20 img 3 (1448x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0020-e3bed48bab35.png)
![page 20 img 4 (2448x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0020-f0835cf4a8ba.png)


<!-- SRC: c10-industrial-areas.pdf | PAGE: 21 -->


## Notes

A stormwater shut-off valve is a device installed in a stormwater drainage system to control or prevent the flow of stormwater in certain situations. These valves are typically used to:

Prevent flooding : By shutting off stormwater flow during heavy rains or floods, the valve helps control water levels in drainage systems and prevents overflow into vulnerable areas.

Environmental protection : They can stop stormwater contaminated with pollutants (like oil or chemicals from industrial sites) from entering stormwater systems that drain to Botany Bay.

Emergency situations : Shut-off valves are used in emergencies, such as fires, chemical spills, where it's critical to block stormwater to prevent contamination of stormwater and Botany Bay.

These valves can be manually operated or automatically activated based on certain conditions, such as water levels or the detection of pollutants.AS/NZS 2293 Series: These standards outline the requirements for emergency lighting and exit signs, ensuring that buildings have adequate illumination during emergencies to facilitate safe evacuation.

# 9. Waste management


## Objectives

The objectives for waste management are to:

- Minimise waste generation and to promote the principles of ecological sustainable development (ESD) including waste avoidance, reuse and recycling
- Facilitate efficient source separation and ensure waste management systems are appropriately designed to integrate with Council and private waste collection and management services
- Ensure waste storage, handling and collection arrangements do not adversely impact the amenity, health or safety of occupants, adjoining properties or the public domain.

## Controls

- Development involving demolition, construction or ongoing use must be accompanied by a Waste Management Plan prepared in accordance with Council requirements
- Development must provide sufficient space for the purposes of on-site separation, storage and handling of recyclables. Waste storage areas must be designated to minimise impacts particularly on nearby residential areas
- For multi-use and industrial units, allocated areas for waste storage and recycling must be provided for each individual industrial tenancy
- The waste storage and recycling area must be easily accessible for occupants, designed to allow safe and efficient access for collection vehicles and be clearly signposted
- Trade/commercial waste materials must not be disposed via Council's domestic waste collection service and must be managed by an appropriate licensed waste contractor
- Waste collection and servicing must be undertaken in a manner that does not adversely impact traffic flow, pedestrian safety, or the amenity of adjoining properties.

## Notes

Waste management and recycling processes of commercial and industrial facilities should be guided by the Waste Management and Recycling in Commercial and Industrial Facilities - Better Practice Guidelines (EPA, 2012).

This guide provides advice on how to incorporate better waste management practice into the design, establishment, operation and ongoing management of waste services in commercial and industrial development

https://www.epa.nsw.gov.au/publications/managewaste/120960-comm-ind

# 10. Amenity and Operation

Council acknowledges that the operation of businesses is not static and needs to evolve over time in response to changing market conditions, technologies and operational requirements. It is therefore important that the configuration, siting and management of activities are carefully considered to minimise operational impacts on adjoining properties in particular residential uses.

This section supports a flexible and performance-based approach to managing industrial operations, ensuring that potential impacts are appropriately mitigated both at the time of development and throughout the life of the use


## Objectives

The objective for amenity and operation is to:

- Enable Council to assess the ongoing management performance of industrial premises
- Provide flexibility to review conditions of development consents to respond to changes in operational management over time
- Mitigate and manage potential adverse impacts arising from changes in business operations - whether proposed or existing industrial development - on the amenity, privacy, air quality, odour, and overshadowing of adjoining or nearby residential properties.

## Controls

- A Plan of Management (POM) prepared by a relevant professional expert must be provided to Council prior to occupation
- This POM must ensure all relevant operations of the premises are documented, and their potential impacts appropriately managed having regard to the having regard to the nature of the use, site constraints, and local context
- The POM must document all operational aspects of the premises and establish measurable management actions and performance outcomes
- As a minimum the following must be included:
- Title and site identification details
- Objectives of the Plan of Management
- Operational details
- Hours of operation, including hours of deliveries
- After hours or emergency contact
- Staffing details
- Guidelines for staff for using the site facilities and equipment
- Deliveries and loading/unloading
- Waste management operation to prevent stormwater pollution and avoid odour
- Traffic movements including vehicle access, routing and manoeuvring
![page 23 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 23 img 2 (175x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0023-b2b889c27ff0.png)
![page 23 img 3 (173x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0023-cc62aad42f81.png)


<!-- SRC: c10-industrial-areas.pdf | PAGE: 24 -->

- Use and management of parking areas
- Managing customers or patrons
- Security details
- Noise Impact Assessment and mitigation measures
- Odour Impact Assessment and mitigation measures
- Complaint recording and response handling procedures
- Monitoring, reporting and review mechanisms to ensure the ongoing effectiveness and continuous improvement of the PoM improvement the PoM.

## Notes

The POM allows Council to exercise control over the ongoing operation of a premises by requiring, as a condition of consent, that the premises operate in accordance with the POM. A condition of consent may require that a POM be regularly revised and submitted to Council.

![page 24 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)

# 11. Fencing


## Explanation

Fencing is often an integral part of industrial development in delineating areas and boundaries and for security purposes. Fencing location, style and height should be integrated with the building form, be unobtrusive and relate to the character of the streetscape. Poorly designed fences can be visually intrusive and dominant in the streetscape and can reduce opportunities for neighbourhood surveillance and social interaction.


## Objectives

The objectives for fencing are to:

- Integrate fencing design and layout with the building entry
- Provide a positive presentation to the streetscape
- Provide site security and passive surveillance to the public domain.

## Controls

- Solid metal panel fences (sheet material etc) of any height are not permitted along the street frontage
- All fencing along the street frontage is required to be permeable metal palisade or picket finishing - dark colours are preferable. Maximum height allowed is 1.8m on street frontages
- For security purposes, taller fencing may be considered forward of the building line (but this fencing must be behind the front landscape strip)
- Fencing should not obscure the main building entry
- If the side or rear boundary adjoins a residential property, provide a timber paling/colorbond fence (commencing at the front of the building line). A maximum 2.2m height will be considered along the common property boundary between an industrial site and an abutting residential property
- Noise walls can be utilised/substituted as boundary fencing where required (see Noise Management Part B13 of this DCP for more information on noise walls).
![page 25 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 25 img 2 (87x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-26f8ed734c74.png)


<!-- SRC: c10-industrial-areas.pdf | PAGE: 26 -->


# 12. Public utilities/infrastructure


## Explanation

For new industrial development, Council requires the undergrounding of electricity connection to buildings to reduce the visual impact of overhead cables.


## Objectives

The objectives for public utilities are to:

- Minimise the visual impact of overhead electricity cables in industrial areas
- Promote common trenching for the provision of services and utilities.

## Controls

- New industrial developments must have an underground service line to a suitable existing street pole; or sheathed underground consumers mains to a customer pole erected near the front property boundary (within 1 metre)
- Bundling of cables in the area surrounding the development may also be required to reduce the visual impact of overhead street cables
- The common trenching of underground power, telecommunications and other services is encouraged.

## Note

For further details see Energy Australia for their requirements.

![page 26 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)


<!-- SRC: c10-industrial-areas.pdf | PAGE: 27 -->


# 13. Signage


## Explanation

Advertising and adequate opportunities for the display of goods and services in industrial areas is important for businesses, however there is a need to ensure this does not detract from the streetscape.


## Note:

Additional signage requirements can be found in B12 Outdoor Advertising and Signage.


## Objectives

The objectives for signage are to:

- Ensure signage and advertising is compatible with the architectural design of industrial buildings
- Minimise visual clutter and protect and improve the visual quality of the streetscape and the public domain
- Prevent excessive and obtrusive signage.

## Controls

- All premises are to provide clear and legible signage, including addresses, for each business
- All signage on the buildings is to be contained within the bounds of the building structure. No sign is to project out from walls or above the roof line
- Signs on multiple tenancies are to be located in the same place on each tenancy
- Stand-alone signs are to be wholly located within the property boundary
- Illuminated and flash signage that incorporates flashing lights or illuminated features is discouraged.

# 1. Introduction

Randwick City is located in proximity to Sydney's Kingsford Smith Airport, a major aviation hub that generates aircraft noise across surrounding suburbs, including Randwick City. To manage and forecast the impact of aviation activity, the airport publishes an 'Australian Noise Exposure Forecast' (ANEF) which models the projected noise levels and flight frequency over a 20-year horizon. These forecasts are represented as noise exposure contours on maps periodically updated by Airservices Australia.

The 2045 ANEF contours identify areas within Randwick City Council where development must incorporate appropriate noise attenuation measures to ensure residential amenity and compliance with relevant standards.

In addition to managing noise impacts, the safe and efficient operation of Sydney Airport requires that new development respects prescribed height limits. These limits are defined by the Obstacle Limitation Surface (OLS) and the Procedures for Air Navigation Systems Operations Surface (PANS-OPS) surfaces, which are prepared by airport operators and endorsed by the Commonwealth Government. Development proposals within affected areas must demonstrate compliance with these aviation safety requirements.

This section of the DCP should be read in conjunction with:

- Part A - Introduction
- Part B - General Controls
- Other sections of the DCP for specific development types, locations or sites, if relevant to the application.

## Objectives

- Minimise the impact of aircraft noise on residential amenity
- Ensure development does not compromise the safe operation of Sydney airport
- Maintain compliance with Commonwealth-endorsed aviation safety surfaces including OLS and PANS-OPS which limit height of structures and cranes (including external lighting)
- Promote sustainable building design that incorporates effective acoustic treatment in areas affected by the operation of Sydney's Kingsford Smith Airport
- Prevent lighting hazards that may interfere with aircraft operations
- Ensure external lighting complies with aviation safety standards.

# 1.1 Legislation and regulatory framework


## Airports Act 1996

The Airports Act 1996 establishes a system for regulating airports and the requirements to create masterplans and environmental standards.


## Civil Aviation Regulations 1988

The Civil Aviation Regulations 1988 establishes standards and regulations for air navigation in Australia to ensure compliance with technical and safety requirements.


## Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998

The Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1988 harmonises aviation safety law and provides administrative provisions for the regulation of civil aviation, including the delegation of powers to the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) and the issuing of Manuals of Standards.

![page 4 img 1 (58x68)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0002-812ca5a4f66a.png)
![page 4 img 2 (1079x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-3fcd452fbfa5.png)
![page 4 img 3 (1117x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-bda9a68e004b.png)
![page 4 img 4 (980x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-11f5dc74450a.png)
![page 4 img 5 (2685x103)](images/randwick-dcp-2025/p0004-1696bb339258.png)


<!-- SRC: c11-sydney-airport.pdf | PAGE: 5 -->

Part 139 (Aerodromes) Manual of Standards 2019

The Part 139 MOS establishes standards and obligations for the operation of aerodromes in Australia.


# 1.2 Prescribed airspace

To ensure the safe operation of the airport, limits on the heights of buildings are prescribed along flight paths. These restricted areas are known as prescribed airspace.

In Randwick City, development proposals (including temporary buildings or structures) with a height of 15.24m AHD or greater must be referred to the Sydney Airport Corporation Limited (SACL) for approval in accordance with Clause 6.8 of RLEP. Any SACL approved height includes lift over-runs, chimneys, aerials, antennas, etc.

A separate approval from SACL is also required to operate construction equipment (such as cranes used for the construction of buildings), prior to the commencement of works.


## Note

- In relation to short term temporary buildings or structures, an application must be made to Sydney Airport at least 28 days before commencement of the activity.
- Additional information and charts showing the current prescribed airspace can be downloaded at the Airspace Protection page at the Sydney Airport website.
- Refer also to the National Airports Safeguarding Framework for relevant guidelines.
- Refer to Clause 6.8 Airport operations of RLEP 2012.

# 2. Aircraft noise

All development located on land near or within an ANEF contour of 20 or greater that Council considers is likely to be adversely affected by aircraft noise must comply with Clause 6.9 of the RLEP.

Parts of Randwick City Council fall within the 20 ANEF 2045 contour. Development proposals in these areas, which involve the creation of additional dwellings or substantial alterations to existing residential buildings, are encouraged to submit a Pre-Lodgement Application to Council. This is to ensure that potential noise issues are identified early and that relevant mitigation

measures are appropriately addressed in the DA.


## Note

The Sydney Airport Master Plan 2039 includes an Australian Noise Exposure Forecast for 2039 (ANEF 2039), as shown in Chapter 16 (Map 29) and Appendix G (Map 33). On 26 February 2026, Airservices Australia endorsed for technical accuracy the new Australian Noise Exposure Forecast for 2045 for Sydney Airport (ANEF 2045) which has replaced ANEF 2039. A copy of ANEF 2045 can be downloaded at: 13836g131c SYD 2045 ANEF Endorsement Chart.

The Sydney Airport Master Plan 2039 is scheduled to be replaced by the Sydney Airport Master Plan 2045. Information about the current state of the draft Master Plan 2045 can be found at Sydney Airport Master Plan 2045 | Preliminary Draft (Sept 2025).

## Note

All development within an ANEF affected area (including ANEF contour 20) must comply with Australian Standard AS 2021-2015.


## Note

Refer also to the National Airports Safeguarding Framework for relevant guidelines (National Airports Safeguarding Framework | Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications and the Arts)


# 3. Lighting hazards

The Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) has the authority, under the Civil Aviation Regulations 1988 and the Airports Act 1996, to control ground lights that may cause confusion or distraction to pilots due to glare. To assist lighting designers and installation contractors near airports, CASA has established guidelines on the location and permitted intensities of ground lights within a six-kilometre radius around an airport, as outlined in the Manual of Standards 2019 - Part 139 (Aerodromes).

This area is divided into four lighting zones (Zones A, B, C, and D), reflecting the degree of interference ground lights can cause as pilots approach landing. External advertising, sports field floodlighting, and street lighting are some of the more likely sources requiring consideration. Parts of Randwick and Kingsford fall within Zone D.

The Manual of Standards 2019 - Part 139 (Aerodromes) requires Sydney Airport to notify CASA in writing if they become aware of any installation, equipment, or laser outside the aerodrome boundary that has or may have lighting intensity greater than specified. CASA may issue a notice to an owner or person in charge of a non-compliant light, directing them to extinguish or screen the light and refrain from exhibiting similar lights in the future.


## Note

The Sydney Airport Masterplan provides a Restricted Lighting map to assist in identifying the covered areas.


## Note

Refer also to the National Airports Safeguarding Framework for relevant guidelines (National Airports Safeguarding Framework | Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications and the Arts)

# 4. Controls


# 4.1 Prescribed airspace


## Controls

- Development applications must include accurate and detailed drawings indicating the height levels (above AHD) of all roof elements including parapet, lift overruns, roof ridges and roof-mounted structures for referral to SACL
- Landscaping must consider bird and obstacle hazard management and ensure trees to be planted are not capable of intruding the Obstacle Limitation Surface when mature (i.e. over 15 metres)
- Details of any cranes or temporary structures proposed during construction must be submitted to SACL, including maximum operating height above AHD.

## Note

Part 12 of the Airports Act defines buildings and structures (such as cranes and concrete pumps) that intrude into prescribed airspace as a 'controlled activity. Details of any potential controlled activities, including the type and anticipated timing of the controlled activity, must be identified and assessed to ensure it does not adversely impact on the safety, efficiency or regularity of air transport operations into and out of Sydney Airport. Further information is available via the following link: https://www.infrastructure.gov.au/infrastructure-transportvehicles/aviation/aviation-safety/aviation-environmental-issues/protection-airspace


# 4.2 Noise


## Controls

- Development within areas affected by ANEF contours must incorporate suitable noise attenuation measures recommended by a qualified acoustic consultant
- Acoustic treatments should support sustainable design principles, maintaining reasonable internal amenity and avoid adverse impacts on the building's architectural quality or surrounding streetscape.

# 4.3 Lighting


## Controls

- Development applications must include detailed drawings indicating any proposed external lighting installations for referral to SACL
- Landscaping and lighting design must consider aviation safety. External lighting must not exceed 450cs (candelas) in intensity within Zone D requirements.
